en: I pay homage to the *Catuṣpīṭha*, which is like a pure forest that yields the fruit of glory; it possesses a charming luster, is beautiful through the arrangement of the words of the Sage,
and, through its awakening, is exceedingly fragrant with the flowers of reality.
The fruit, being of various forms, ripens there at a corresponding time.
Though its qualities are pure throughout, it is occasionally impure within;
the *Tantra* called *Amṛtodbhava-catuṣpīṭha* is like the stalk of a lotus.

Who, apart from a divinity of supernatural power, would be able to clarify the meaning of this [text], which is like the Golden Mountain (Meru)? As for us, we are merely semblances of men; what capacity have we in that regard?
How can he be considered capable of seizing the jewel from the elephant— a task achievable only by the prowess of the lord of beasts—
when this ascetic deer wanders here, [eating] grass that must be severed with tears?
Now, I am unable to divide this [poison] which has been rendered potent by the words of my guru;
for even iron, when softened by medicine, a person can indeed consume.
Sentient beings possess diverse inclinations; who knows the range of their various desires?
Composing this work, I shall set forth its meaning by examining it in accordance with the inclinations of my instruction.
In this work, all that is highly unconventional—meter, gender, case, number, and so forth—is to be adorned with the intent of being ornaments of meaning; such is this *Tantraratna*.

[1.1.1] This tantra, which is extracted from the *Catuṣpīṭha* consisting of thirteen thousand verses contained within the eighteen-lakṣa [collection], was introduced at the beginning by the compiler with the words "Thus have I [not heard]" (*evaṃ mayā*), because it is situated therein. Regarding the phrase "Thus" (*evam*) and so forth: "Thus" refers to the entire tantra about to be spoken, ending with the word "iti," which consists of both the expression and the expressed, and is declared as the teaching.

"Spoken" means that he has spoken and taught the tantra without error; thus, the teaching (*deśanā*) is demonstrated. Furthermore, by this [term], the expression (*abhidhāna*) is also established. By the words "I wish to hear," etc., the subject matter (*abhidheya*) will be established. The relationship between these two, characterized as that of the expression and the expressed, should be understood. The purpose (*prayojana*) is the direct realization of the deity. And the purpose of that [realization] is the favoring of the world. To explain how the teaching is without error, he says: "Omniscient," and so forth.

One who knows the entire collection of entities (*padārthagrāma*) in their momentary and other such forms is "omniscient" (*sarvajña*). In reality, such knowledge arises only for the Blessed One. By this, the perfection of his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpad*) has been stated. Regarding the phrase "the Lord (*īśvara*) is the knowledge of the *rigīs*": "knowledge" (*jñāna*) means that which is known, i.e., the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Because he is called the Great Lord of Merit (*puṇyamaheśākhya*) and because he is the progenitor of all Buddhas, he is the Lord Mahāvajradhara. He is both the knowledge of the *rigīs*—that is, the Buddhas—and the Lord. And thus it is said:

"The glorious Lord of all Buddhas, the state of the Great Vajra-holder, is the goal of all Buddhas; that indeed is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena" (GST 18.178). Or, as it is said: "The progenitor of all Buddhas" (MNS 1.60a). By this, the perfection of the means for achieving one's own welfare is indicated. Through a qualification of the Blessed One, he speaks of the perfection of his abode: "the dwelling place of the Śuddhāvāsikas. The Śuddhāvāsikas are the gods; that which descends upon them is the Śuddhāvāsika, namely Mount Sumeru.

In this context, "one who has that place" (*tatra-sthāna*) means one whose station (*sthiti*) is there; the meaning is that he is situated in a gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. He states a qualifying attribute indicating the perfection of the welfare of others: "the *saṃvara* of the *yoginī-jāla*. *Yoga* is the non-dual gnosis of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). Wisdom is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); skillful means is completely pure compassion. It is called *yoga* because it is the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and skillful means, according to the statement: "Wisdom is that which is without intrinsic nature; skillful means is characterized by existence. (GST 18.33)

Those who possess that [knowledge] are the *yoginīs*; their "net" (*jāla*) is a completely pure emanation (*nirmāṇa*). Because by means of it he covers—that is, protects—all sentient beings from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), he is so [designated]. Yoga itself is the perfection of the means for accomplishing the welfare of others. Therefore, it is established that what has been taught in this manner is indeed non-erroneous. Thus, the perfection of the object to be taught, the teaching, the teacher, and the place has been shown in sequence.

[1.1.2] Furthermore, the assembly must be presented in the tantra; thus the tantra says: "The qualities of purification (*dhutaguṇa*)," and so forth. Maitreya possesses the qualities of purification. Vajrapāṇi is the loathsome one (*bībhatso*). Samantabhadra is the one who hangs down (*lambaka*). Gaganagarbha is the three-thorned one (*trikaṇṭha*). Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin is Meru. Kṣitigarbha is the peak of Meru (*meruśikhara*). Lokeśvara is Padma. Mañjuśrī is Padmodara. These eight bodhisattvas are mentioned as being preeminent.

With these as their leaders, the eighty *koṭis* of *yogīśvara* Bodhisattvas, looking toward Vajrapāṇi among them, smiled—that is, they manifested a slight smile. The word "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) is to be understood as the subject. The intention is this: the Blessed One, through his knowledge of the minds of others, perceiving that the assembly desired to hear the *Catuṣpīṭha*, and seeing that Vajrapāṇi was capable of chanting it, showed his favor by means of a smile, thinking, "Let him request me."

[1.1.3] Showing that he too proceeded to request [the teaching], he says: "Immediately thereafter," and so forth. "Immediately thereafter" means without interval. "Vajrapāṇi" refers to Vajrapāṇi. "From his seat" means from the moon-maṇḍala. "With one shoulder bared" means that which has one shoulder [exposed]; this is because of the manner in which he stood. "Upper garment" (uttarāsaṅga) means a cloak (uttarīya). "On the ground" means not on a seat. "With palms joined" means one by whom a hollow (puṭa) was made of the two hands; the meaning is "with hands in the añjali gesture.
Furthermore, this is an instruction regarding the request even for those who have not yet arrived.

[1.1.4] He states the request: "I wish to hear," and so forth. Regarding "Jñānendra": *jñānas* refers to the mirror-like and other [wisdoms]; *indra* is the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*), the teacher. Alternatively, since they have the nature of the mirror-like and other wisdoms, the *jñānas* are the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana and the rest. Their *indra* is the one under discussion, because he is their progenitor. His address is "O Jñānendra. Regarding "the characteristic of secret yoga": *rahas* means secret; and that consists of the knowledge of the *mudrās*, the pledges (*samaya*), and so forth.

"Yoga" refers to rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), or else it refers to the *yogas* beginning with Vāruṇa. "The characteristic form of secret yoga": how is it that "O beautiful one, the sky"? Here, "beautiful one" (*sundarī*) is the earth, and "sky" (*ākāśa*) is the atmosphere. One should not examine here whether these are correct words (*śabda*) or corrupt words (*apaśabda*), because they are merely conceptual constructs. How water (*āp*) could become fire (*tejas*) is easily understood.

[1.1.5] Regarding "of inhalation and exhalation" (*anāpāna*) and "of breaths" (*śvāsānām*): *anā* is the going out; *apāna* is the entering, according to the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*). "Of breaths" refers to the wind. As for "how meditation (*dhyāna*) is meditated upon": the sense is, how does meditation come to be with respect to the wind whose nature consists of going out and entering? What would the mandala of the deities such as Rāṣṭrapāla be like? They are called "protectors of the realm" (*rāṣṭrapāla*) because they protect the realm, which is the body; these are the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana and others.

They are called *devas* because from the very beginning they play for the sake of sentient beings, acting through various emanations of accomplishments such as Vajraḍākinī and others. Their *maṇḍala* is their accomplishment; it is so called because it takes (*lāti*) the essence (*maṇḍa*), which is the welfare of sentient beings, as its purpose. Alternatively, the *rāṣṭrapālas* are the guardians of the fields (*kṣetrapālas*); they themselves are the primordial gods (*ādidevas*). What is their *maṇḍala* like? It is together with those who belong to the *maṇḍala* (*māṇḍaleya*). Alternatively, the *rāṣṭrapālas* are the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields (*skandhadhātvāyatana*); they themselves are the primordial gods because they have the form of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].

"How could action and so forth apply to one whose body consists of knowledge and discernment?"—the meaning is this: "knowledge" (jñāna) is the cognition of existence, non-existence, and so on; "discernment" (vijñāna) is the vital breath (jīvitam); how then can action and so forth, such as meritorious deeds and the like, be joined to a body endowed with those two?

[1.1.6] "Listen, O Vajra, to the characteristic of the further shore of saṃsāra according to reality": the connection is as follows—"O Vajrapāṇi, listen to the characteristic of the further shore of saṃsāra according to reality (*yathātattva*), that is, by way of its true nature (*tattvena*). That which is characterized by the further shore of saṃsāra, namely enlightenment (*bodhi*), is indicated by the *vāyu-tattva* (the reality of wind) which is about to be explained; such is the meaning. He states this very point: "The breath-work (*śvāsakarma*) and so forth are the activities of all wise ones. "Breath-work" means the activity of the breath. And "that and so forth" means it is the foremost, the most excellent, the primary thing.

For all wise living beings, the practice of yoga is joined and the activity of the breath proceeds. To the question "How so?", he says: "By action" (*karma*). This is a compound word with the elision of the instrumental case ending; the meaning is "by means of the yogic action of Māhendra and the others."

[1.1.7] Demonstrating the activity of the breath (*śvāsakarma*), he says: "Two ten-thousands, one thousand, and six hundred—thus by calculation; sixty *ghaṭīs* is proclaimed as the number of breaths in a day and night. Regarding "two ten-thousands": this means two *ayutas*. Regarding "one thousand": this means one *sahasra*. Regarding "six hundred": this means six *śatas*. Thus, in this manner. "By calculation" (*m-aṅkataḥ*) means by means of numerical counting. Regarding "sixty *ghaṭīs*": by the word *ghaṭī*, a *daṇḍa* (forty-eight minutes) is meant; "sixty" means sixty.

There are twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths. Where? He says: "in sixty ghaṭīs," meaning in sixty ghaṭīs. The sense is that there are sixty ghaṭīs in a day and night, and there are that many breaths in a day and night.

[1.1.8] Regarding the phrase "the breaths of the necklace-swing (hārādola) are counted as marked by the swing (dola)": *hāra* is the entry of the wind; *dolā* is its exit. Between those two—the breaths of the necklace and the swing—*gaṇitā* means by counting (*gaṇanayā*); *dolā* means by the swing (*dolayā*); and *m-aṅkitam* means marked (*aṅkitā*) or characterized (*lakṣitā*). The sense is that the counting of the wind should be performed by means of the exit. "The necklaces of the swing dissolve for the wise one within the two breaths": within the two breaths, the necklaces dissolve into the swing.
The meaning is that he becomes one with Dolā. "O wise one" (*buddhiman*) is an address to Vajrapāṇi.

[1.1.9] "The external should be marked" means something other than the practice of breath (*śvāsakarman*). "Marked" (*aṅkita*) means inscribed. If one asks what that is, he says: "The world (*bhuvana*) likewise twelve. The "world" refers to twelve squares (*koṣṭhaka*). Just as there is the placement of twelve squares for the marks of the days starting from the first day of the month (*adinabhi*), the meaning is that in those squares one should write the marks—the inscriptions of the days—of whichever month they belong to; that is, one should write the lunar dates (*tithi*) starting from the first day (*pratipad*) up to the twelfth, in a counter-clockwise direction (*vāmāvartena*).

[1.1.10] "One should remain in Puṣya and so forth first; that which follows is the sequence of twelve. This means that having written the month of Puṣya at the beginning in the first square, one should write the remaining months, beginning with Māgha, in the subsequent squares in order, proceeding counter-clockwise (*vāmāvartataḥ*). "That which follows" refers to the yogi who is intent on devotion. The zodiac signs, beginning with Aries (*meṣa*), are also to be understood here. He states the actual writing: "Rohitā," and so forth.

In each month, the days beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), the months beginning with Puṣya, and the zodiac signs beginning with Aries are designated in sequence by the words *rohitā* and so on.

[1.1.11] "The twelfth is the Lord of the Worlds" (bhuvaneśvara) means that Rohita and the others are the lords of the twelve world-cells (*koṣṭhaka*). It should also be understood that there are twelve [lords], beginning with Rohita, within a single day and night.
As it is said: "Three in Rohita and Makara; four in Moha and Kūrma;
five in Bhadra and Vṛṣabha; and five in Raṇḍā and Kāma."
The sixth [suffix] is applied after the roots *bhid* and *driv*, and the seventh after *ākul* and in the sense of "in a dream" (*svapne*).

Thus: at dawn, three *daṇḍas* are *rohitā*. Beyond that, four *daṇḍas* are *mohitā*. Beyond that, five *daṇḍas* are *bhadram*. Beyond that, as many *daṇḍas* as that are *vṛṣabhaḥ*. Beyond that, four *daṇḍas* are *kūrmaḥ*. Beyond that, three *daṇḍas* are *makaraḥ*. Beyond that, five *daṇḍas* are *raṇḍā*. Beyond that, seven *daṇḍas* are *mikiraḥ*. Beyond that, six *daṇḍas* are *bhidriḥ*. Beyond that, as many *daṇḍas* as that are *vyākuliḥ*.

Beyond that, seven *daṇḍas* are *svapna*; beyond that, five *daṇḍas* are *kāma*. Thus, in one day and night (*ahorātra*), there are sixty *daṇḍas*. By combining the *daṇḍas* of the lunar days (*tithi*), months, and zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) according to the stated rule, the result is obtained. Concluding the arrangement with its various permutations, he says: "One should place [the numbers] in these established squares in the order starting from the East. The meaning is that once these squares have been established, the placement must be performed in the sequence beginning from the East.

However, in the months beginning with Māgha, the lunar days (*tithi*) revolve under different names; for instance, in Māgha, the first day (*pratipad*) is called *mohitā*, while the days from *bhadrā* up to *rohitā*, and from the second day up to the twelfth, follow accordingly. This is the case elsewhere as well. Starting with *bhadrā* and so forth, the days beginning with the first (*pratipad*) should be counted. [1.1.12] Regarding *rohitā*: it means on the day called *rohitā*. *Saubhāgya* means a beloved wife. *Krūracittā* is called *mandāgni*; one with a cruel mind remembers harm, not benefit. *Mandāgni* means having weak digestion. *Videśāprabhu* means that one will constantly obtain sovereignty and such in a distant land.

[1.1.13] "One who loves sexual intercourse" means that for the sake of pleasure, he does not exercise discernment regarding what is appropriate or inappropriate. Regarding the statement about the constant [deities], "the omniscient one" refers to one who speaks without harshness at all times. Since Rohitā is a deity to be worshipped, one born under Rohitā becomes a worshipper of the deities. Likewise, by the phrase "with seventy years," his lifespan is seventy years.

[1.1.14] "The red one (rohitā) bestows wealth; all [desires] turn back"—the meaning of this is that when wealth is given through another art or similar means, it turns away from everything by way of pleasure, or rather, all wealth [turns away]. "A wound on the limb of the red-born" means that the limb of one born of the red one becomes wounded. "And union with splendors" means that she attracts fortune (*lakṣmī*) from others.

[1.1.15] “Having resorted to the place, wealth is established”: the meaning is that by resorting to the Rohitā as a place, one becomes established in wealth, friends, and so forth. “The Rohitā goes to the place”: the sense is that one must go somewhere within the Rohitā. “Everything is accomplished through thoughts”: the meaning is that once gone, one achieves what is desired. “They employ the marriage rite, the fire-ritual, and the pacification rites.”

The sense is that in the *rohitā* [year], the marriage-homa and other rites become fruitful. Some maintain that the alchemical process (*dhātuvāda*), the making of images, jewelry, and so forth, constitutes the fire-rite (*agnikārya*).

[1.1.16] "Those who are deluded [know] by means of the calculation of the application of meanings": in the *mohitā* [year], "the application of meanings" refers to the collection of wealth, and that is to be known as what ought to be done through the calculation of twelve compartments (*koṣṭha*).

[1.1.17] "But those with little wealth" refers to those who do not possess abundant fortune. "Always fond of sexual union" means one for whom sexual union is dear (*priyamaithuna*). "The cruel ones always speak unpleasant things to the addicted" means that the "addicted" (*vyasanin*) is a litigant.

[1.1.18] "Constantly angry, full of egoism, an evildoer, and evil-natured": "angry" means one who is enraged; "full of egoism" means one who is conceited; "evildoer" means one who commits acts such as taking life; "evil-natured" means one whose body is deformed. "Speaking incoherently and harshly": he is one who possesses both incoherent speech (*saṃbhinnālāpa*) and harsh speech (*pāruṣyālāpa*). "The falling away from all volition": the falling away (*cyuti*) of volition (*cetanā*), that is, of life, occurs in every respect and by every means.
Regarding the reading *cyuta-śastrābhi-cetanā* found in some places: the meaning is that for one who has been deluded (*mohita*) and not yet born, consciousness (*cetana*) is lost due to weapons.

[1.1.19] As for the statement "the lifespan is proclaimed to be eighty-four years": the sense is that the life span is eighty-four years. Regarding *ucchāhya-yoga-bhūmy-ādi*: the meaning is "having encouraged oneself, one stands on the ground of yoga" (*ayoga-bhūmi*). Regarding *vicchāhya-yoga-bhūmy-aśaḥ*: *vicchāhya* means *vicchāhin*, which means "lacking enthusiasm" (*anutsāhin*). Where? He says: "on the ground of yoga" (*yoga-bhūmi*), meaning in a state of being established (*sat-sthāna*).

[1.1.20] "The injury of a limb" and "the encounter with deaths of bodies": this is the detailed explanation of that which was indicated by the phrase "consciousness struck by fallen weapons. "Whatever wealth is to be given does not return once it has gone": the meaning is that wealth given on account of debts and the like does not return.

[1.1.21] "Bhadra" means auspicious food: agriculture and the like are food, and that should be performed auspiciously (*bhadre*). "One should cause auspicious rites and so forth to be performed": this refers to rites such as those for pacification (*śāntika*). "A son born of a *bhadra* woman lives for a hundred years": the meaning is that one born of a *bhadra* woman lives for a hundred years.

[1.1.22] "But the poor man who practices the Dharma": "poor" means devoid of wealth. "Dharma" is merit (*puṇya*), which is the cause of heaven and liberation (*apavarga*). "He becomes one whose wife is devoted to a single husband, possessing a divine body and speech, and is a leader": "one whose wife is devoted to a single husband" means having only one wife. He becomes one who possesses a divine body and speech. "Leader" (*nāyaka*) means a controller (*niyāmaka*).

[1.1.23] "Skilled in all arts and crafts" (*sarvaśilpakalābhijña*): *śilpa* refers to painting and so forth; *kalā* refers to the sciences (*vidyā*). As it is said: "The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the extensive Nyāya, the Dharmaśāstra, and the Purāṇa—all this is called the Trayī (the threefold knowledge). Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda—these three, together with the Arthaśāstras, should be known as the eighteen sciences. (MBh 1.113.40b, 12.122.25d) Thus.

The six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍ-aṅga*) are phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), etymology (*nirukta*), prosody (*chandas*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*). Phonetics refers to the treatises on the training of elephants and so forth. Ritual refers to the secondary rituals (*anukalpa*), the law codes (*smṛti-śāstra*), and the like. He is proficient in all arts and crafts as appropriate; for the word "all" indicates a great abundance. He is one who possesses affection for his own kin. Regarding the phrase "he should enjoy the family by means of punishment": he should bring his own family to a state of being enjoyed through discipline. Alternatively, he enjoys [the family] by virtue of its greatness. Regarding "death occurs in water in that same way": death is the falling away of the body into water.

[1.1.24] "A son born under Vṛṣabha will be heroic against powerful enemies": a son born under Vṛṣabha becomes valiant toward strong foes. "He possesses passion, wealth, and sovereignty": he possesses passion, wealth, and lordship. "He should honor many wives": he should show respect to many wives.

[1.1.25] "Among all, there are many kinsmen": the meaning is that one is always endowed with many kinsmen. "The lifespan of the father is destroyed": as soon as he is born, he destroys the lifespan of his father. "By means of trade, one fashions a livelihood": the meaning is that one makes a living through commerce. "But one should fashion a lifespan of sixty": the meaning is that one's lifespan shall be sixty years.

[1.1.26] "Laziness and talkativeness": the meaning is that he is lazy and garrulous. "Cruel in action and evil-natured" has already been explained. "They become like the weapon of death, or else like poison for living beings": the sense is that he dies by means of a weapon or by snake venom.

[1.1.27] "A son was born to the tortoises, who is always established in anxiety": there is an alternative reading, *citte 'navasthitaḥ* ("unstable in mind"). The meaning is that one born among tortoises is constantly abiding in anxiety, being intent on worry (*cintāpara*). Or, "unstable in mind" (*citte vānavasthitaḥ*), meaning one whose mind is unsettled (*anavasthitacitta*). "Angry at even a slight offense" (*svalparoṣa*): he is such as one who has anger toward even a minor transgression. "Content with even a little" (*alpato tuṣṭa*): the meaning is that he is satisfied with only a small amount. "Talkative and fond of his own kin" (*bahubhāṣī svajanapriya*) is easy to understand.

[1.1.28] *Atikrodhī ugrasya*: the meaning is that he is exceedingly wrathful and fierce. *Īśvaraḥ sarvadāyakaḥ*: the meaning is that he is a lord and a giver of all his possessions. *Hanyāt paṇṇikaputrāṇām*: he destroys both wife and son. *Svadeśe prabhu nityaśaḥ* is easily understood.

[1.1.29] “He ordains agricultural activities for the aeon” means that he arranges for agricultural activities. “He is seized by the leprosy of disease” is easy to understand. “The lifespan is eighty years” means that the life span is eighty years. “Likewise, one dies at home” means that one dies with composure.

[1.1.30] "A boy was born under the sign of Capricorn (makara), with a lifespan of ninety-three years": for one born under Capricorn, the lifespan is seventy-two years. "Ninety-three" means sixty plus three. Alternatively, it may be explained as having a lifespan of ninety-six years. "Virtuous" (*puṇyavān*): that which purifies is merit (*puṇya*), such as giving, worship of deities, and so forth. "Endowed with ethical discipline" (*śīlasaṃpanna*): ethical discipline (*śīla*) is threefold—engagement in the wholesome, abstention from the unwholesome, and conduct for the benefit of others; or it refers to a state of excellent character. "Guarded by the practice of discipline" (*vinayācārarakṣita*): [this refers to...]

*Vinaya* is the conquest of the senses; *ācāra* is worldly conduct. The rest is easily understood. [1.1.31] Regarding the phrase "shining with good fortune and fame" (*saubhāgyayaśa-rājate*): the sense is that he shines by means of both good fortune and fame. Regarding "resplendent with a single wife" (*ekapaṇṇī-prabhāsvara*): he is one whose excellent wife is singular; thus he is so described. There is an alternative reading: *ekapatnī-vratāsana*. *Vrata* means firm resolve; it is derived from the analysis that he abides in the vow of having a single wife.

[1.1.32] Regarding "the mind of the ever-indolent": those who sit in a contemptible manner are *kusīda*; one whose mind is constantly such is "one of a perpetually indolent mind"—this is the intended meaning. Regarding "under one umbrella with kinsmen": it should be understood as having wealth in common with one's relatives. Regarding "words of affection for all": there is affectionate speech in every respect. Regarding "death in battle is certain in that way": the meaning is that death occurs for him in battle. Regarding "fifty-five years of life": [this refers to the duration].

The meaning is that the lifespan is fifty-five years. Alternatively, "by sixty and thirty" means a lifespan of sixty-three years. By these two sequences of life-span numbers, untimely death (apamṛtyu) is described. Alternatively, some maintain that by the phrase "by sixty and thirty," the conclusion of the previous explanation of "nine and sixty-three" is being made.

[1.1.33] “A son was born to a widow” means: a son was born to a widow (*raṇḍā*). “But with an evil intent” means: an intent to commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) and so forth. “Speaking confusedly among beings” means: one who speaks confusedly toward sentient beings. “Poor” means: one who is poor. “Always sweet-spoken” means: always exceedingly sweet in speech. [1.1.34] “Sick” means: one who is ill. “One whose self is struck by royal punishment”: he whose self is struck is a “struck self” (*hatātmā*); [the phrase] “by royal punishment” means *rājadaṇḍena*. “Of those always fond of sexual intercourse” is easy to understand. “Confidence” means: a favorable state of mind.

[1.1.35] *Saubhāgyam* means "fortunate" (*subhaga*). Regarding *viṭa-śilpādi*: *viṭa-śilpa* refers to painting and so forth. One who knows all that, beginning with those—such as everything from elephant-riding onwards—is a "knower of all arts and so forth" (*śilpādi-sarvavit*). The rest has been explained. [1.1.36] Regarding *mikiram*: the accusative case is used according to *Aṣṭādhyāyī* 2.3.5, which states that the accusative is employed to express the continuous connection of time or distance. Regarding *svakuloccayam*: he is so called because he "gathers" (*uccinoti*) or increases his own lineage. Regarding *nītiśāstrāṇi saṃpannā vidyā vividhaśilpakaiḥ*: he acquired the treatises on ethics (*nītiśāstra*) along with various sciences and diverse arts.

[1.1.37] Regarding "of words that are terrible and harsh": one whose speech is terrible (*ghoravāk*). Regarding "but those whose nature and meaning are slight": he whose meaning (*artha*) and essential form (*svarūpa*) are slight is such. Regarding "light and performing all tasks": the meaning is that he is one who quickly carries out every duty. What is beautiful form (*surūpa*)?

[1.1.38] "When cast into the water together with bodies, there is no doubt regarding deaths": the meaning is that it is certain he dies once his body has been thrown into the water. "Eighty years for the eighth": the sense is that his lifespan is eighty-eight years. "Likewise, death by the king's weapon": the meaning is that his passing, his death, occurs by the king's weapon.

[1.1.39] Regarding the expression *bhidrikā dārako jātaḥ*: it means "a son has been born to Bhidrika. As for the statement that "as soon as he is born, he kills his mother," it is said: "once born, he kills his mother. Regarding "he kills his father at eight years": the meaning is that he kills his father in the eighth year. At that very time, being deprived of both mother and father, he becomes the master in his own house according to his own will.

[1.1.40] "Of one with little substance and anger" means one who has little wealth and is prone to wrath. "Like a fool" means a fool. "One's own minds and actions" means that one performs actions by means of one's own mind. In some places, the reading is "actions performed by outcasts" (*śvapacitāni karmāṇi*); in that case, it means one who performs the deeds of a *caṇḍāla*. "Leaders of force" refers to army commanders.

[1.1.41] “His lifespan is eight hundred”: the meaning is that his lifespan is one hundred and eight years. “Death is certain in his own home”: the meaning is that he dies in his own house. “He has affection for all his kinsmen”: the meaning is that he possesses affection toward all his relatives. “Compassionate toward the lowly and the miserable”: the lowly (*hīna*) are those inferior by birth and so forth; the miserable (*dīna*) are those who suffer. [1.1.42] “A restless boy was born”: he was born agitated. “Of little intelligence” (*alpabuddhimān*): he is of limited intellect. “But of little wisdom” (*alpaprajña*) means he is dull-witted (*jaḍa*).

[1.1.43] "Affection for kinsmen and good fortune": this means affection for one's kin and good fortune. "A lord through wealth and cattle": the meaning is that he is a lord by virtue of his wealth and cattle. "Satisfied with a house and so forth": the meaning is that he has three wives in his home. [1.1.44] "Long-lived parents": both his father and mother are long-lived.

[1.1.45] "But for a merchant, by means of the pair with Death at the end of the eon": in the very act of trading, his pairing occurs together with Death. The intention is that there is a conjunction with Death. "By means of" (*hetunā*) means "in this manner. The sense is that in this very way—through the act of trading alone—there is a conjunction with Death. "The signs for the commencement of conjunctions are known through calculation for the wise": these are the signs stated to be known by the wise. Those whose commencement occurs within the *rohiṭa* and other conjunctions are described as such.
He explains how they are to be known: "by calculation," that is, by counting the twelve squares.

Regarding the phrase "of dreams": it means "in a dream. Regarding the phrase "all enemies are burned": the sense is that all his enemies are burned. Regarding the phrase "but having kinsmen though without a protector": it refers to one who has relatives but is deprived of a mother and so forth.

[1.1.47] Regarding "poor at all times": he is always poor. Regarding "but intent on an evil mind": one whose intellect (*buddhi*) is directed toward evil is thus described; "intent on that" (*tatpara*) means one who performs those actions. Regarding "himself with a lion-like nature": the action should be understood as him considering himself to be great, thinking, "There is no one else more excellent than I. Regarding "O Pāruṣāpāla, you are all-knowing," this is easily understood.

[1.1.48] "Free from disease at all times" means he is healthy from birth onwards. "But the acquisition of enjoyments" is easy to understand. "The servant must enjoy" means the servant must perform service. "Enjoying by mounting the woman" means he engages in sexual intercourse by mounting her. [1.1.49] "A lifespan of fifty years" means a life expectancy of fifty years. "His lifespan is thus determined" implies that there is no other calculation for his life span. "Of him who is slain" (*hanyasya*) means of one who has been killed (*hatasya*).

[1.1.50] Regarding "of desires" (*kāmānām*), it means "in desire. "He lives for sixty-eight years" means he lives for sixty-eight years (*aṣṭaṣaṣṭivarṣāṇi*). Regarding "in villages and cow-pens," the meaning is that he possesses villages and possesses cattle. Regarding "but horses and so forth," the meaning is horses, elephants, and so forth.
[1.1.51] "One who acts for the welfare of all beings" is easily understood.

[1.1.52] Regarding "saubhāgya sarva sarveṣu": the meaning is that he is fortunate in every way toward all. Concluding the arrangement of the twelve squares, he says: "one should display the sign of yoga. One should characterize by this sequence whatever sign or mark belongs to the yogas, such as Rohitā and the others. "My word, there is no doubt": "this is my word; no doubt should be entertained here"—such are the words of Vajradhara.

[1.1.53] Now, performing the calculation for determining a lost lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), he says: "In Rohiṇī," and so forth. One born under Rohiṇī is, from childhood onwards, invariably a worshiper of deities. One born under Mṛgaśirā has obtained wealth; that is, one born under Mṛgaśirā invariably obtains wealth in that very manner. One born under Ārdrā eats excellent food; that is, one born under Ārdrā invariably obtains excellent food in that very manner. One born under Punarvasu is exceedingly wrathful; that is, one born under Punarvasu invariably possesses excessive anger in that very manner.

[1.1.54] It is easily understood that one born under Kūrma is known as being intent on anxiety. One born under Makara is invariably a storyteller; likewise, one born under Raṇḍā, having contemplated sin, is intent on sexual intercourse—this is easily understood.

[1.1.55] One born under Bhidri is invariably sleepy. One born under Vyākulī is invariably possessed of slander, foul speech, and the like. One born under Svapna is invariably possessed of anxiety, valor, and so forth. One born under Kāma is invariably a *gandharva*.

[1.1.55 (Excursus)] For instance, at dawn, during the three *daṇḍas* of the Sun’s transit through Aries, one knows that there is a portion of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā. Then, during the four *daṇḍas* of the transit through Taurus, there is the remaining three quarters of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and half of Mṛgaśīrṣa. Then, during the five *daṇḍas* of the transit through Gemini, there is half of Mṛgaśīrṣa, Ārdrā, and three quarters of Punarvasū. Furthermore, during the same number of *daṇḍas* of the transit through Cancer, there is one quarter of Punarvasū, Puṣyā, and Āśleṣā.

Then, in the four *daṇḍas* of the Leo (*siṃha*) portion, there are Maghā, Pūrvaphālgunī, and one quarter of Uttaraphālgunī. Then, in the three *daṇḍas* of the Virgo (*kanyā*) portion, there are the remaining three quarters of Uttaraphālgunī, Hastā, and half of Citrā. Then, in the five *daṇḍas* of the Libra (*tulā*) portion, there are half of Citrā, Svātī, and three quarters of Viśākhā. Furthermore, in the seven *daṇḍas* of the Scorpio (*vṛścika*) portion, there are one quarter of Viśākhā, Anurādhā, and Jyeṣṭhā.

Then, within six *daṇḍas* of the passage through Capricorn (*makara*), there are the asterisms Mūlā, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and one quarter of Uttarāṣāḍhā. Furthermore, within as many *daṇḍas* of the passage through Aquarius (*kumbha*), there are the remaining three quarters of Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇā, and half of Dhaniṣṭhā. Again, within seven *daṇḍas* of the passage through Pisces (*mīna*), there are half of Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, and three quarters of Pūrvabhādrapadā. Finally, within five *daṇḍas* of the passage through Pisces, there are one quarter of Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, and Revatī.
Thus, even in this manner, three asterisms are known [for each sign], yet not a single one is definitively fixed.

[1.1.56–57] He states that among those things denoted by the word *rohitā*, such as the three staffs (*daṇḍatraya*) and so forth, the rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and others should be performed in their respective order: "The *rohitā* is for the rites of pacification," etc., which is easy to understand.

[1.1.58] "Success for the bulls and the *repha*s; the nectar of yoga is born": success is attained with the bull (*vṛṣabha*); "of the *repha*s" means that the four yogas—Rohitā, Makara, Raṇḍā, and Mikirā—are born for the sake of immortality (*amṛtatva*). Restricting the time for drawing the wheel, he says: "having established [them] starting from the eastern direction," and so forth. The meaning is that first, having established Rohitā in the eastern direction, one should establish Mohitā and the others in the northeast (*aiśāna*) and so on. The wise person should perform the calculation (*gaṇita*), which is carried out by counting, in the forenoon.

[1.1.59] Indicating that which was introduced by the words "The meaning given to Rohitā," etc., he says: "Rohitā," etc. The sense is that the meaning given to Rohitā, while returning, returns as something abundant. He indicates that which was introduced by the words "The meaning of the applications for Mohitā," etc., with the words: "Mohitā," etc. The meaning thus grasped is not subverted by others.

[1.1.60] "The commencement of a house and the arrival of prosperity": when there is the commencement of a house, O auspicious one, prosperity arises. "A bull for the conjunction with the deities": the commencement of an image of a deity and so forth is recommended under the asterism Vṛṣabha; he says that the commencement of a mantra is also recommended: "One succeeds even through a mantra."

[1.1.61] Regarding the statement "In marriage, through the *kūrma-yoga*, there is non-separation in every respect": the meaning is that in a marriage under the *kūrma-yoga*, there is both sexual enjoyment and affection between the couple. Regarding the statement "When the *makara* ascends the field, the crops certainly flourish": the meaning is that when a field is commenced under the *makara-yoga*, there is an increase in the harvest.

[1.1.62] "A *raṇḍā* does not release her tasks among women, even when dead": the meaning is that when a woman is won over through the *raṇḍā*-yoga, she becomes his wife even in another birth. "One obtains a merchant (*vaṇij*) at *mikira*; the object is seen to be present": through the *mikira*-yoga, at the commencement of obtaining a merchant's goods, one obtains them; at the commencement of pleasure (*prīti*), a penetration into the next birth is observed.

[1.1.63] *Bhidrikā*, having grasped it, becomes long-lasting through the action and so forth, meaning "always": the meaning is that whatever is grasped by means of the *bhidri* yoga is long-enduring. *Vyākulī*, going abroad, a place free from disease is attained: by means of the *vyākulī* yoga, one goes abroad; therein, one remains in a state of health.

[1.1.64] "One certainly and eternally encounters everything through everything in sleep": the meaning is that whatever has been experienced in a dream returns. "And indeed, what has gone for the sake of an object does not return for one who has gone": the sense is that whatever object has been attained through the power of desire does not return.
[1.1.65–67] Showing that even serpents are denoted by words such as *rohit* and so forth, he says: "Vāsuki," etc.; this is easily understood.

[1.1.68] Regarding the statement "one should specifically make known by means of the sequence of their poisons": the meaning is that the progression of the poison of these [serpents], Vāsuki and the others, is to be understood through the specific distinctions of the conjunction with Rohitā and the other [constellations]. The passage beginning with "siddhi-vṛṣabha" has already been explained.

[1.1.69] "Of whom it is suspected that he has been bitten": having recognized the being by whom one was bitten, the progression of the poison is known; this is the connection with what precedes. "But the encounter with deaths": if it is a bite at the time of death, then knowing that it is indeed death, one should desist; such is the meaning. By the principle to be stated later, the proper and improper time must be discerned. Otherwise, having prepared the poison and having neutralized the poison through yoga—

If it is a bite at an improper time (*akāladaṃśa*), then one should neutralize the poison by means of the application (*yoga*) to be described hereafter. Regarding the phrase "having combined the poison": this refers to the combination of poison at an improper time. The meaning is that whether it is the proper or improper time must be known by means of the messenger, the location of the bite, the lunar day (*tithi*), the asterism (*nakṣatra*), and the hour (*velā*).

[1.1.70] Now, in order to demonstrate the rule for the days, nights, and *ghaṭīs* of the months, he says: "It should be performed in successive order according to the time, marked with the letter *m*. Having written the months beginning with Puṣya in twelve squares in a counter-clockwise direction, the calculation should be performed. The meaning is: having written whichever month belongs to whichever square, one should proceed therefrom.

Regarding "the sequence beginning with Pauṣa, [starting] with Āditya": the meaning is that the new moon of the month of Puṣya and so forth is determined by the movement of the sun. As for "the journey of the seasons," this refers to both the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) and the northern course (uttarāyaṇa). The meaning is that between these two, the northern course is primary. The intention is that of the southern and northern courses, the northern course is the principal one.

[1.1.71] "Ten, doubled, four days, and one *ghaṭikā* for each; ten, three, and six—the wise one (*budha*) should begin the *ghaṭikā* of the night. Regarding this: in the month of Puṣya, which is designated as the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), there are ten *ghaṭikās* doubled for each day; these are the "doubled-tens" (*dviguṇadaśa*). There are another four *ghaṭikās*. "The wise one" (*budha*): the verb is supplied as "the wise one should know that it is thus."

In each night, there are again ten *ghaṭīs* [per period]; those nights which consist of three such periods are called "ten-triads" (*daśatrikā*). Regarding the phrase "of the six," it refers to six *ghaṭīs*. Thus, it should be understood by applying this logic consistently everywhere. The summary meaning is that in the month of Puṣya, the days consist of twenty-four *ghaṭīs*, and the nights consist of thirty-six *ghaṭīs*.

[1.1.72] "Just as each day, when combined with the calculation... means that whichever day belongs to whichever month, that day is to be known through the calculation situated within the twelve compartments. And this is the mnemonic verse (*grahaṇakavākya*). Having shown the month located in the first compartment, he says "by the second," etc., while showing the month located in the second compartment.

[1.1.73] "Ten times twice six" means twenty-six *ghaṭikās*. "By two days" means days. "Ten, three, four" means thirty-four *ghaṭikās* for the nights. And this refers to the month of Māgha. [1.1.74] Showing the case of Phālguna, he says "ten," etc. Twenty-eight *ghaṭikās* are the days. "Two of one" means two; thirty-two *ghaṭikās* are the nights.
[1.1.75] "In the middle of the equinox, having joined two, thirty *ghaṭikās* are established": the meaning is that in the month of Caitra, a day and night consists of thirty *ghaṭikās*.

[1.1.76] He states the days and nights of Vaiśākha: "Ten by three, two kinds, with two here at the end. This means that thirty *ghaṭikās* [make a day], and here at the end there are two *ghaṭikās*. Thus, the meaning is that the days consist of thirty-two *ghaṭikās*. "Ten by two, of the eighth": this means the night consists of twenty-eight *ghaṭikās*. [1.1.77] He states the day of Jyeṣṭha: "Ten by three," and so forth. The sense is that the days consist of thirty-four *ghaṭikās*. "From the previous two days," a day proceeds. "Ten doubled," and so forth: this means the night consists of twenty-six *ghaṭikās*.

[1.1.78] Regarding Āṣāḍha, he says: "ten times three," and so forth. "Of the sixth" means six. "By two days" means days; that is, thirty-six *ghaṭikās* constitute the days. The intention is that the nights consist of twenty-four *ghaṭikās*. [1.1.79] It is declared that the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) shall make known the time of the seasons (*ṛtukāla*): having established a month as thirty days starting from the new moon (*amāvāsī*) of the month of Puṣya, six months constitute the northern solstice (*uttarāyana*). Now, starting from the new moon of Āṣāḍha in the same manner, six months constitute the southern solstice; such is the meaning. In this way, let the time of the seasons be known.

[1.1.80] Regarding Śrāvaṇa, he says: "ten times three," and so forth. This means the days consist of thirty-four *ghaṭikās*. Regarding the sixth [lunar mansion], there are six; the meaning is that the nights consist of twenty-six *ghaṭikās*. [1.1.81] Regarding Bhādra, he says: "ten times three," and so forth. Regarding "two of one," there are two; the days consist of thirty-two *ghaṭikās*. Regarding the eighth: there are eight; the implication is that the nights consist of twenty-eight *ghaṭikās*.

[1.1.82] Regarding Āśvina, he says: "Ten times three for the days of a *lakṣa* is the day and *ghaṭī*; ten times three for the nights is likewise the day in the middle of the *viṣuva*. The term "*lakṣasya*" means *lakṣaya*. The meaning is that there are thirty *ghaṭīs* for the days and thirty *ghaṭīs* for the nights. Regarding "the day in the middle of the *viṣuva*": this indicates that the days of the bright fortnight (*viśu*) of Caitra are also like this.

[1.1.83] He states the days of Kārttika: "Ten times two," and so forth. Regarding "of eight" (*aṣṭasya*): it means eight. The days consist of twenty-eight *ghaṭīs*. The remainder is easily understood.
[1.1.84] Regarding Mārgaśīrṣa, he says: "Ten doubled," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

[1.1.85] "Ten doubled and four make the number of ghaṭīs for the day; ten tripled and likewise six are established as the ghaṭīs of the night": thus the summary of the ghaṭīs of the day and night for Puṣya is completed.

[1.1.86] "Three times ten multiplied by ten, or fifty, breaths from the *ghaṭī*s, like a *nālī*": three times ten multiplied by ten is three hundred; "or fifty" means sixty. "Like a *nālī*" means that just as there are three hundred and sixty breaths in one *daṇḍa*, so it is in other *daṇḍas* as well. He provides the explanation for what was indicated as "sixty *ghaṭīs*": "The day and night (*ahorātra*) of a number consisting of sixty *ghaṭīs* is measured. The meaning is that a day and night consists of sixty *daṇḍas*.
There is a reading in some places as "three hundred and likewise sixty," and that number is exactly the same.

[1.1.87] "In the same manner as the sequence of the months, so too is it marked by the sequence [of the breaths]" means that just as there is a sequence of months according to their order, so too should the sequence of three *ghaṭīs* and so forth be observed within the compartments (*koṣṭhas*). "The *ghaṭīs*, breaths, and so on are complete" refers to the *viśuma*. "But the *cchindikā* moves in sequence" means that, setting aside the *viśuma*, the increase and decrease of the day and night occur in regular succession.

[1.1.88] Regarding the phrase "having grasped the sequence of breaths, one should especially perform rites and non-rites": the meaning is that by means of the sequence of breaths, having understood the fourfold yoga of Vāyu and the others, one should specifically perform auspicious rites such as *śāntika* and so forth, as well as inauspicious rites such as *abhicāra* and so forth. In this regard, the Vāyavya [yoga] is six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the Āgneya is four finger-breadths, the Vāruṇa is twelve finger-breadths, and the Māhendra is sixteen finger-breadths. He states the explanation of what was indicated by the word "ten thousand" (*ayuta*) and so forth, beginning with "for fear of the harsh [breaths]" (*kharādibhiḥ*).

*Kha* and *ra* are the *kharau*. Those two are at the beginning of which two groups (*rāśi*), those are the *kharādī*. There are twenty-four syllables beginning with *kha*, and six beginning with *ra*. Thus, there are two groups: those beginning with *kha* and those beginning with *ra*. The meaning is "by means of these two groups, beginning with *kha* and *ra*. By this, the number twenty-four and the number six are to be taken. Regarding the phrase "having made a season" (*ṛtuṃ kṛtvā*): there are six seasons; their number is to be taken. By the unification of twenty-four and twice six, thirty-six results. Regarding the phrase "marked by *ya*, *na*, *da*, *e*, *bhi*, and *m*": [these letters represent specific numbers].
The number thirty-six itself is to be placed in two positions; from that, there are eighteen and eighteen.

[1.1.89] "Having multiplied the two by ten" means: having made both parts tenfold; thus, in each individual part there becomes one hundred and eighty. Then, having joined one digit of the two hundreds with one digit, and the eight digits with the eight digits, one should place a dot below and a dot near the top. This results in twenty thousand, one thousand, and six hundred. In a single day and night, there are that many breaths. Therefore, he will say:

"By its [the breath's] mark (m-aṅka), it should be joined with a day-and-night; thus it is 'pertaining to respiration' (śvāsika). And in a year, there are that many *daṇḍas*. Therefore he says: 'And in a year, only the *ghaṭī*. By the word *ghaṭī*, the *daṇḍa* is meant."

[1.1.90] Showing the science of astrology (*jyotiṣa*), he says: "Having grasped the vowel in the sentence, the vowel is established by means of a numerical mark (*aṅka*). One should cause the questioner to state the name of a flower. Having grasped as many vowels as there are letters—beginning with *ka*, etc.—in the sentence stating that flower-name; or else, one should establish those very vowels associated with *ka*, etc., by means of a numerical mark. It was not stated what would result from this, because that will be explained later. "Having established it by means of the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*)," [he says].

The lords, beginning with the letter *a*, are to be established in the twelve compartments of the worlds. Having done what? He says: "excluding the neuter vowels and so forth. This means having excluded these vowels: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. By this, the method for determining auspicious and inauspicious results has been stated.
[1.1.91–101] He explains that very same point starting with the word "the letter *a*"; and that is easily understood.

[1.1.102] "As for the letter *a* at the beginning, so too at the end": the meaning is that just as there is a result for the letter *a*, so too there is for the letter *aḥ*. Regarding the question of what kind of syllables of the name of the flower should be taken from the sentence, he says: "sixfold," and so forth. Those syllables in the sentence which have been mounted upon numerical figures (*aṅka*) must be made sixfold. And "of the preceding, threefold": the preceding portion of the syllable-numbers that have been made sixfold must be made threefold.

[1.1.103] "This mixed [number] is sixty-fifth": one should add fifty-five to it. Regarding the syllables in the sentence, having multiplied them by six and then again by three, one should divide [the result] by the world, which is twelve with its twelve parts; the meaning is that one should take the quotient. "But having grasped the remaining syllable" means that once the numerical values of the name's syllables have been thus processed, whatever number remains is the fruit of that letter. And these twelve vowels are denoted by the words beginning with *rohit*.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "and of the previous [number] tripled": those numerical values of the syllables of the flower-name that were previously taken should first be tripled; subsequently, those same [values] should be sextupled. The remainder is as before.

Alternatively, regarding the calculation of the vowels and so forth from the hour-sign (*horācihna*): having consecrated a piece of chalk with the mantra of Jñānaḍākinī, one should draw a line in the form of a stream of cow-urine while reciting the mantra of Jñānaḍākinī once. One should draw the line for as long as the mind remains at rest; then, having counted the line, the result of the vowel corresponding to that number is to be understood according to the previously stated method—this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively, having cast a flower, one should likewise discern the ground and so forth: having placed the twelve vowels in order within twelve squares and having fixed the matter in mind, one should cause the flower to be dropped. Wherever that flower falls, the result of that vowel occurs. The "ground and so forth" refers to the twelve squares. "One should perceive everything according to truth" means that one should see all things, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as they truly are. Concluding that this is indeed true, he says:

"But the Yogaśāstra is praised," it is said. The *Yogaśāstra* is the Mantra system (*mantranaya*). It is purposeful by virtue of its specific rule, because it has been praised by all the Buddhas. [1.1.col. Thus, in this section, regarding "the seat of the self" (*ātmapīṭha*): the self itself—the very body—is the seat (*pīṭha*), the throne, the support of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with wind. According to the sequence thus stated, the principles beginning with wind are set forth and introduced. By this, or rather, this section is precisely the "seat of the self. Thus ends the first chapter in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*, in the section on the Seat of the Self.

[1.2.1] Now he speaks the chapter on the knowledge of time, its deception, and so forth: "O Blessed One, I wish to hear the reality of knowledge (*jñānatattva*) in detail. The reality of knowledge refers to such things as the removal of poison. "How is this a sign? means it is a sign of death. "How is the reality relied upon? means the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*).

[1.2.2] Listen, O Vajramahārāja, to what is shown regarding the mark of the limb: he who reigns by means of the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and others is a "king" (*rājan*). He for whom the Vajra—that is, Akṣobhya himself—is the Great King is addressed as "Vajramahārāja. The mark of the limb has been shown; it shall be demonstrated immediately hereafter—listen! "Standing like the time of death" means that the time of death is known with certainty; such is the sense.

[1.2.3] He states the sign: "the fluctuations of the breaths," and so forth. The fluctuation (*visphuraṇa*) of the breaths is their alteration, their being either deficient or excessive—an alteration from their natural state. After six months, emission (*cyuti*) necessarily occurs. Alternatively, at the time of dawn, by the mere fluctuation of the breath through its turning, revolving, and exiting. Having done what does this fluctuation occur? He says: "having seen some fear, and likewise [other things]. Here, physical injury, fatigue, and so forth are also included, since "fear" is used as an illustration.

And thus, the implication is that if there is a throbbing of the breath without fear or other such causes, then death occurs; for through fear and the like, one's natural state becomes otherwise. Regarding the phrase "with joints rolling on the cheeks" (*kapole ghūrṇasaṃdhika*), it means that if the two hollows of the cheeks (*kūpaka*) should become joined, this should be understood to apply elsewhere as well—provided it is without fear and so forth—at which point death will certainly occur.

[1.2.4] Therefore he says: "If, in times of distress, by means of a mother. The meaning is that this refers to the domain of emergencies. "The breath falters, it falters" refers to an abnormality of the breath. "In the forenoon, the portion of Rohitā" means when there are three staffs at dawn. It should be understood that in the absence of fear and other such factors, truth becomes the cause in all circumstances.

[1.2.5] "In the case of the cutting of the nasal flesh" (*nāse māṃsika vicchidyeti*) means when there is a severance of the flesh of the nose. "In seven days, there is no doubt" (*dina saptā na saṃśaya iti*) means that death occurs without doubt after seven days. The sense is that when the cutting of the nasal flesh occurs, the nose becomes crooked, and death happens within seven days. "In the case of the cutting of the eye and the water, death is likewise after five days" (*cakṣurambarasaṃchede troṭā pañcāhikas tatheti*): "Water" (*ambaram*) means *udaka*, which is to say *lota* (fluid). "Cutting" (*saṃcheda*) means non-existence. "Death" (*troṭā*) refers to the end of life. The sense is that when the eyes are deprived of fluid, death occurs after five days.

[1.2.6] "But by the cheeks and the sides, death occurs after one night": when the two channels at the side of the cheeks are severed, then the cheeks become long, sunken, and support a protruding chin; at that very moment, death becomes imminent within a single day—this is the meaning. When, however, the two depressions (kūpaka) on the cheeks are [severed], it should be known that death will occur in six months. "Upon the severance of the ear-lobe, death in five *ghaṭīs*, there is no doubt": by the word *udu-karṇa*, the ear-flap (*karṇapuṭa*) is meant.

When the two channels of the two ear-pits break, then the ears fall from their respective positions, and death occurs within five *ghaṭikās*. Regarding the statement, "The tongue is the *kālasūtra*; for embodied beings, death occurs after two nights": the meaning is that when the *kālasūtra* appears on the tongue, then death occurs after two days. Regarding "when stuck between the jagged teeth, death arrives after three nights": when the channel at the junction of the teeth breaks, then the two rows of teeth become separated from their joints, and death occurs within three days.

[1.2.8] "The vessel on the side of the neck": when two vessels on the sides of the neck become visible externally, and both sides of the chest become elevated, then death occurs within a fortnight; there is no doubt regarding this limit of a fortnight. Regarding the statement "doctors may treat for a fortnight when the vessels are sunken in the cage of the heart": when the vessel submerged in the cage of the heart breaks, a cavity then forms in the heart, and at that time, death occurs within the limit of a fortnight; and in that case, there is no medical treatment whatsoever.

[1.2.9] "The nails and blood of bodies [disappear] in eight days; of this there is no doubt": when the channels carrying the nails break, then the nails become bloodless. The meaning is that they suddenly turn white. At that time, death occurs in exactly eight days. If these signs appear quite suddenly, then it should be understood that death is certain. Thus, the eight signs have been shown as indicating the time of death for the body.

In the sense of "he reaches" or "he pervades," when the sixth case ending is elided, the word *aṣṭā* (eight) serves as a qualifier for the time of death (*mṛtyukāla*). [The term] *aṅgasya* means "in the limbs. *Mṛtyukālam* means "of the time of death. *Darśitam* means "shown" or "demonstrated. The meaning is that the signs which pervade the time of death have been previously shown as signs in the limbs. Wherever any one of these signs should appear on the limb of a living being, there death is certain.

[1.2.10] Now he speaks of the deception of death: "In the case of the cutting of the nose or the monthly [menstrual] flow, one should press with the seed-syllable of gnosis (jñānabīja). This means that when the nasal channels are severed, for the purpose of filling them, one should press with the seed-syllable of gnosis—the seed-syllable of Jñānaḍākinī, which is the syllable *HŪṂ*—by means of which, being formidable with a stream of nectar, one should press. The meaning is that one should nourish that location. Alternatively, one should visualize Jñānaḍākinī, transformed from the syllable *HŪṂ* and possessing the form to be described later, in that location. Consequently, that channel becomes full.

For death enters by way of the severance of the channels (*nāḍī*); the sense is that if that [channel] is full, death also turns back. In all cases, whatever nourishment is performed by means of a seed-syllable (*bīja*), it should be done through union with the corresponding deity. Regarding the statement "one should energize the eyes and the *ambaratroṭā* with the *vajrī*-seed":

if a *troṭā* occurs upon the severance of the two eye-channels, then at that location one should perform nourishment with the *vajrī*-seed, which is the syllable *suṃ*, or by means of Vajraḍākinī, whose form is terrifying yet holds a stream of nectar, transformed from that seed-syllable. This is the intended meaning.

[1.2.11] "One should press with the *kapola* by means of the seed-syllable of *Ghorī": the meaning is that when the channels of the *kapola* and the sides are severed, one should effect a filling by means of the seed-syllable *kṣūṃ*—the seed of *Ghorāḍākinī*—or by means of *Ghorāḍākinī* herself who has been transformed from that seed-syllable. "The ears are severed at their ends; the seed-syllable of *Vetālī* is recited": when the channels of the two ear-cavities are severed, one should visualize there the seed-syllable *yūṃ*, the seed of *Vetālī*, or *Vetālī* herself who has been transformed from that seed-syllable.

[1.2.12] "The tongue, this thread of time, and the seed-syllable of Caṇḍālī are contemplated": it should be understood that one should meditate there upon the syllable *huṃ*, the seed-syllable of Caṇḍālī, within the "tongue-thread of time" (*jihvākālasūtra*), or upon Caṇḍālī herself as its transformation. "Struck by the seed-syllable of Siṃhī for that which is stuck between the teeth": when the channels of the teeth are severed, one should contemplate the syllable *smryuṃ*, the seed-syllable of Siṃhī, or Siṃhī herself as its transformation.

[1.2.13] "One should press the channel on the side of the neck with the *vyāghrī* seed-syllable" means: when severing the two channels on the sides of the neck, one should meditate there upon the *vyāghrī* seed-syllable *hmr-yūṃ*, or upon a *vyāghrī* (tigress) transformed from that syllable. "The *jambukī* seed-syllable is held for those low in the cage of the heart" means: when severing the cage-channel in the heart, one should contemplate there the *jambukī* seed-syllable *ymr-yūṃ*, or a *jambukī* (jackal) transformed from that syllable.

[1.2.14] "The nails, blood, and hands are seized by the *ulūkī* seed": this means that one should visualize the severing of the channels of the hands and nails as the *ulūkī* seed (*kṣmryuṃ*), or else one should visualize the *ulūkī* itself as having evolved from that. Regarding the statement "the signs of death of the body are protected by these seeds": the meaning is that whatever signs of death are present in the body should be protected by means of the seeds associated with the Yoginīs such as Jñānaḍākinī and the others, according to the sequence previously described.

[1.2.15] "Afterwards, according to the rule, the wheel is protected by knowledge and realization" (*jñānavijñānarakṣitam*): the phrase "I shall state another rule afterwards" is to be supplied. He states that very rule with the words "according to the rule," and so forth. The sense is that a rule must be performed in order to protect realization through knowledge. There is a variant reading in some places: *aparair rakṣāṃ vakṣye*. In that case, the explanation is: "I shall state protection—namely, the maintenance of the vital breaths—in another manner. He states the rule: "ām," and so forth. "Two *āma*-vessels" means two unbaked clay bowls.

Regarding the phrase "with *rocanā* and saffron" (*rocanakuṅkumaiḥ*): it means with either *gorocanā* or with saffron. Alternatively, the connection is that one should draw the wheel with saffron and *rocanā* mixed together.

[1.2.16] "The nine compartments and so forth": by the intersection of four lines in the lower bowl (*adhaḥśarāva*), there are nine divisions, that is, nine compartments. To the question "Why 'lower'?", he says: "Above, like twelve divisions. By the intersection of four lines at the four corners of the upper bowl (*uparitanaśarāva*), there are twelve divisions, that is, twelve compartments. "Like twelve divisions" means "like twelve compartments. "One should write the name in the center," however...

One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the central square of the wheel. Regarding the phrase "by means of the enclosures of the seed-syllables" (*bījaveṣṭanaiḥ*): the "seed-syllables" (*bīja*) are the syllables of the mantra; "enclosures" (*veṣṭana*) refers to those [syllables] by which [the name] is surrounded. The meaning is that one should write the name having enclosed it within the mantra-syllables.

[1.2.17] He states the *garbha* (the womb/core): "The sound of the *praṇava* comes first. Regarding "the sound of the *praṇava*": the meaning is that the *praṇava*-sound is the syllable *oṃ*. That is what occurs first, at the beginning. To the question of why it occurs first, it should be understood as being "from the name of the *sādhya*" (the one to be accomplished). And as to where the name of the *sādhya* is, he says: "In the preceding [part], from the word *rakṣa*. That is, before the word *rakṣa*. "But at the end of the seed-syllable, it is adorned by the five Buddhas":
at the end, the conclusion of that word *rakṣa*, the seed-syllable is adorned by the five Buddhas; the meaning is that it is the syllable *hūṃ*.

[1.2.18] "At the end of the *hutākṣara*": even at the end of the syllable *hūṃ*, there is the *hutākṣara*, which is the word *svāhā*. The collective meaning is: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ svāhā*. The word *rakṣa* is stated twice because of the oral instruction (*upadeśa*). "But the vowels above with the low ones": the word "above" (*ūrdhva*) denotes the exterior. "With the low ones" (*nimnakaiḥ*) refers to the rim (*nemi*). The sense is that the sixteen vowels are to be placed on the rim, which consists of two lines outside the nine squares. The same vowels should also be written on the rim of the upper bowl.

Alternatively, "above" (*ūrdhvam*) means an upward-facing bowl. "With concave [vessels]" (*nimnakaiḥ*) means downward-facing bowls. The remainder is as before. He speaks again of the encircling: "of the seed-syllable doubled by *kha* and *pha*. *Kha* is the syllable *huṃ*; *pha* is the syllable *yuṃ*. The "doubled seed-syllable" is the syllable *kṣuṃ*. Regarding "by the name of the deity Vajrī": Vajrī is the deity named Vajraḍākinī; her seed-syllable is *suṃ*.

[1.2.19] Regarding "the seed-syllable conjoined with five": the seed-syllable conjoined with the five Buddhas is the syllable *hūṃ* everywhere. Regarding "at the beginning": the *praṇava* (oṃ) is at the beginning everywhere. Regarding "at the end": the *svāhākāra* is at the end everywhere. This is the meaning:

*Oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ hūṃ svāhā; oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa yuṃ hūṃ svāhā; oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa kṣuṃ hūṃ svāhā; oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa suṃ hūṃ svāhā.* This is the extraction of the mantras according to the sequence of the Yoginīs. Regarding the fact that the syllable *hūṃ* consists of the five Buddhas, he says: "The staff," and so forth. The "staff" (*daṇḍa*) is the line at the bottom of the letter *ha*. Lokeśvara is Amitābha. The "crooked one" (*kuṭila*) is the letter *ū*; he is Vajrapāṇi, Akṣobhya.

[1.2.20] "The limb" refers to the letter *ha*; he is Mañjuvara, Ratnasambhava. "The bell" refers to the half-moon (*ardhacandra*); he is Maitreya, Amoghasiddhi. "The blazing *ma* above"—he is indeed the liberator from *saṃsāra*: the letter *ma* is the *anusvāra*, and that itself is Vairocana. Thus, the syllable *hūṃ*, whose nature consists of the five Buddhas, is the liberator from *saṃsāra*.

[1.2.21] "Having established the goddesses in the eastern direction and so forth, [one places] Vajraḍākinī": one should write the mantra of Vajraḍākinī in the eastern square of the nine-square wheel. *Oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa suṃ hūṃ svāhā*. "In the north, one should apply the seed-syllable of those named Ghorā": proceeding counter-clockwise, in the north is the ḍākinī named Ghorā; one should apply her seed-syllable, that is, her mantra. The meaning is "one should write. *Oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa kṣuṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

[1.2.22] “Vetālī is situated in the west”: one should write the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*) of Vetālī in the west: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa yuṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Regarding “Caṇḍālī” and so forth: one should write the seed-mantra of Caṇḍālī in the south, perfectly complete according to the full instruction: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa huṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is the sequential writing of the mantras.

[1.2.23] "Īśāna," and so forth: the mantra of Siṃhinī in the northeast corner is *smryuṃ*. The mantra of Vyāghrī in the southeast corner is *hmryuṃ*. The mantra of Jambūkī in the southwest corner is *ymryuṃ*. The mantra of Ulūkī in the northwest corner is *kṣmryuṃ*. Regarding "the utterance of *hūṃ*": this refers to the Ḍākinī whose nature is the pronunciation of the syllable *hūṃ*, because she imitates an owl. In this case, there is no *vidarbhaṇa* (intercalation), due to the absence of such instruction.

[1.2.24] “But by means of the seed-syllables at each corner, there are four with six syllables”: the meaning is that, according to the stated sequence, the four six-syllable seed-mantras of Siṃhinī and the others, in their combined forms, are to be deposited in each corner. He states the conclusion of the mantra-deposition with the words beginning “yathā” (as): the sense is that one should deposit whichever seed-syllable belongs to whichever direction in that very direction.

[1.2.25] “One should place twelve above the locus of the seed-syllable of sound”: this means that one should write the twelve vowels in twelve compartments within an upper bowl (*ūrdhvaśarāva*). Regarding the placement of the mantra in the central compartment, as in the case of the lower bowl, he says: “*praṇamā*, *huta*, and at the end. By the words *oṃkāra* and *svāhākāra* are meant the terms *praṇamā* and *huta*. By the word “at the end” is meant the syllable *hūṃ*. Thus, the meaning is this: the mantra to be written in the center of the wheel is: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ svāhā*.

In the eastern square is *ṛ*, in the north *ṝ*, in the west *ḷ*, and in the south *ḹ*. This is precisely what is meant by the statement: "One should place the neuter vowels in the directions": one should place the neuter vowels in the cardinal directions according to the sequence already stated. In the intermediate directions (*vidik*), one should place the others according to the oral instruction: in the northeast (*aiśāna*) by clockwise rotation *i* and *ī*; in the southeast (*āgneya*) *u* and *ū*; in the southwest (*nairṛta*) *e* and *ai*; and in the northwest (*vāyavya*) *o* and *au*. This is the collective meaning of the phrase "one should place the seed-syllables of the vowels."

[1.2.26] The four neuter [syllables], beginning with *dīpinī*, are the seed-syllables (*bīja*). He explains this very point with the words "the inflamer" (*dīpinī*) and so forth. "They should be placed in their respective locations, preceded by *praṇava*, followed by *svāhā* and *hūṃ*": the meaning is that just as previously the *praṇava*, *svāhā*, and *hūṃ* were established in the center of the nine-square diagram, exactly the same applies here in the twelve-square [diagram]. For example: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ svāhā*.

[1.2.27] Showing which seed belongs to which [deity] according to their respective directions, he says: "In the east," and so forth. The eastern square belongs to Ḍākinī; from that comes the syllable *ṛ*, which is her seed-syllable (*bīja*). The northern belongs to Dīpinī; from that comes the syllable *ṝ*, which is her seed-syllable. The western belongs to Cūṣiṇī; from that comes the syllable *ḷ*, which is her seed-syllable. The southern belongs to Kambojikā; from that comes the syllable *ḹ*, which is her seed-syllable.

[1.2.28] He provides a further explanation for the instruction beginning with "yathā" (as): "in the middle," and so forth. The name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), together with the mantra, is to be written in the center of the wheel. To the question "How?", he says: "just as the name goes upward. This means that just as the name was previously written going upward in the nine-square wheel, so too [should it be done here]. Alternatively, the explanation is that the name of the person to be accomplished should be written between the words *praṇava* (oṃ) and *rakṣa rakṣa*. The remainder is as before.

Regarding the reading "just as the downward [moves] upward" found in some places: *nimnam* means the center; *ūrdhvagam* means the upper bowl. Thus, the meaning is this: just as the previous wheel was placed in the center, so too here. Regarding the phrase beginning with "two," etc.: having joined two bowls together to form a casket, one should wrap them with a red thread...

[1.2.29] Having placed it on a level spot on all sides and smeared with red sandalwood, one should worship it. Regarding the worship, he says: "various," and so forth. As for "the offering at the time of installation": before placing the *yantra* on the sandalwood-smeared spot, an offering (*bali*) must first be presented. The offering at the time of installation is that which is given with raw fish, meat, onions, blood, and so forth, as well as with flour-cakes and the like.

[1.2.30] "Having placed [the yantra] in the middle" means that having placed the yantra in the center of the site, one should recite "I am Vajrasattva"—this is the connection. To the question "What kind of yantra?", he says: "Five," and so forth. The meaning is that upon a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*), one should perform the visualization of Jñānaḍākinī, Vajraḍākinī, Ghorī, Vettālī, and Caṇḍākṣī. Regarding "of the yoga with the self-Vajrī": having emanated oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī, one should recite "I am Vajrasattva"—this is the connection.

The meaning is: having meditated upon the Wisdom-Ḍākinī, whether alone or with her retinue. Regarding the phrase "I shall recite 'Vajrasattva'": the sense is that one who has realized the yoga of the Wisdom-Ḍākinī should assume the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of Vajrasattva. Alternatively, one should meditate upon the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*).

[1.2.31] "With a vajra in his hand, one should touch the vajra visualized at the tip of the hand": having grasped the vajra with the hand, one should touch the pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*). Regarding "in the center of the stated seed-syllable": one should recite eight hundred times the mantra-word that has been written in the center of the bowl, as follows: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ svāhā*.

[1.2.32] He states the benefit of this rite: "One should envelop the deity and so forth with the evil of previous births and the like. This means that the evil committed in previous lives should envelop the deity and others; the sense is that the body of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is not protected by this rite alone. "There is no affliction for the limb, nor indeed untimely death": neither bodily affliction nor premature death occurs for the one being accomplished.

[1.2.33] "Free from disease at all times" means: as long as one has set up the *yantra* and performs the recitation (*āvarta*) of the mantra eight hundred times, for that long it shall be so at all times. However, when untimely death (*akālamṛtyu*) or illness is observed, then by means of the mantra recited eight hundred times a single time, that death or illness is destroyed. "The sick person is joined to the side": having set up the *yantra* at the side of the sick person, one should mutter the mantra. For one whose life has been exhausted, the lifespan of the body shall be increased by six months. This means: having set up the *yantra* at the side of the sick person, one should chant the mantra.
Then, even for one whose life-span and body have perished, an additional lifespan of six months shall occur.

[1.2.34] "It should be installed in another place, with constant worship, intent upon that": having installed the *yantra* elsewhere as well, when the mantra is recited preceded by worship, the previously mentioned result occurs. Therefore he says: "Whose liberation is through consciousness? The meaning is: who becomes liberated from consciousness by means of this procedure?

[1.2.35] Now he speaks of the treatment for poison, beginning with the words "by others" (*apara*). The connection is that another ritual action is being described. Regarding the phrase "one's own breath should be examined": having examined one's own breath, effort should be exerted in that procedure for removing poison. He states this very point with the word "from the cause" (*kāraṇāt*). He explains the examination of the breath with the words "with equal breath" (*samaśvāsena*), and so forth. In whichever place the wind flows, if the questioner is present there, then at that very moment that place—the nostril—becomes a state of equal breath. And when that occurs, all success is achieved.

[1.2.36] "With the right [breath] in the place of the right, or with the left in the place of the left, the wise one [attains success]; but in its place, regarding all statements, total accomplishment is declared. By this, he clarifies what was stated previously: when the messenger asks while the wind resides in the right nostril and the messenger himself is situated on the right, and likewise when the wind resides in the left nostril and the messenger asks while situated on the left, then there is total accomplishment (*sarvasiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "but in its place, regarding all statements": [this refers to the following].
Wherever the wind is located, staying there, the messenger utters his speech; at that time, it is a state of equal breath, and the meaning is that all success is attained.

[1.2.37] Regarding the phrase "the turning back (*vivarta*) of breaths and sentences": because there is a cessation (*nivṛtti*) of the breath—the wind—from one of the two nostrils, whether the right or the left, it is called "the turning back of breath. The meaning is that the nostril is devoid of air.
