Regarding the word "sentences" (*vākyānām*): the connection is that when one utters a sentence while remaining in the empty nostril, then success (*siddhi*) is far off. An example of such a question is: "Devadatta has been bitten by a snake; what should be done in that case? and so forth.

Having thus examined the breath and understood both success and failure regarding the bite, one should determine whether it is appropriate to proceed or not. Explaining this very point, he says: "At the moment," and so forth. "Moment" refers to the entry of the wind. "Of the vital breath" (prāṇasya) refers to the exit of the wind. Regarding the phrase "the conjunction of the two": the connection is that one should indicate [the state] by means of the "moment" between those two conjunctions.

[1.2.38] To the question "What is that?", he says: "In all undertakings. To the question "And what are those all undertakings?", he says: "The nourishing rite (*pauṣṭika*) is proclaimed. The meaning is that these are the undertakings such as the nourishing rite and so forth. The point is that the application of the *kṣaṇa* [breath-moment] is praised not only for the treatment of poison. He says "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*), etc., because that which is commenced when the wind is exiting does not succeed. "Success is far off": the meaning is that the success of that undertaking remains at a distance.

[1.2.39] "But one should consider the poison of those who have been bitten and so forth; medical treatment is the means therein" means that, having considered whether the removal of the poison from the bitten person is curable or incurable according to the method previously described, medical treatment should be administered there only if it is curable. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who are ill and the like are also included. He asks again, "How? and replies with the words "by the previous," etc. This means that the treatment for the *nāgas* should be performed after knowing their command through the application of the characteristics stated in the preceding chapter. "The All-Knowing One" refers to the yogin.

[1.2.40] He states the previously mentioned characteristic: "For one bitten by the deaths [of the yogas], there is no doubt. This means that in the *mikirā* yoga one is bitten by Kuliśa, in the *bhidrikā* by Śataśīrṣa, in the dream state by Karāla, and in the *kāma* yoga by Kāladaṣṭa; for one bitten in these four yogas, death alone is certain—there is no doubt. Regarding the remaining [yogas], there is a summary. He says that very thing: "The treatment is other," and so forth. Treatment is for one bitten by any of the other yogas. How so? He says: "By the yoga for the neutralization of poison.
That is, by the yoga for the removal of poison which will be explained below.

[1.2.41] He describes the procedure for neutralizing poison: "The knower of all should perform the placement of syllables upon the body of the bitten one. The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the eight syllables in various ways. He explains this very point with the words beginning with "eight" (*aṣṭa*): "Of the eight-syllable mantra": the eight syllables are the mantra. "But established in the eight limbs": the sense is that, being established in the eight limbs beginning with the head, they protect the one who has been bitten.

Just as *kṣūṃ* is at the crown of the head, *yuṃ* at the two nostrils and ears, *huṃ* at the two eyes, *suṃ* at the throat, *smryuṃ* at the neck, *hmryuṃ* at the two shoulders, *ymryuṃ* at the heart, and *kṣmryuṃ* at the navel.

[1.2.42] "Having visualized them as white in color": although those seed-syllables (*bīja*) may be of various colors, nevertheless, for the purpose of neutralizing poison, they should be visualized as white. Having done so, one should remove the seed-poison from the mind. One should remove the seed according to the sequence to be described. The seed is the cause of death. "Poison is the mind" means that this poison is nothing but one's own mind (*svacittamātra*); such is the intended meaning. "In the middle, in the place of the mandala": the mandala is the body; in its middle, that is, in the heart. "Knowledge and discernment are paralyzed" means:
The meaning is that by means of the knowledge of the syllable *hūṃ*, the consciousness of the one who has been bitten becomes paralyzed.

Regarding the statement, "After protecting the limb through yoga, one should subsequently perform the external [rite]": once the body of the bitten person has first been protected according to the previous sequence, one should thereafter perform the external rite using vessels and so forth. As for the phrase, "filled with water mixed with milk": it refers to a vessel made of clay or similar material filled with water mixed with milk...
[1.2.44] ...In its center is a white eight-petaled lotus; upon its pericarp is a moon mandala; and above that is [the goddess], transformed from the syllable *suṃ*, adorned with a white parasol...
[1.2.45] ...two-armed, seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, adorned with serpent ornaments, white in color, her two hands occupied with a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup, and elegantly dressed...

[1.2.46] ... One should visualize Vajraḍākinī seated, having stepped upon the eight serpent heads situated between the filaments and the moon. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "In the center, a lotus" (44a). Now, he describes the serpents whose tails rest upon the lotus petals, beginning with "In the east," and so forth. On the eastern petal is white Vāsuki; in the north, yellow Takṣaka; [1.2.47] in the west, red Karkoṭaka; in the south, black Padma; in the northeast corner, white-yellow Mahāpadma; and in the southeast, white-black Śaṅkhapāla.

[1.2.48] In the southwest (nairṛta) is Kuliśapāla, red-black; in the northwest (vāyavya) is Huluṇḍaka, yellow-red. Concluding that these are the eight nāgas, he says: "One should visualize the seat as treading upon the heads of the eight nāgas. The meaning is that Vajraḍākinī is seated while treading upon the heads of the nāgas.

[1.2.49] He speaks of worship: "one should worship," and so forth. This means that all things [should be offered] with all things—namely, with flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and food offerings (*naivedya*). He speaks of the sacrificial offering (*bali*): "one should give the *bali*. By saying "the self," and so forth, he shows that even at the time of removing poison, the yoga of Vajraḍākinī must be performed; the meaning is that one should contemplate the yoga of Vajraḍākinī within one's own body.

[1.2.50] He states that one should remove poison with a peacock feather immediately after the previously mentioned procedure: "with a peacock," and so forth. "Like the yoga of *m-manya*" means that one should draw it out and then discard it. Where? He says: "of the foot drawn from all [directions], the water of the feet dissolves. The meaning is that the drawn-out poison should be cast as far as the soles of the feet, and from there into a vessel containing milk mixed with water.

[1.2.51] He states the mantra for removing poison: *oṃ hrīḥ ṭaṭṭaṇḍara hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. According to the oral instruction (*upadeśa*) here, three *hūṃ* syllables and three *phaṭ* syllables are to be understood [as being present].

[1.2.52] He states that the accomplishment of the goal cannot be achieved without prior service: "Vajrasattva," and so forth. At the outset, through the yoga of Vajrasattva, one should recite each of the mantras associated with Vāsuki and the others one hundred thousand times.
[1.2.53–60] He states the mantras: "Oṃ Vāsuki," and so forth.

[1.2.61] He states the *vidarbhaṇa* (interweaving) at the time of removing poison: "Oṃ Hrīḥ," and so forth. In the phrase "of such-and-such" (*amukasya*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.

[1.2.62] He states the instruction beginning with "drawn forth by all" (sarvākarṣitā): "having drawn forth," and so on. Having arranged other mantras in this manner—such as *oṃ vāsuki hrīḥ ṭaṭṭaṇḍara devadattaṃ nirviṣaṃ kuru hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*—and while reciting them, one should repeatedly wipe from the head down to the feet with that very [mantra] and throw the poison into milk and water. Regarding the phrase "the milk becomes black immediately": thereafter, the milk turns black.

When the milk has turned black, he states another application, beginning with "mustard seeds" (*sarṣapa*) and so forth. Having mixed white mustard seeds, white flowers, and white sandalwood [1.2.63], one should strike the heart of the person bitten while reciting the mantra, all these substances having been consecrated with mantras. When struck, the heart of the bitten person quivers. To the question of what should be done once the heart has quivered, he says: "consciousness is paralyzed and held" (*jñāna-stambhita-dhāritam*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is to be paralyzed by means of "knowledge," that is, by the syllable *hūṃ*. The sense is that one should visualize the syllable *hūṃ* in the heart and thereby paralyze consciousness.

[1.2.64] When consciousness has been sustained, the breaths quiver; thus he says: "With knowledge," and so forth. "One should press with one's own breath" means that with one's own breath, one should press the breath of the victim as it exits, turning it back and causing it to enter—this is the intended meaning. [1.2.65] When that occurs, the breath dissolves within. Upon the dissolution of the breath within, the hands, feet, and so forth move. To the question of what one should do when there is trembling of all the limbs, he says: "But one should cause the self-sung [song] to be performed. The practitioner of mantra should utter the self-sung song, such as "Oṃ hūṃ te na... and so forth (4.4.93cd).

[1.2.66] This very point is indicated by the passage beginning with "hūṃkāra" and so forth. He states that the singing is preceded by the giving of three snaps of the fingers: "extracted by means of three snaps. The meaning is that the bitten person rises by means of the three snaps. Once risen, the bitten one must be made into the embodiment of the yoga of Vajraḍākinī; thus he shall be protected. He says this very thing: "As soon as the bitten one is extracted, one should perform protection for him alone."

[1.2.67] He says that one should throw that milk-and-water mixture, turbid with poison, into a lake inhabited by a *nāga*: "removable," and so forth. Now he describes the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for the primary mantra of poison: "in the moon," and so forth. Visualizing Vajrasattva as white, two-armed, seated in the vajra-posture, situated upon a moon-maṇḍala on a lotus, holding a bell and a vajra in his left and right hands respectively...

[1.2.68] ... One should recite the mantra beginning with *oṃ hrīḥ* three hundred thousand times. The meaning is that by means of this, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for that mantra is accomplished. It is certain that the recitation of the first mantra is three hundred thousand times, while for the remaining ones it is one hundred thousand each. Thus he says "poison," etc., to explain how the poison-removing mantra is perfected: the destruction of poison occurs for the yogins.

[1.2.69] He states the locations where [the poison] is incurable: "In the mouth," and so forth. "Tilaka" refers to the space between the eyebrows. "Of the eyes" refers to the two eyes. "Above the neck, however, in the nostrils" means: in the palate above, in the neck, and in the two nostrils. "Heart, private parts, and the navel" means: the heart is the penis, the private parts are the anus, and "of the navel" means in the navel itself. "The two thumbs of the feet" means: in the thumbs of the hands and feet, and in the feet.

One who is bitten in these locations is not fit for treatment. This very point he states: "But of one bitten by an incurable [snake]," meaning that the one bitten becomes incurable. Regarding the phrase "however, death caused by a cause": the remainder of the sense is that the bite is the cause of death. [1.2.70] Now, in connection with the topic of the *nāgas*, he states the procedure for the *varṣāpaṇa* (the rite for bringing rain), beginning with "Listen," and so forth. "O Great King" is an address to Vajrapāṇi. Regarding "delightful," and so forth: he states that the maṇḍala should be constructed near a lake presided over by a *nāga*, or in a general reservoir, in the north-western corner.

[1.2.71] Regarding "vitāna" and so forth: one should draw the maṇḍala with five colored powders, provided with a canopy and the like, devoid of an archway (toraṇa), possessing squareness and other such features, and adorned by eight nāgas.
[1.2.72] At its four gates, there are two pairs of nāgas situated on both sides, with their hoods raised, their bodies coiled around one another, and each pair encircling the other.

[1.2.73] He speaks of the *nāgas*: "Jayabhadra’s," and so forth. Jaya and Bhadra are on the two flanks of the eastern gate. The same applies to the others. "Śrīnanda to the north" means Śrī and Nanda. "Suvṛṣṭipriya in the west" means Suvṛṣṭi and Priya. "Dhruvaghora in the south" means Dhruva and Ghora. These are connected to the eight families (*kulāni*) respectively; they possess their respective colors and serve as the enclosure walls.

Therefore, it says: "The eightfold enclosure of the Nāga. Regarding "the group of eight families in the intermediate directions": this means that the eight Nāgas are located upon the petals of the eight-petaled lotus in the center of the maṇḍala. "In the intermediate directions" (vidiśa) means in the directions between the cardinal points. He states this very point with the words beginning with "Vāsuki. Their colors are exactly as previously described.
[1.2.76cd] Furthermore, the eight cloud-kings are to be drawn outside the maṇḍala. He states that very point with the words beginning with "Megheśvara."

[1.2.77] In the eastern direction it is thundering; in the southeast, it is rolling; in the south, it is terrible; in the southwest, it is swirling; in the west, it is dense; in the northwest, it is fierce; in the north, it is raining; and in the northeast, it is filling. The colors of these directions, intermediate directions, and *nāgas* should be understood in their respective order.

[1.2.78] This very point he states: "Having established the directions starting with the east, one should meditate upon their colors. And these [deities] have human bodies with the faces of single-hooded serpents. Regarding "seated in the lotus posture upon Vajraḍākinī in the center": the meaning is that Vajraḍākinī is situated in the lotus posture upon the pericarp of the lotus. [1.2.79] The passage beginning with "khaṭvāṅga" (the skull-topped staff) is easy to understand.

[1.2.80] Regarding "of the lotus encircled by a serpent": the previously mentioned lotus itself should be drawn as encircled by a serpent. Alternatively, upon the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of the previously mentioned lotus, another lotus encircled by a serpent should be drawn, and thereupon Vajraḍākinī, as previously described, should be drawn seated upon a serpent-throne. Therefore, it says: "one should employ the serpent-throne. Regarding the worship, it says: "of the noble ones," and so forth. Worship consisting of eight bowls of milk and other offerings should be presented.

[1.2.81] “Vividhamanyakah” means: *vividhā pūjā* (various worship) and *manyakah* is the yogin. To explain what kind of person he is, it says: “the yogin of knowledge. The meaning is that he is one who has attained knowledge (*jñānasamāpanna*). The ellipsis is that, having meditated upon himself in the form of Vajraḍākinī, he should recite the mantra. The sense is that after having drawn the previously mentioned maṇḍala, he should subsequently recite the mantra while in the form of Vajraḍākinī. [1.2.82–83] “Upacāramantra” means: the mantra for the ritual services (*upacāra*) such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), sipping water (*ācamana*), and so forth.
[1.2.84–92] “Oṃ vāsukī,” etc., are the mantras of the eight nāgas.

[1.2.93–94] *Oṃ ghilli*, etc., is the mantra for the eight cloud-kings (*megharāja*). Here, by means of the three *ṭha* syllables, the three *phaṭ* syllables are indicated. Therefore, in place of the three *ṭha* syllables, there are three *phaṭ* syllables; namely: *phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. [1.2.95–96] “Having performed the *pānāvarta*, one should show it toward the eight directions”: by the word *pāna* is meant the hand (*pāṇi*). When the *āvarta* is performed with both hands, it becomes a mudrā. One should display that mudrā to the clouds in the eight directions. Thereby, the clouds will be summoned. For this reason, it was stated previously: “drawn toward the eight directions” (76d).

[1.2.97] Regarding "the left hand," etc.: having formed a fist with the left hand and extended the thumb and little finger, one should place the right elbow upon them and hold the right hand in the shape of a hood; this is the *mudrā* of the *nāgas*. The mantras have been stated previously, and this *mudrā* is distinct from the mantra, not in its form (*ākāra*), but in its application. [1.2.98] Therefore, it says: "The eight are the *mudrās* of the *nāga*-kings. For the clouds (*meghas*), however, there is no distinction between the mantra and the *mudrā*. The previously mentioned *kamalāvarta* is the *mudrā*, and the mantra is: *oṃ ghili*, etc. (93).
[1.2.99] *Oṃ vajraḍākini varṣa varṣāpaya hūṃ bhū ho svāhā*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) for Vajraḍākinī for the purpose of causing rain.

[1.2.100] Although mantras have been taught for the sake of causing rain by both the *nāgas* and the clouds, nevertheless, among them, the mantra of Vajraḍākinī is the principal one. Therefore, it is called the "root mantra."

[1.2.101] Regarding the statement "one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) for the recitation (*jāpa*) of three hundred thousand [mantras] and so forth": the meaning is that when the recitation of three hundred thousand for each individual mantra has been completed at the outset, the preliminary service is accomplished. Regarding the phrase "by these" and so on: the remainder of the sense is that once the rites such as the drawing of the mandala have been performed subsequently with these mantras whose preliminary service has been perfected, the yogin’s attainment of rain invariably succeeds.

[1.2.102] "By others, the sign of the female messenger (dūtīnimitta)" means that another characteristic of the messenger will be stated; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Its "otherness" consists in its being distinct from the characteristics of the wind and the characteristics of the bite. Regarding "the squint-eyed, the grey-haired, and the hunchbacked": "squint-eyed" (kekara) refers to one with grey hair on the head; "hunchbacked" (kubja); "with terrible garments, etc. (ghoravastrādi) refers to one wearing black clothes; and "with a staff" (daṇḍaka) refers to one carrying a staff.

[1.2.103] “He has come with women in pairs”: the meaning is that he has come together with women. “With disheveled hair, etc. means one whose hair is disheveled; by the word “etc.,” one who speaks with a nasalized initial sound is included. “Having cried” means weeping or wailing. “Having approached a naked person in his speech”: “naked” refers to one who speaks with forceful insistence. “The four are like the yoga of cyuti”: the four yogas are *miki*, *rabhidrika*, *svapna*, and *kāma*. The sense is that whichever messenger arrives during these [states] is a cause for death (*cyuti*).

[1.2.104] As in the case of the messenger: "I shall examine myself for two reasons. The meaning is that, having thus observed the characteristics of the messenger and the characteristics of the internal winds and so forth, and having understood success or failure through these two, one should determine whether it is appropriate to go or not to go. Regarding the phrase beginning with "yadi": if the yogin goes when auspicious signs are present, there is success; otherwise, there is loss, which means failure.

Regarding the phrase "in this treatise" (*itiprakaraṇe*): it is called a "treatise" (*prakaraṇa*) because the characteristics of death, the methods for deceiving it, and so forth, are set forth (*prakriyate*) herein according to the sequence already described. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Ātmapīṭha*, within the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*.

[1.3.1] Having first abandoned the ordinary aggregates (*skandha*), one should perform the meditation on the deity; thus he speaks the Chapter on Emptiness (*śūnyatāpaṭala*) beginning with “O Blessed One,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “specifically at the commencement of yoga”: the connection is that he wishes to know specifically—that is, with excellence—the commencement of the meditation on the deity. Regarding “by what should they be known among the mantras?": the meaning is, "How should the mantras be known? Regarding "how, then, should one maintain knowledge?":
how should one maintain—that is, stabilize within the mind—knowledge for the sake of attaining accomplishments such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth?

[1.3.2] He gives the reply: "Listen," and so forth. "According to reality" means without error. "By those whose nature is the deity" means for the sake of cultivating the yoga of the deity, or else, "listen to what will be taught so that one may become the very self of the deity. He states what is to be heard: "First," and so forth. The meaning is that after first contemplating the body as empty through the cultivation of the deity, one should subsequently cultivate the deity. He says this very thing: "Having washed away the impurity of embodied beings.
The meaning is that having washed away the impurity of the body—the attachment to objects of perception and so forth—by means of emptiness, the deity is to be cultivated.

[1.3.3] He states its explanation: "Form," and so forth. It is called *rūpa* because it is manifested (*rūpyate*); thus, the five aggregates are *rūpa*. Regarding "empty, etc.": that form is empty of intrinsic nature, signs, and aspirations. By the word "etc. in "empty, etc.," it is meant that form is to be cultivated by means of the three liberations characterized by emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Since it is not only the five aggregates that are to be cultivated as purified by the three liberations, he says: "up to the eighteenth, the mind."

The six faculties are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The six objects are form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). Their six consciousnesses are likewise. Thus, there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*). And these are purified by the three liberations; they should be meditated upon beforehand, because of the statement "of the former. To the question, "What is the proof that these are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth? he says: "Mind. If their form were something other than mere conceptual construction, then one's own mind alone would be the proof.

The meaning is that the mind alone imagines everything in the form of existence and non-existence. Now, demonstrating the various distinctions in whatever way possible, he says: "The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)," and so forth. It is called a *dhātu* because it maintains (*dadhāti*) form—such as white, yellow, and so on—and its own specific characteristics such as long and short. That which is both form and a *dhātu* is the realm of form, the object of the eye.

And that [form-realm] is empty by its own nature of the characteristics of the apprehended object and so forth; just as when it is said that "a jar is empty," it is understood to be empty of water and the like, but not that the jar itself does not exist. Now, one might ask: what is the form (*rūpa*) of this form-realm other than the forms of the apprehended object and so forth, by virtue of which it may be conventionally designated as "existing"? True. By that very [nature] which cannot withstand analysis and is devoid of both truth and falsehood, it is conventionally designated as "existing," like the moon in water. In this matter too, one's own mind alone is the authority. One should cause sound to be produced for that [mind] alone:

The meaning is that sound, likewise, is empty of being an object of apprehension and so forth. The same applies to what follows. [1.3.4] Regarding "one should effect its form": it is called *rūpa* because it is formed (*rūpyate*) and differentiated across all objects; thus, *rūpa* refers to the sphere of the *dharmadhātu*, which has the nature of bliss.

[1.3.5] Immediately after the objects such as form, he shows the sense faculties beginning with the eye: "the eye," and so forth. The intention is: since both the eye and form are empty, how could consciousness—which lies between them—not be empty? The meaning is: "How can the consciousness born from that be [anything other than empty]?"
[1.3.6] In this way, the ear, nose, and tongue, as well as their respective consciousnesses, are to be viewed as empty.

[1.3.7] "The body" refers to the tactile faculty (*tvagindriya*). Regarding "the mind," which is external among those that are empty, and "the mind would also conceptualize": the mind is empty both internally and externally. One instance of the word "mind" refers to the internal. This entire mind and thought (*citta*), acting as the agent, would conceptualize.

[1.3.8] "It dissolves," and so forth: even the mind goes to dissolution in the form of space. In this way, one should contemplate everything as empty (*śūnya*). He speaks of everything as being obstructed: "destruction," and so forth. Having taken the threefold world (*tridhātuka*), Mount Meru, and the other continents as objects through emptiness—[1.3.9]—namely, the sky above, the earth in the middle, and the netherworld (*pātāla*) below—one should contemplate all of them as empty destruction and then perform the yoga of the deity; this is the meaning. As for those world-systems in the ten directions...

[1.3.10] ... They too are exhausted and rendered empty. Regarding "of the personal existences" (*ātmabhāvānām*): even the grasping at a self (*ātmagraha*) must be made empty. Regarding "existence merged with space": the meaning is that one should meditate upon the deity after having contemplated the entire collection of existences as empty through the state of equal flavor with space (*ākāśasamarasasamatā*). Regarding "of the yogis": a yogi. Regarding "the discerning one": one who is empty of grasping.

[1.3.11] Regarding the question, "How should one maintain knowledge? (1d), he provides the explanation beginning with "paśyanta" and so forth. Thus, while cultivating emptiness and maintaining the mind in a state of equanimity, one should examine the cause by means of that mental equanimity. The meaning is that the cause—the *nimitta*—is to be examined. The point is that while cultivating emptiness, one should perceive the signs (*nimitta*) for the accomplishment of pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites. He states this very point with the words beginning "dīpena" and so forth.

When one sees it in the form of a lamp, then pacifying (*śāntika*) is accomplished. Regarding "dust-colored": when one sees it as red in color, then enriching (*pauṣṭika*) is accomplished. [1.3.12] Regarding "the sun" and so forth: when one sees it in the form of a solar disc, then rites such as the red ones—namely, subjugation (*vaśya*) and summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*)—are accomplished. Regarding "it becomes black and smoky, the rest": when one sees it in a black form or a smoky form, then malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) is accomplished.

[1.3.13] Regarding "of the color of turbulent wind": when one sees the color of the wind as turbulent—that is, agitated and black in form—then the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*) is accomplished. When one sees a white-colored form in the shape of the moon...

[1.3.14] ... Then there is the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "one who possesses knowledge of movement and configuration": by this sequence, one knows whatever movement occurred previously and will occur in the future. The meaning is that when the form of the moon has become stabilized, one understands the movement. Now, in order to show that one should meditate upon the deity immediately after emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he says: "Afterwards," and so forth. "Afterwards" means immediately following emptiness. "Yoga has arisen" means that the yoga of the deity is to be generated. To the question "By what?", he says: "By the seed-syllable of the sprout and so forth."

The seed-syllable is that which is like a sprout and so forth; the meaning is that one should contemplate that very [syllable] as consciousness (*cetanā*). The summary meaning is that the deity is generated by means of the seed-syllable and so forth. This he will explain in various places, but here only the introduction has been stated. The instruction is that if the yogi, having grasped the entire collection of objects with his mind, should remain for two moments, he then knows everything, including the past and so forth; this is another fruit of the cultivation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

[1.3.15] To address the question, "What contradiction is there in deity yoga without emptiness? he says: "He who, having known emptiness, [practices] with the mind, will quickly attain liberation. This means that the yogin who, having understood the emptiness of all phenomena, performs deity yoga, shall become liberated swiftly. Addressing Vajrapāṇi by saying, "Awaken yourself with the mind," the Blessed One spoke. To the question, "Why is it thus? he says: "By means of gnosis," and so forth.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: having perceived the objects of knowledge (jñeya), such as the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth, by means of knowledge—that is, the knowledge of emptiness—and having examined the course (gati), meaning the essential nature (svarūpa), of the deities who are the objects of knowledge, he who practices that yoga shall quickly become liberated.

[1.3.16] He provides the explanation for the phrase "having washed away the impurity of embodied beings" with the words beginning "the mother," and so forth. "The mother" means that the mother is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is insatiable desire for sense objects. Just as a mother does not abandon her son even at death, so too does craving [not abandon] a person. Because of this similarity to a mother, craving is called "the mother. "The father" means that the father is delusion (*moha*), the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. Just as a father procreates, so too does delusion. For it is through the power of delusion that a sentient being is born. "Having killed" means having caused [them] to fall from their true nature.

Regarding "the king": the king is the *ahaṃkāra* (ego-sense). For everything has its origin in the *ahaṃkāra*. Thus it is said: "everything arises from the *ahaṃkāra*. Regarding "two Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*)": these are passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), according to the technical terminology of the Dharma. Regarding "the kingdom with its followers (*sānucara*)": the kingdom is the body (*śarīra*). This is because the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth reign within it. They are called "followers" (*anucara*) because they move along with (*anu*) or together with (*saha*) it. And since the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) exist together with them, it is "with its followers."
Thus, by rendering all this free from appearance (*nirābhāsīkṛtya*), one becomes pure. And that is likewise described by others. This verse expresses the summarized meaning of the chapter.

Regarding the phrase "in this section" (*itiprakaraṇe*): in this manner, emptiness and the signs for nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*) and so forth are treated herein; thus, the "section" (*prakaraṇa*) is the very seat of the self (*ātmapīṭha*). Thus ends the third chapter in the *Ātmapīṭha*, which is a commentary on the *Catuṣpīṭha*.

[1.4.1] Now, immediately following the section on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the fourth chapter is taught to show merely the portion concerning the yoga of the deity, beginning with the words "Listen" (*śṛṇu*) and so forth. "O Vajra" (*vajra*) means O Vajrapāṇi. The connection is: "Listen to the non-dual gnosis" (*advayaṃ jñānaṃ*). "According to the path" (*yathāmārgam*) means without deviating from the path. "Free from duality" (*dvayavarjitam*) means devoid of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and so forth. By this, the following is stated: non-dual gnosis itself is the path to awakening (*bodhimārga*) whose nature is the deity. And that path is the yoga of the deity, which consists of non-dual gnosis.

For whose sake? He says: "In the ocean of saṃsāra," and so forth. Saṃsāra itself is an ocean because it is difficult for the foolish to fathom. It is "terrible among the terrible" because it is hard to cross. Again, of what kind is it? He says: "crossed over," meaning excellent. By whom? He says: "by those who have enemies in the water. Attachment and the other afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves the water-enemies, such as sea-monsters (*makara*); the meaning is that it is filled with them.

[1.4.2] Regarding the phrase "of those whose bodies abide in the midst": this refers to those whose bodies are situated in the middle of that ocean of saṃsāra. To the question "What is for them?", he says: "The goal to be reached is declared. For them, the goal (*lakṣya*) is the yoga with the deity. "To be reached" (*uttārya*) means excellent, in the sense of being for the purpose of crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. "Is declared" (*ucyate*) means it is spoken by the sages throughout the duration of saṃsāra. He first states the definition of non-dual knowledge: "the goal," and so forth. The goal is the yoga with the deity; the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is the act of observing that.
One who perceives is a *lakṣa*, that is, a yogin. *Vijñā* means consciousness (*vijñāna*). By "by means of knowledge" (*jñānena*), it refers to knowledge as the cognition of objects.

[1.4.3] "By means of knowledge" (*jñānena*) means by means of the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñānena*). "The object of knowledge" (*jñeya*) refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. By this, the following is stated: these things, beginning with the characterized (*lakṣya*), as well as the aggregates and so forth, are to be contemplated as empty. The intended meaning is that non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*) is the realization that the characterized and so forth are devoid of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the like. Why is this so? He says: "Because the understanding of the objects of knowledge occurs through observation. For, by defining the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the objects of knowledge—the characterized and so forth—there arises an understanding, which is the knowledge of their intrinsic nature. And: "Understanding occurs in the mind through observations."

Regarding the question of what is gained for the yogin who knows reality through the investigation of the knowable, he says: "The path," and so forth. "Path" means the way; it is the path of deity yoga permeated by non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). By this, it is shown that awakening may be attained according to one's own will. Therefore, he says: "May it be attained according to one's own will."

[1.4.4] He speaks of the benefit of penetrating the emptiness of the path, beginning with the words "Let them be," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "or the snare of saṃsāra": let there be the snare of saṃsāra; nevertheless, "the elephant is fainted at the vital point. The "elephant among men" is the yogin; he is "fainted"—that is, intensified—at the "vital point," which is the knowledge of the true nature. To the question "What does that effect?", he says: "And by a single thousand, the non-yogin has gone to the state of a previous birth."

Even if one has previously experienced a thousand births in unfavorable conditions (*akṣaṇa*), one nevertheless goes to a good rebirth (*sadgati*). The meaning is that even if a non-yogi is bound by the snares of *saṃsāra* and has experienced a thousand births in unfavorable conditions, if he now practices the path of deity yoga permeated by the knowledge of emptiness, he attains a good rebirth upon death, even if he has not yet achieved [the ultimate] accomplishment (*siddhi*).

[1.4.5] He says this very thing: "equality," and so forth. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the deity after having thoroughly contemplated equality through emptiness, characterized as previously described. To the question, "Having meditated upon emptiness, for what purpose is the deity to be meditated upon? he says: "empty," and so forth. For one whose body and field are purified by the empty—that is, by emptiness—he is one whose body and field are empty; for such a person, the sowing of the seed, namely the imposition of the mantra, is praised. To the question, "Of what kind is he? he says: "the wise one."

The discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) is intelligence (*buddhi*); one who possesses this is "one endowed with that" (*tadvān*), referring to the intelligent person. The summary meaning is that for such an intelligent person, the imposition of the mantra upon the body purified by emptiness brings about awakening. And likewise, it is observed that a seed sown in a thoroughly purified field invariably produces a sprout.

[1.4.6] To the question "What is it like?", he says: Just as the section concerning the divine presence (*devādhiṣṭhāna*) of the fire at the house of Mātaṅga is described—wherein a wise woman from a noble family had taken refuge—so too are the dwellings [described] by the thought of meditative concentration (*samādhi-cetanā*). Just as the house of Mātaṅga was consumed by fire, so it should be understood. He asks what such a thing would be like, and replies: it is a "divine presence," meaning the installation of a deity; it is so called because the ritual procedure (*prakriyā*) is performed and applied therein.

"It is fit for the consecration by a deity; let this be said"—this is the meaning of "it is said. For the implication is that it is purified by burning. It is not only suitable for the invocation of a deity; [the phrase] "having resorted" means that, considering it to be a noble family, that house of the *mātaṅga* was purified by fire. To the question "Who are they?", he says: "the learned," meaning the wise. The sense is that in that house of the *mātaṅga* which has been burnt by fire, there exists the abode of deities and the wise.

Just as it is thus, so too the palaces and bodies are burned by the fire of emptiness; the meaning is that "the volition of meditative absorption" constitutes the bases for the superimposition of the deity-yoga.

[1.4.7] Pointing out what was indicated by the statement, “The eight-syllable mantra is assigned to eight locations” (1.2.41cd), he speaks the words beginning with *nyaset* in order to resolve the question, “By whom should it be known among the mantras? (1.3.1c). The connection is as follows: once the union with the deities and so forth has been accomplished, one should perform the arrangement of the syllables (*akṣaravinyāsa*). The word *nyaset* means “one should assign” (*nyasyet*). He states the assignment (*nyāsa*) with the words beginning with *ūrdhvam*. “Above” refers to the palate; there, one should visualize the fire-seed-syllable *kṣuṃ*. Regarding the phrase “of the two earth-seeds”:
"Two *huṃ* syllables: one should apply them to that very eye" means that one should apply those two *huṃ* syllables to the two eyes.

[1.4.8] Regarding "the seed-syllable of wind, space, and so forth": the connection with what precedes is that one should apply the syllable *yuṃ*, the seed of wind purified by emptiness (*śūnyatā*) (7d). As for where: he says, "in the nose, ears, and so forth, by means of the mind. This refers to both nostrils and both ears. "By means of the mind" means by means of the essential nature of consciousness (*citta*). Regarding "of the seeds of nectar and water": the seed of nectar is the syllable *suṃ*, and that is purified by water. Regarding "the Lord is the master of the tongue-faculty": that seed-syllable is to be applied to the tongue-faculty.
Why? Because his sovereignty resides therein. "Sovereign" (*prabhu*) is explained here as "Lord" (*īśvara*).

Regarding the phrase "whose peak-syllables are to be grasped in order": the connection is that one should apply the seed-syllables (*kūṭabīja*), which belong to him and their respective places, in those respective locations among the four positions. He says this very thing: "on the neck," and so forth. On the neck, the seed-syllable *smryuṃ*, which is the purification of delusion (*moha*); likewise, on the two arms, the seed-syllable *hmryuṃ*, which is the purification of affliction (*kleśa*).

[1.4.10] "It has moved to the region of the heart": *calita* refers to the vital air (*vāyu*). That pure seed-syllable is *ymryuṃ*; the ellipsis is that one should join that in the heart. "By means of the two *paśus* at the navel and the root": by the word *paśu* is meant *ullūkī*; its seed-syllable is *kṣmryuṃ*, and that is at the navel and the root. These are "peak-seed-syllables" (*kūṭabīja*) because they exist in the form of peaks (*kūṭa*), being situated one above the other. Regarding "by the eight parts of *kalana*": the sense is that this is a statement concerning the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*). What is that? He says: "The seed-syllable is protected by the eight limbs. The meaning is that which is the protection of the eight limbs by means of the eight seed-syllables.

[1.4.11] "Endowed" (*yukta*) and so forth: the meaning is that one should visualize oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī and be endowed with the seed-syllables in the eight limbs. He describes the form of Jñānaḍākinī with the words "lotus-seat" (*padmāsana*) and so forth. "Adorned with a solar disc" (*sūryamaṇḍalam-aṇḍita*) means she is seated upon a solar disc atop a lotus.
[1.4.12] She is covered by a white parasol situated above. This very point he expresses with the words "white" (*śveta*) and so forth.

[1.4.13] Regarding "kirīṭi vajrā-ūrdhvānām": he holds a vajra upon the crown of his head. "Paṭṭāveṣṭavilambitam" means he wears a crown bound with cloth. He holds three eyes on each face; this is what is meant by "trinetram. "Hasitakrodham" means his left face is smiling, his right face is wrathful, and his principal face is characterized by the languid grace of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). "Suśobhā" means he is endowed with exceedingly white garments. [1.4.14] Regarding "asī" and so forth: his three right arms hold a sword (*asi*), an axe (*paraśu*), and a vajra. His three left arms hold a raised index finger (*tarjanī*), a spear (*śakti*), and a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*).

[1.4.15] One should meditate upon oneself as the form of Jñānaḍākinī, emitting a vast cloud-like multitude of Vairocana and other Buddhas, thereby accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, and radiant with various rays of light. "With breath motionless" (*śvāsaniścalam*): that in which the breath is motionless is "with breath motionless. One should meditate in such a manner; this is an adverbial modifier. By this, one-pointedness of mind is indicated, since when that is present, the breath becomes motionless.
The sense is that one should meditate until the breath dissolves right within the body.

[1.4.16] Now he explains the subtle yoga, beginning with "the mind" (*mana*). "The mind" refers to the syllable *hūṃ*. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) are synonyms for that very same thing. "One should contemplate it as having the form of crystal": the meaning is that one should contemplate the white *hūṃ*. Regarding "ālī" and so forth: *ālī* is the vowel *ū*; *kālī* is the consonant *ha*. Through their conjunction, that seed-syllable is extracted.

[1.4.17] To the question "Where should one meditate on that? he says: "In the middle of the eyebrows," and so forth. Regarding "but in the place of the *bindu*": the sense is that one should meditate on the syllable *hūṃ* after placing the *bindu* of the downward-facing *hūṃ* between the two eyebrows. Here too, the phrase "the breath is motionless" (15d) is to be applied. And this is to be meditated upon immediately following the yoga of the deity. The meaning is that the state of the seed-syllable (*bījabhāva*) is to be meditated upon as the syllable *hūṃ* itself. By whom? He says: "of the yogins"; that is to say, by the yogin.

The intended meaning is that one should contemplate the syllable *hūṃ*, seated upon a lunar disc, with a drop (*bindu*) attached between the eyebrows, from which a stream of nectar flows. Immediately after that, he says "one should recite the mantra," and so forth. One should recite the "syllable-seed" (*akṣarabīja*), which is the seed-syllable of the Knowledge-Ḍākinī (*jñānaḍākinī*). To the question "Which is that?", he replies: "adorned by the five Buddhas. That this [syllable] is adorned by the five Buddhas has already been shown previously.

[1.4.18] He states the extraction of the syllable *hūṃ*: "for the sake of the seventh of wind and fire. By the word *sapti* (seventh), the seventh [letter] is meant. The seventh of *anila* (wind), which is *ya*, is *sa*. The seventh of *anala* (fire), which is *ra*, is *ha*. It is the seventh of both wind and fire. It is called *artha* because it is sought (*arthyate*); the meaning is that it is to be grasped. The singular number is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*). "Impelled by the seed-syllable of Vajrī": the seed-syllable of Vajrī is the seventh of wind (*ya*).

Because the letter *sa* and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) share the common quality of having the nature of nectar (*amṛta*), the term "seed-syllable of the Vajrin" refers specifically to the half-moon; for the letter *sa* is indeed the seed-syllable of the Vajrin. Consequently, "impelled by the seed-syllable of the Vajrin" means joined with the half-moon, [resulting in] the letter *ha*, which is the seventh of the fire-syllables (*anala*). "One should recite" (17c) is to be connected with what precedes. To explain further what kind [of syllable] it is, he says: "with a drop," and so forth. One should recite the letter *ha* as being surmounted by a drop above the half-moon, and below, surmounted by the resonance (*nāda*) and the long vowel *ū*.

The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is [to be understood] as a whole [representing] Jñānaḍākinī. Regarding "the shower of rain": it is called "shower of rain" because it rains down a stream of nectar; that is the *hūṃ*-syllable as it is traditionally taught. The intended meaning is that one should recite it.

[1.4.19] To explain how one should recite that seed-syllable (*bīja*), he says: "Of the guru," and so forth. The "syllable of the guru" is the syllable *oṃ*. It should be seen as preceding the syllable *hūṃ*. Regarding "the burnt syllable at the end": the "burnt syllable" at the end of *hūṃ* is the syllable *svāhā*. Even in the reading where it follows immediately after (*antikāpāṭhe*), it is indeed at the end. Thus, the whole becomes *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Regarding "one should recite," and so forth: one who is perfected in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Jñānaḍākinī should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times. By that, the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.

[1.4.20] Regarding the phrase "in this [practice], for those engaged in recitation": the meaning is that for whatever yogi is joined with recitation through this sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), everything he intends is accomplished. He states the intended purpose: "the eight [types of] actions and so forth, as before. These eight actions—pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākṛṣṭi*), malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), and immobilization (*stambhana*)—are first accomplished prior to awakening; the sense is that subsequently, even awakening itself is attained.

He provides the explanation for the passage beginning with *japet* (19c): "The preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and so forth" means that what was previously mentioned will be accomplished at the time of the ritual (*karmakāla*). The sense is that everything is accomplished merely by recitation (*jāpa*) preceded by *vidarbhaṇa*.

[1.4.21] Now he states the mantra of the Vajra-sickle (*vajrakarttarī*): "Listen," and so forth, which is easy to understand. Regarding "of the Vajra-word": the meaning is that the word "Vajra" (*vajraśabda*) should be placed first. Regarding "the letter preceding the first group": the meaning is that the letter preceding the first group is the letter *ka*.

[1.4.22] “The first syllable of the fourth class”: this means that the first syllable of the fourth class is the letter *ta*. And he says “doubled” because that [syllable] is to be doubled. “*Repha* for the upward [vowels]”: this means that the *repha* (the letter *r*) is placed above the doubled *ta*. “The vowel *i* joined with *repha*”: the meaning is that subsequently another *repha* is to be joined with the vowel *i*.

[1.4.23] "As for the second of each class, with two syllables, it is called *binduka*": the second syllable of the second class is the letter *cha*; one *bindu* (dot) should be placed near it. "But by the goad, one should press": here, by the word "goad" (*aṅkuśa*), the short vowel *i* is taken; by that, one should press—that is, one should join—the letter *cha*. "The third of the fourth": the third of the fourth class is the letter *da*.

[1.4.24] "The two should be uttered twice" means that the pair consisting of the syllable *chiṃ* and the letter *da* should be pronounced twice; for example, *chiṃda chiṃda*. An *anusvāra* or the letter *na* should not be employed. "But it is embellished by the fifth" means that the fifth is the syllable *hūṃ*; the mantra is embellished (*carcita*) by that. "Preceded by the syllable of salutation" means that first, at the beginning, there is the syllable *oṃ*. "With the terrible syllable at the end" means the terrible syllable is *phaṭ*; the sense is that this should be placed at the end. Thus, the complete mantra is: *oṃ vajrakartari chiṃda chiṃda hūṃ phaṭ*.

[1.4.25] He states its benefit: "Its seed," and so forth. Since "stambhana" (paralysis) is illustrative, the intended meaning is that by reciting this mantra, one accomplishes all tasks. He describes the mudrā: "With two," and so forth. Regarding "the mixing of the hands": having joined the two hands together; "one should apply it to what has been eaten" means that "eaten" (*bhuñjita*) signifies food or eating. Therefore, one should join the two mixed hands.
By this, the sense is that one should join the two hands and show the mouth with the gesture of eating.

[1.4.26] Having joined the two hands together, he explains what should be done: "Having extended both the *krodha* and the middle fingers, one should touch them finger-to-finger. Having joined the two hands and subsequently formed two *vajramuṣṭis*, one should extend both the *krodha* (index) and the middle fingers and touch them to one another with the gesture of cutting. One should also perform the gesture of devouring with the mouth. By employing this mudrā while joining it with the preceding mantra, one shall accomplish all rites.

Inserting the thumb into the palm and pressing down with all the fingers constitutes the *vajramuṣṭi* (thunderbolt-fist). Regarding the phrase "by these" and so forth: "by these" refers to this mudrā. "All things are cut" means that it cuts and accomplishes [the task]. As for what those things are, he says: "or the neck of the enemy," and so on. The sense is that when one applies this mantra—which has been mastered through prior service (*pūrvasevā*)—preceded by this mudrā, it cuts the neck, ears, nose, and other parts of the enemy. To the question "What would necessarily happen? he replies: "the mind. The meaning is that this is merely a play of the mind.

[1.4.27] “Now,” and so forth. “The stopping of all effects such as water” means the immobilization of rainwater; this is the intended sense. “Just as,” and so forth. “Just as” (*yathā*) is used as an illustration. “Of the class, by three letters of the final ones is grasped”: the final class is the *pa*-class (*pavarga*), when counted from the *ka*-class. “By three letters of that”: the third letter is *ba*; it is taken first.

[1.4.28] "The third of each class with three syllables": the third syllable of the third class, the *ṭa*-class, is the letter *ḍa*. "But by means of *e* for the preceding, with the seed-syllables of the third part": having placed the preceding *e*, the letter *ba* is taken by the word "seed-syllables of the third part. Consequently, it becomes *baḍabe*.

[1.4.29] "But of the fifth, the preceding": this refers to the letter *pa*, which is the first of the fifth group (*varga*). Regarding the phrase "by means of the hook" (*aṅkuśena tu*): here, the short vowel *i* is understood by the word "hook. One should join the letter *pa* with that. Regarding the phrase "the visarga-syllable in the middle": the visarga-syllable is the letter *ba*; it is in the middle of the seed-syllable of Vajrī. He says that very thing: "The seed-syllable of Vajrī is indeed near (*antiketi*). The final seed-syllable of Vajrī is the letter *ha*.

[1.4.30] "The letter *ra* with the hook on its side": having placed the letter *ra* below the letter *ha*, one should place the long *ī* vowel as a hook on its side. "Ghāta," etc.: the syllable *phaṭ* is at the end. "The *praṇava* should be placed first": the *praṇava* (Oṃ) is to be given first. Thus, the complete mantra is: Oṃ *baḍabe piba hrīḥ phaṭ*. "The seed-syllable fashioned for immobilization": this is the mantra for the immobilization of water.

[1.4.31] He explains the *mudrā*: "The two hands," and so forth. Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, one should draw out the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*) from their bases to their tips; then, having drawn the tips of the two ring fingers with the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), one should join the tips of the two thumbs (*jyeṣṭhāṅguli*) at the base of the two middle fingers (*madhyamāṅguli*). This is the *vaḍavāmukha-mudrā*. "May Meghadeva and the others be devoured" means the paralyzing (*stambhana*) of Meghadeva and the rest.
[1.4.33] "A hundred thousand," and so forth, is easy to understand.

This fourth chapter is the exposition of the yoga of the deities and so forth; by means of these four chapters, the Ātmapīṭha is completed. Therefore it says: "Thus the Ātmapīṭha is finished. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the *pīṭha*. Thus ends the first *pīṭha*, the Ātmapīṭha, in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*.

[2.1.1] Now, in order to explain the characteristics of the disciple, as well as the fire-offerings (*homa*) and the presentation of oblations (*balidāna*) for pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites according to the systems of others, he speaks the first chapter beginning with "O Blessed One" and so forth. The connection is: "I wish to hear. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Of what nature is the reflection? How are the rites of pacificatory fire-offerings, the application of oblations, and so forth? Regarding the rites of pacificatory fire-offerings and the like, what is the "reflection," which is the yoga with the deity? This is a question concerning the very rites of pacification and so forth, because their constituent parts have been asked about.

Regarding the phrase "the offering of oblations (*bali*), the application (*yukti*), and so forth": the sense is, at the time of offering the oblation, what kind of "application" is there—that is, what kind of union with the deity (*devatāyoga*)? Alternatively: what kind of ritual action is there, such as the *śāntika* fire-offering (*homa*) and so on; what kind of "reflection" (*pratibimba*)—that is, the union with the deity—is there therein; what kind of oblation-offering is there; and by the word "and so forth," it should be connected to the question of what kind of characteristics the disciple possesses.

[2.1.2] Expounding this very point, he says: "Listen," and so forth. Regarding "the supreme consciousness of the image (*bimba*) and so on": listen to the mind whose essential nature is the deity’s image; the sense is that you will hear it. Regarding "of the mantra and the mudrā": it should be construed as "listen to the mantra and the mudrā. To the question "Whose?", he says: "of the *homa*. The explanation of "mantra" is "recitation (*japa*)," meaning the recitation of that mantra. "Meditation and cultivation" is the explanation of the deity’s image. The sense is: at the time of the *homa*, listen to the deity-yoga, the mantra, and the mudrā.

[2.1.3] Furthermore, "the wise one will know the fire-ritual and so forth prior to the recitation" means that the wise person should first understand the fire-ritual (*agnikarman*) and the oblation-ritual (*homakarman*) from the recitation of mantras; the sense is that prior to the oblation, the recitation and other such acts must indeed be performed. Alternatively, the sense is that prior to the recitation, the oblation and other acts are to be understood. "By merely purifying the ground, the altar (*vedī*) is characterized as being subsequent to that": first, the purification of the ground must be done for the sake of the oblation. "Subsequent to that" means: after that, one should dig the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) whose characteristics have been understood.

[2.1.4] "Starting from eight finger-breadths up to a thousand cubits" means up to a thousand finger-breadths. Alternatively, it means starting from the measure of eight finger-breadths up to the measure of one cubit, and from the measure of one cubit up to the measure of a thousand cubits; this is stated as the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*. There is a reading in some places: "The eight finger-breadths are taken as the excess. The explanation is that when the measure exceeding eight finger-breadths is taken, it is taken up to the measure of a thousand cubits. He states the measurement: "But the eighth is the slayer of enemies."

The meaning is that a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) should be made for the purpose of slaying enemies; the intention here is that this is for an *abhicāra* (malevolent) fire-offering (*homa*). "The tenth is likewise for nourishment" means that one measuring ten finger-breadths is for the purpose of a nourishing (*pauṣṭika*) fire-offering. "The twelfth is connected with subjugation" means that one measuring twelve finger-breadths is for the purpose of a fire-offering for subjugation (*vaśa*). "The fourteenth is for peace alone" means that one measuring fourteen finger-breadths is for the purpose of a fire-offering to remove diseases and so forth. "The sixteenth is connected with *ākrānta*" means that one measuring sixteen finger-breadths is for the purpose of a fire-offering for the increase of sons, grandsons, and so on. Even by one who is childless, a fire-offering should be performed for the sake of obtaining a son.

[2.1.6] "It increases by eighteen places starting from Gokula": this means that the place measuring eighteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) is for the purpose of *pauṣṭika* (prosperity) and *śānti* (pacification) fire-offerings (*homa*) for cows, elephants, horses, and so forth. "Twenty [finger-breadths] for the altars (*vedi*)" means that the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the altars is twenty finger-breadths.

[2.1.7] “Of that which is covered, two parts are dug out by the third”: regarding the phrase “of that which is covered,” this refers to the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*. Regarding “by the third”: having divided it into three parts, the digging of the *kuṇḍa* is done with the measure of two parts. The meaning is that, having divided the measurement of the mouth of the *kuṇḍa* into three parts, the digging is performed with two parts. This is the general characteristic of the digging for all *kuṇḍas* alike. Regarding the phrase “but the eighth part of what is dug out”: this means by the eighth part of the excavated portion.

He asks, "What is that? and replies: "The *kuṇḍikā* is even by means of the lip (*oṣṭha*). The sense is that it is the lip of the *kuṇḍa*. [2.1.8] "One should cause the outer rim (*nemi*) to be half a part of the lip": this means that the lotus is joined with a rim exceeding [the lip] by one-eighth; thus, the lotus situated on the lip is one-eighth the size of the rim. "One-eighth of the petal" means that the lotus petal is one-eighth the size of the lotus. Alternatively, "exceeding the rim by one-eighth" refers to the ninth part of the rim; the eight-petaled lotus situated on the rim is of that same measure.

[2.1.9] Regarding "of the outer": outside the rim (*nemi*), there is a lotus enclosure (*padmaprākāra*) one finger-breadth wide. Regarding "of the vajras": the emblems of the *yoginīs* should be drawn upon the lotuses in the center of the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*). Alternatively, the emblem of Vajrasattva is the vajra. [2.1.10] With the words "But for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), a triple-altar," and so forth, he states the specific characteristics of the fire-pits. Regarding "but for malevolent rites, a triple-altar": this means triangular. Regarding "perfectly full, conjoined with subjugation (*vaśa*"): this means circular. Alternatively, "and likewise for nourishing rites (*pauṣṭika*)," meaning that the nourishing fire-pit is also circular.

[2.1.11] "The half-moon for eradication" means having the shape of a half-moon. "An eighth part for attraction and immobilization" means that for both attraction and immobilization, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be one-eighth [the size of the standard]. "It should be applied in successive order for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, and so forth" means that within the aforementioned pits, pacification and the other rites are to be understood according to their respective sequence. This is the intended meaning.

[2.1.12] He provides the explanation for the passage beginning with "In the center of the *kuṇḍa*," etc. (9c): "Five," and so forth. One should place the emblems of the yoginīs, who are the very nature of the five Buddhas, according to their respective directions. He explains that very point: "One should place them in each direction according to its direction. Therein, upon the lotus in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, on a solar seat, one places a *vajra*; and on the petals in the east, north, west, and south, one places a *khaṭvāṅga*. Regarding "four," and so forth: one should draw a wheel, a jewel, a lotus, and a sword in sequence on the four sides of the rim (*oṣṭha*). He states this very point: "Adorned with the emblems of the Buddhas."

[2.1.13] A vajra should be drawn above the half-moon at the corners of the *varaṇḍaka*. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "in the moon" (*candretyādi*). Regarding the phrase "as Kailāsa is lofty and auspicious through its seats and abodes": Kailāsa should be fashioned on the left side of the front of the teacher’s seat.

[2.1.14] As to what its measurement is, he says: "joined with half a *pauruṣa*. A *pauruṣa* is the measure of a cubit (*hasta*), and half of that is a span (*vitasti*). The meaning is that it measures one and a half cubits in both width and height. Regarding "but with twelve [fingers] for the thumb": the intention is that the staircase there should be seen as twelve finger-breadths wide. Regarding "on the petal, by eight, one should establish the place of the deity in sequence": [this refers to the placement].

Outside the *kuṇḍa* in every respect, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus, and upon its petals—in sequence on the eight starting from the east—one should write the emblems of the goddesses. There, on the eastern petal, is the emblem of Ḍākinī: two hands entered into the mouth. On the north is the emblem of Dīpinī: the form of a head in the *añjali* gesture. On the west is the emblem of Cūṣinī: the form of drinking an *añjali* of blood. On the south is the emblem of Kāmbojī: the shape of a pestle (*musala*).

On the petals beginning with that of Īśāna, one should draw only the goad as the symbol for Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Ulūkī. Regarding the question of what color these symbols are, he says: “of those that are stepped upon,” and so forth. This means: of the symbols that have been stepped upon—that is, superimposed. “Of the yoginīs” means: by the yogin. “But specifically” means: according to the specific ritual action such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. Thus, the meaning is this: the distinction of the colors of the symbols is to be understood from the distinction of the ritual actions. [2.1.15] *Oṃ hili hili oṃ kili kili oṃ vettāli hūṃ*—this is the mantra.
[2.1.16] “Ritual service” (*upacāra*) refers to the ritual service consisting of the sprinkling of the materials to be offered into the fire and so forth.

[2.1.17] Starting from the purification of the ground, one should meditate on oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī; thus he says: "One should visualize," and so forth. One should visualize Jñānaḍākinī. Regarding the phrase "created by means of one's own body": the meaning is that one should visualize oneself as Jñānaḍākinī. He states the singular number: "the act of imagining," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "abiding in oneself": this refers to the form of oneself as Jñānaḍākinī. Even if the reading were "one should place oneself in the locus," the meaning would be the same.

[2.1.18] "The tongue and this water": "this water" means the nectar-water; that is the seed-syllable *suṃ*, and it is located on the tongue—this is the meaning. Even in the reading "the tongue and indeed water," the meaning is the same. "Space in the ears and nostrils": space is the seed-syllable *yuṃ*, and it is located in both ears and both nostrils. "Earth and this water are joined": the earth-purified seed-syllable *huṃ*; and that is in the two eyes, which are the waters—so it should be understood.

"Agni, this is Brahman, thus [it is said]: Agni is the seed-syllable *kṣum*, and that is in the place of Brahman, meaning in the palate. These are to be known as the seed-syllables of Vajraḍākinī, Vettālī, Caṇḍālī, and Ghorī, respectively."

[2.1.19] Regarding "from the necks of the charioteers of delusion" (*moha-sārathi-grīvebhyaḥ*): the seed-syllable *smryuṃ* is purified of delusion, and it resides in the neck as the charioteer. The wind that has moved is purified by that; the seed-syllable *ymryuṃ* resides in the heart. Regarding "the afflictions in the chests of all": by the word "chest" (*uraḥ*), the arms are meant. The seed-syllable *hmryuṃ*, purified of the afflictions, resides at the roots of the two arms. Regarding "by the two beasts" (*paśubhyām*): by the word "beast" (*paśu*), the female owl (*ulūkī*) is meant; its seed-syllable is *kṣmryuṃ*, and it resides at the root of the navel. These are the seed-syllables for the lioness, the tigress, the jackal, and the female owl, respectively.

[2.1.20] The calculation (*kalana*) that follows from the context is specified: "One should cause the eight limbs of the deity to be known by means of the eight [syllables]. The meaning is that the calculation of the eight limbs is performed with the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the eight goddesses. To explain how this is done, he says: "With the *tripatāka* [gesture]," and so forth. By pressing the little finger with the thumb and releasing the remaining fingers, the *tripatāka* mudrā is formed. With that, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) for each seed-syllable. [2.1.21] Reminding us that "it should be offered by way of the union with Jñānaḍākinī," he says: "The emanated," and so forth, which has already been explained.

[2.1.22] Regarding the phrase "those with khaṭvāṅgas and vajras in their hands": the meaning is that they hold a vajra in the right hand and a khaṭvāṅga in the left. Regarding the term "composed" (*samāhita*): it refers to a yogin who has turned away from worldly concerns; the syntactical connection is that one should meditate upon the Jñānaḍākinī as distinguished by such attributes. The sense is that one should meditate upon oneself—that is, the self as one's own body—as the Jñānaḍākinī. The expression "steady in breath" has already been explained.

[2.1.23] Now, regarding the purification of the ground: first comes the yoga with the deity, then the purification of the ground, and then the digging of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); such is the sequence. Therefore, immediately after the yoga with the deity, the purification of the ground must be performed. [2.1.24] He states that very point: *oṃ hana hana krodha hūṃ phaṭ*.

[2.1.25] “Extending the left hand and striking while meditating on the vajra”: having extended the right hand and visualized a five-pronged vajra therein, the yogin of his chosen deity should meditate that, with that vajra-adorned hand, he strikes the five locations down to the subterranean realm (*rasātala*), which consists of vajras, through the purification of the five goddesses; this is the mudrā. The mantra has been stated previously.
[2.1.26–27] “Both hands, with fists joined, should extend the two middle fingers”: having formed two fists, one should extend the two middle fingers.

"Extending the two middle fingers in the shape of a needle and joining them, one should hold [them]"—this is the *mudrā*. "The purification of all substances" means the purification of all substances such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and so forth. "The mantra is distinct for each": by means of this single *mudrā* and the distinct mantras to be mentioned, the purification of the clarified butter and other substances must be performed.
He states the mantras: *oṃ śriṃ svāhā*, etc.

[2.1.30] Beginning with the purification of ghee and continuing up to the purification of the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*), this very same mudrā is used. [2.1.31–39] He explains the summoning of fire, beginning with the words "in the middle of the fire" and so forth. Having kindled the fire in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and having visualized within its center a lotus, and in the middle of that, the Fire-god—arisen from the transformation of the syllable *raṃ*, seated upon a sun-disc, wearing tawny matted locks, honey-colored in hue, holding a water-pot and a rosary in his left and right hands, and surrounded by flames—one should summon such a fire and cause it to enter therein.

[2.1.40] He says this very thing with the words "vāma" and so forth. Having placed the left hand fist upon the rim of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a bundle of kuśa grass, having raised the middle and index fingers, and having placed the bent index finger upon the line of the third joint of the middle finger—with this mudrā...
[2.1.41] ...one should summon [the fire] with the mantra: *oṃ āgaccha āgaccha agne jaḥ svāhā*.
[2.1.42] Regarding the form of the fire, he says "bhāvayet" and so forth; this is easily understood.

[2.1.43] With the words "one should worship" (*pūjayet*) and so forth, he describes the worship of the fire (*vahni-pūjā*). This is what is stated: having drawn in the fire according to the previously mentioned method and having offered the *argha*, *pādya*, and other offerings to it, one should worship it with flowers, incense, and so forth, after having brought the *samaya*-fire—which has been visualized within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)—into a state of equal flavor (*samarasīkṛta*) with that fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*). Regarding the phrase "having performed worship there as far as possible": the connection with what follows is that, having performed the worship according to one's means (*yathāvibhava*), one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*). Regarding the phrase "with three for all": [this refers to the three oblations].

The meaning is that one should offer all substances three times. As for where: he says, "In the midst of the fire, upon the tongue. This means upon the tongue of the fire. [2.1.44] Regarding "the two," etc.: having formed the *añjali* gesture and opened it in the shape of a lotus, when the two middle fingers are raised in the form of a *madhyamā* among all the fingers, this is the *mudrā* of the Heart of Fire. [2.1.45] One should display this *mudrā* to the Fire with the mantra: *oṃ agne juhu juhu svaḥ svāhā*.

[2.1.46–47] He states what should be done next: "One should carefully give three snaps. The meaning is that, having formed the mudrā and reciting this mantra, one should snap the fingers three times. When this is done, the fire drawn into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) merges in the form of a flame and becomes of one flavor (samarasībhavati); such is the meaning. Regarding the statement "here purification begins; however, all-knowing [one should purify] in the midst of the fire":

the meaning is that at the time of meditating on one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the midst of the fire, one should purify the interior of the pit and the substances to be offered by means of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
[2.1.48] He explains how one should perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*): *oṃ hūṃ ṭaṭṭi phaṭ*, and so forth.

[2.1.49] "Water, mustard seeds, flowers, and the vajra... This is what is meant: having grasped the vajra with the hand, together with water mixed with mustard seeds and flowers, and employing this mantra along with the previously mentioned sprinkling mudrā (*prokṣaṇamudrā*), the purification of all things should be performed; such is the sense. [2.1.50] Regarding the "purification mudrā and mantra": the sense is that the mudrā for the purpose of sprinkling is the one previously mentioned.
[2.1.51] *Oṃ vajraprākāra* and so forth is easy to understand.
[2.1.52] "Starting from the northeast corner, one should rotate [it]" is the meaning of the passage beginning with *aiśānyā*.

[2.1.53–54] "Extending both hands, one should touch the tips, but not like a bird's beak": having extended the two hands above the head, one should draw out the fingers of each other from the base and hold them; this is the *pañjara-mudrā* (cage mudrā).
[2.1.55] *Oṃ vajra svāhā* is the mantra.
[2.1.56–57] The meaning of the passage beginning with "the left" (*vāma*) is that one should form a fist with the left hand and hold the thumb facing downwards.
[2.1.58–59] This should be understood during the purification of the ground and in the yoga of the deity, such as for the construction of a perimeter wall (*prākāra*) and so forth.

[2.1.60] Showing that one should offer oblations to one’s own chosen deity after having offered to Agni, he says: "In the middle of the fire," and so forth. In the center of the fire situated within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), there is a lotus; above that, a solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*)... [2.1.61] ...above that, a five-pronged vajra transformed from the syllable *hūṃ*; having visualized the syllable *hūṃ* in its hub (*varaṭaka*), one should meditate upon [the goddess] who is the transformation of all of that, red and other colors, holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a vajra in her right and left hands.

[2.1.62] “Emerged by means of the breath of the self” (*ātmaśvāsena niḥsṛtam*) means that the *jñānasattva* has issued forth from the body of the self. Regarding “the colors of the ritual action itself” (*karmasyaiva tu varṇānām*): the *jñānasattva* possesses colors corresponding to the specific ritual, such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. It should be understood that the *samayajñānaḍākinī* also possesses a color corresponding to the ritual. As was stated previously: “of red color and so forth” (*raktavarṇādīti*); by the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), the other colors are also to be included. “The seat of yoga” (*yogapīṭhikā*) means she is seated upon the *sattva*-cushion.

Having emanated from one's own body such a Jñānasattvī, one should meditate on the mantra of the Samayajñānaḍākinī. And that Jñānaḍākinī, situated in the midst of fire, has the nature of one's own body.
Therefore, he says: "yataḥ" and so forth. "Pūjayet" and so forth is easily understood.
[2.1.64–65] Regarding "oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha svāhā": by the word *ṭha*, the three *hūṃ* syllables are meant. Thus, the mantra should be "oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā."
[2.1.66] "Staff" refers to the *sruva* ladle.

[2.1.67] Regarding the statement, "one should extend the two middle fingers of the two hands joined in the hollow-fist gesture," this is the seal (*mudrā*) for purifying all objects; its mantra is: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. [2.1.68] This very point is stated as: "the mantra of the root-seal. Following the purification of the ground, the purification of all objects is to be performed with the root-seal using the individual mantras, both at the time of meditating upon one's chosen deity in the center of the fire and by means of this mantra with the aforementioned seal. Thus, the purification of all objects should be carried out.
[2.1.69] He states the mantras for all offerings, beginning with *oṃ*.
[2.1.70–75] Extending the right hand and making the gesture of offering scented unguents is the *gandhamudrā*.
[2.1.76–77] Extending the right hand and joining the thumb and forefinger while extending the remaining fingers is the *puṣpamudrā*.
[2.1.78–79] The *dīpa-mudrā* (lamp gesture) is formed by raising the thumb from the fist of the right hand.
[2.1.80–81] Regarding the phrase "in the *puṣpa-mudrā*": the *dhūpa-mudrā* (incense gesture) is formed by raising the middle finger from the *puṣpa-mudrā*.

[2.1.82–83] Extending both hands, one should touch the two middle fingers to the two thumbs; this is the *bali-mudrā* (offering gesture). The application of these mudrās with their respective mantras follows the sequence [as given].

[2.1.84] “Having recited once, one should offer once to the two fires with the *mukhajihvikā* [mantra]: this means that having recited the *āhuti-mantra* once, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Having recited the mantra “Oṃ hūṃ 3 svāhā” upon the tongue of the fire’s mouth, one should offer it—this is the meaning. There is an alternative reading: “*sakṛj jāpyāhutyā mukhajihvikaiḥ*,” but here too the meaning is the same. “But having taken seven more, in the middle, on the *madhyamapiṇḍikā*”: seven oblations are to be offered. “In the middle” refers to the fire; [it is offered] in the middle of the tongues of one’s own chosen deity. “*Madhyamapiṇḍikā*” is the technical name for the oblation.

[2.1.85] "But the remnants from the oblation, in their form as remnants, are for that purpose": when the oblation has been performed, the remaining substance is to be offered. It should be understood that this refers to what remains after the first full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) has been given into the mouth of the fire. The meaning is that even after that has been offered—preceded by the giving of the full oblation—what remains is different from that. By this it is stated: having first offered one oblation into the mouth of the fire, one should offer all the substance.

At the conclusion of the oblation of all the substances, there is once more a single *pūrṇāhuti*.
