Immediately thereafter, having offered a *pūrṇāhuti* into the fire as the mouth of one’s own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), one should offer the remaining substance. Then, at the end of that [subsequent] homa, there is a *pūrṇāhuti*. Again, having asked one’s chosen deity for forgiveness and having re-visualized the deity of the fire, one should offer a *pūrṇāhuti* into its mouth and offer the remainder. Following that as well, at the end of the homa, there is a *pūrṇāhuti*. Immediately after that, a single *pūrṇāhuti* should be caused to be offered into the fire by the hand of the patron (*dānapati*).

Thus, it is established in the *Catuṣpīṭha* that seven oblations are completed. Regarding the phrase "the course of the fire": the meaning is that the deity's own body dissolves [into the practitioner]; that is, once the homa has been performed, the visualized chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) should be made to enter into one's own self.

[2.1.86] "Complete" means that everything, including the *pūrṇāhuti* mantra and the mudrā, should be performed; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "one should cause [the offering] to be given into the midst of the fire with a vessel full of ghee": this provides the specific instruction for the matter previously indicated—that once the *homa* has been performed, [the deity] dissolves into the body of one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

When the homa has been completed in every respect, at the conclusion of the seven oblations, one should visualize one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in the midst of the fire. Having placed a vessel filled with clarified butter and a *sruva* ladle before its mouth, a single oblation is to be offered. Then, two full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) are to be given to one's own chosen deity. After that, following the chosen deity, one full oblation is to be given into the fire. There should also be two oblations for the fire itself. Previously, a single oblation each was cast for the chosen deity and the fire.

[2.1.87] "But draw in the self-form; let the self-form dissolve"—this shows how the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) dissolves into oneself. The sense is that she should be made to enter into oneself by means of one's own breath. "Thereafter, let the wise one contemplate with his own body"—the meaning is that thereafter he should contemplate her, who has entered into himself, as being identical in form to his own body.

[2.1.88] “The wise one should meditate upon the fire-god in the center”: the meaning is that immediately after the entry of one’s own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) into oneself, having performed the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites upon the fire, one should visualize the fire within its center according to the method previously described. “The remainder by three oblations, through the offering of worship and *bali*”: once the fire has been visualized, one should offer the remaining sacrificial material (*havya*) three times, preceded by the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and having given the *bali* and performed the worship and so forth, one should ask the fire for forgiveness (*kṣamayet*).

First there are seven oblations, afterwards two oblations, and now three oblations; in total, twelve oblations. Regarding "maṅgala" and so forth: he will speak of the auspicious song (4.4.93). With the words "two hands in front" and so on (44a), the mudrā has been described [2.1.89]. Regarding "I shall explain another classification of the fire-offering rites in brief": the meaning is that I shall explain briefly another classification of rites such as the *śāntika* and others [2.1.90]. Regarding "to be drunk with milk": this refers to milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Some say it refers to the cream of milk (*kṣīramaṇḍa*).

[2.1.91] He speaks of the fuel for the kindling of the fire: "five," and so forth. Wood from the *āmra*, *vaṭa*, *nyagrodha*, *parkaṭī*, and *aśvattha* trees is to be taken. "As if stepped upon by fourteen thumbs" means the fuel is fourteen finger-breadths long. The procedure regarding the appropriate time for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) has been stated previously.
[2.1.92] Now he describes the rite of prosperity (*puṣṭika*): "black sesame," and so forth; the meaning is black sesame seeds.

[2.1.93] *ghṛtakṣīrasya peyena*: milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee. *ākrāntā daśam-aṅgulam*: fuel ten fingers long. Even in the alternative reading *ākrānta daśamas tathā*, it is exactly the same. [2.1.94] He states the *vaśa* [mantra]: *tilaraktasya*, etc. *kṛṣṇasya*: black sesame; *raktapuṣpam*: red flower. *aśurī*: black mustard. Some say it means the fruit of a creeper. *madhu sarpiṣayojitam* is easy to understand. In the alternative reading *madhusarpeṇa yojitam*, the meaning is "mixed with honey and ghee."
[2.1.95] *nāgakāṣṭham* means the wood of the *nāgakesara* tree. *Raktakarmādīti* means that one should accomplish subjugation (*vaśa*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).

[2.1.96] *Phalakālaketi* means the fruit of the *mahākāla* tree. [2.1.97] *Kālavṛkṣasya* refers to the tree commonly known as *hariṭhā*. *Kubjasya* refers to the tree commonly known as *kujākaṇḍa*. *Bhallātaguḍim eva ca* means the wood of the *bhallātaka* tree. *Aṣṭāṅguṣṭhakrāntasya* means that for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), the fuel should be eight finger-breadths in measure.

[2.1.98–99] "But of *kāñcana*": this refers to the *dhuttūra* tree. For the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*), the fuel should also measure eight finger-breadths. [2.1.100–101] "Wood of the house-crow and so forth": this means wood from the nest of a crow. "With tooth-sticks that have been spat out" (*m-utsiṣṭā dantakāṣṭhakair*): with tooth-sticks that have already been chewed. Wood of *devadāru*, *vāsā*, and *nāgakesara*; wood of the black tree (*kālavṛkṣa*), *kubja*, and *bhallātaka*; wood of *kāñcana* and *vāsā*; wood of the crow's nest and wood from chewed tooth-sticks—these are for the purpose of kindling the fire; the remainder is to be offered as oblation (*hotavya*).

[2.1.102–105] Regarding "Sundarī": this refers to the earth (*pṛthvī*). "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ" means again the earth, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and heaven (*svarga*). The sense is that she accomplishes either the earth alone or the three worlds.
[2.1.106] With the words beginning with "atha," he states the characteristics of a disciple.

[2.1.107] "Complete in every limb" means one whose constituent parts are complete. Alternatively, by the word *aṅga* (limb), one refers to the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) and so forth. He states this very point with the words beginning "disciplined" (*vinīta*). "Disciplined" means one who has mastered grammar and the other sciences. "Peaceful in conduct" (*śāntacārika*) means one who has conquered the senses. "Delighting in the three Dharmas" means one who takes pleasure in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Mahāyāna. "Always possessing a Mahāyāna mind" means one whose intellect is devoted to the practice of the Mahāyāna. And thus it is said: "One who abides in the vows of a Śrāvaka and has generated the resolve for the Mahāyāna."

[2.1.108] *Mantraprayogaḥ* (the application of mantras) refers to the employment of mantras for pacification (*śāntika*) and other rites. *Tantraprayogaḥ* (the application of tantra) refers to such things as drawing mandala circles (*cakra*) for pacification and other rites. *Abhirato yogadhyānaṃ ca* (and delighting in yoga-meditation): he is one who delights in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). *Śrutapāṭhāditatparaḥ* (intent upon hearing and reciting the scriptures): he is devoted to listening to the *pravacana* and to its recitation. [2.1.109] *Gurubhaktaḥ* (devoted to the guru): he serves the guru through body, speech, and mind. Following the qualities, he states the faults: "But not... and so forth, which is easy to understand.
The sense is that some reality (*tattva*) is to be imparted to one who is distinguished by such qualities and free from defects; or else, that such a person is to be made a disciple in this *tantra*.

Thus, because the ritual procedures beginning with the fire-oblation (*homa*) are performed in this manner according to the stated sequence, it is called a "section" (*prakaraṇa*), namely the "Supreme Seat" (*parapīṭha*). Thus ends the first chapter in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha* concerning the Supreme Seat.

[2.2.1] Now he speaks the chapter on the water-oblation (*jalahoma*): "It has been heard," and so forth. The intention is that a curiosity regarding the water-oblation exists in him to hear it. He provides the explanation for this very point: "How," and so forth. The intention is: what is the definition, the essential nature, and the true reality of the water-oblation?

[2.2.2] “Listen,” and so forth: *tattvam* refers to the essential nature of the water-oblation (*jalahoma*). “Just as” (*yathā*) is used as an illustration; the meaning is: “listen to the essential nature of the water-oblation exactly as it is. He explains that very point: “One should properly observe the water and so forth”: the sense is that one should perform the oblation with proper effort after first inspecting the water thoroughly. One should take water that is free from living organisms, originating from a good location, and clear. “And with canopies spread out and various hanging cloths”: where the oblation is to be performed, there one should stretch out a canopy and various banners.

[2.2.3] "On all sides," and so forth: In a secluded place, smeared with cow dung and provided with canopies and the like, a square mandala measuring four cubits on each side should be prepared using fragrant substances. By the instruction "very extensive," the measurement of four cubits is indicated. "In the center, a water-vessel, etc.": In the center of the fragrant mandala, there should be an earthen vessel fourteen finger-breadths in height; its depth should be two-thirds of its mouth-measure, following the proportions of a *śāntika* sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (cf.)

2.1.7ab) “And one should place the vessel free from blackness and so forth”—this is the ellipsis. “One should smear it with white fragrance and so forth”: one should make the vessel smeared with white sandalwood.

[2.2.4] Furthermore, as to what kind [of vessel], he says: “mixed with water and milk. Having placed that vessel, filled with the previously mentioned purified water mixed with milk, in the center of the mandala, one should place eight vessels in the eight directions, filled with fragrant water and having their mouths adorned with sprouts (5ab); this is the intended meaning. Therefore, he says: “of the jars,” and so forth.

[2.2.5] Having instantaneously manifested oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī, with three faces, six arms, and so forth, he says "instantly," etc., regarding the task to be performed as it will be described below.

[2.2.6] Regarding "one should worship," etc.: the meaning is that one should worship, by means of flowers, incense, and so forth, the assembly of deities residing within the vessel, which will be described below. To explain the visualization of the deities within the vessel, he says "afterwards," etc. The sense is that immediately after visualizing oneself as Jñānaḍākinī, one should visualize the form of the deity situated externally in the vessel for the purpose of the water-oblation (*jalahoma*).

[2.2.7] "The two hands," and so forth: having joined the two hands in the shape of a lotus through slight opening, one should display the *kamala-mudrā* (lotus gesture) to the vessel, conjoined with the mantra *oṃ kamalābhe svāhā*.

[2.2.8–10] Then a lotus is seen in the midst of the water. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "in the midst of the water. Regarding "one should place": by the mere display of the mudrā, the lotus arises; thus it is called the "placement of the lotus" (*padmanyāsa*).

In the midst of water is a lotus, and upon that, a moon mandala; therein is the seed-syllable *hūṃ*. From that seed-syllable, one should visualize Jñānaḍākinī—two-armed, seated in the sattva-paryaṅka posture, holding two staffs marked with vajras in her two hands, white in color, and possessing a principal face on the right and left that is wrathful, laughing, and amorous respectively. Having emanated from oneself a Wisdom Being (*jñānasattvī*) identical to her, one should cause her to enter [the visualized form]. He explains this very point with the words beginning with "white" (*śvetā*):
One should meditate upon Jñānaḍākinī, who holds a white parasol. To the question "How?", he says: "In the center of the seed-syllable. This means having visualized the seed-syllable within the moon.

The sense is that one should first produce the form of Jñānaḍākinī from water by means of that seed-syllable, and subsequently, through one's own breath, emanate the Knowledge Being (jñānasattvī) from one's own body and cause her to enter. He describes the form of the Knowledge Being with the words "two-armed," and so forth.

[2.2.12] Regarding "of the two-armed one": the meaning is that there are two staffs (*daṇḍa*) in the two hands. By the phrase "laughter, anger, and passion," three faces are understood. The form of the *samayasattva* is likewise. Having shown the *mudrā* to the *jñānasattvī* within the *samayasattvī*, he says "he should show her" and so forth, meaning that he should cause her to enter. [2.2.13] He describes the *mudrā*: "with two hands" and so forth. Having formed fists with both hands and joined back to back, one should make a knot with the two extended index fingers; this is the *samayamudrā*.
[2.2.14–15] One should display that [mudrā] with this mantra: *oṃ samaye tiṣṭha hūṃ phaṭ*.

[2.2.16] He explains the placement of the yoginīs (*yoginīnyāsa*) in the vases starting from the east, beginning with the words "In the vase," etc. In the eastern vase is Vajrī; the rest is easily understood.

[2.2.17–18] “One should show the individual signs” means that, having visualized the assembly of Yoginīs—beginning with Vajrī and the others—arisen from their respective seed-syllables within the vases starting from the east, one should show the mudrās to be described individually to each Yoginī in due order; this is the intended meaning. “Like the *samaya*-mudrā” means that just as the previously mentioned *samaya*-mudrās are to be shown to each of the Yoginīs and Jñānasattvas, so too is the root-mudrā to be shown to them; this is the intended meaning.
Then he says that one should perform the worship: "With flowers," and so forth. "The wise one" means one who is free from distinctions such as the worshipped and the worshipper.

[2.2.19] He describes the root mudrā: "With the vajra," and so forth. Having placed the left fist at the heart, one should place the right fist upon it; this is the root mudrā. [2.2.20] One should display it with the mantra: *oṃ jrūṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

[2.2.21] Regarding "the root mantra": this means the mantra of the root mudrā. This is also to be recited (*japya*). When three hundred thousand recitations have been performed, it should be understood that the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is complete. Thereafter, one should offer oblations with this mantra.

[2.2.22] Regarding "of the white flower, etc., such as the *kunda*": whatever white flower there may be, the *kunda* flower must certainly be employed. Regarding "one should cause the tip of the *dūrvā* grass to be given": having placed the tip of the *dūrvā* grass upon the root of the flower, one should offer oblation while striking the crown-vajra of the Goddess visualized within the vessel, reciting the previously mentioned mantra with that flower. He says the same thing: "one should strike," and so forth, which is easy to understand. [2.2.23] Regarding "once," and so forth: the sense is that one should offer each individual flower one by one, reciting the mantra again and again for each.
[2.2.24] "Combined with *dūrvā*" means that one should offer oblations of red *karavīra* flowers interspersed with *dūrvā* grass; this is the intended meaning.

[2.2.25] "With fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *nāgapuṣpa*" means that the flowers of the *nāgakesara* tree themselves serve as the fuel-sticks; this is the intended meaning. [2.2.26] Regarding "one should employ" and so forth: the meaning is that once the fire-oblation has been performed with lotus fuel-sticks, one may perform various ritual acts. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "ten thousand" (*ayuta*).

[2.2.27] "A handful," and so forth: the meaning is that having seen the previously mentioned Bhagavatī situated within such a vessel, one should offer her one hundred and eight handfuls of water while reciting the root mantra. "Prosperity" (*pauṣṭika*) means that there is an increase of wealth and so on. [2.2.col. This is the section (*prakaraṇa*), because the ritual procedures such as the water-oblation (*jalahoma*) are performed herein according to the stated sequence. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha* concerning the other seat (*parapīṭha*).

[2.3.1] To clarify the yoga of the deity and to explain the commitment (*samaya*), he speaks the third chapter, beginning with "Listen, O Vajra," and so forth. The intended meaning is: "Listen to the characteristics of that non-dual gnosis by which one goes to the further shore of saṃsāra. Indeed, the yoga of the deity was already asked about previously; therefore, no further request was made for the instruction on its limbs and sub-limbs.
That same subject matter is repeated here, though it relies upon a different point of meaning.

Thus, from the statement [of the scripture]. In order to clarify the yoga of the deity, he first speaks of emptiness, beginning with "bhāva" and so forth. *Bhāva* is existence; *abhāva* is non-existence. It is liberated from both. If entities do not exist because they are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can their non-existence exist either? Because there is no substratum (*dharmin*). As for the phrase "one should avoid purity and impurity": purity is the state of being free from afflictions (*niḥkleśatā*); impurity is the state of having afflictions (*sakleśatā*). The meaning is that it is devoid of both.

Because non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) is pure by nature and because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are adventitious, even that form which is free from existence, non-existence, and so forth, does not exist for the non-dual. If existence and so forth do not exist, how can there be "freedom from them"? Thus it is said: "‘It exists’ and ‘it does not exist’—these are both extremes. ‘Pure’ and ‘impure’—these too are extremes.
Therefore, having abandoned both extremes, the wise person does not take a stand even in the middle."
Thus.

[2.3.2] He states that such non-dual knowledge is itself all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) with the words beginning "adaitya" and so forth. All phenomena, that is, all entities, are designated as non-dual; the sense is that they are devoid of duality.
Indeed, all phenomena are non-dual and devoid of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Because of this statement: "In this way, all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature; thus the world is empty of intrinsic nature. And it is signless:
"Never, anywhere, do any entities exist that have arisen from themselves, from another, from both, or without a cause."

Because of this statement, [there is also] the wishless (*apraṇihita*). For indeed, in a world that lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), a wishful aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is not tenable. He shows that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is to be cultivated at the beginning, middle, and end of the undertaking of the yoga of the deity: "Form," and so forth. The meaning is that the emptiness of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the others is to be cultivated in the beginning, the middle, and the end.

[2.3.3] "Impure," and so forth: "impure" (*aśucyam*) refers to the state of being intensely greedy for impurity. "Pure" (*śuci*) is its opposite. "Intermediate" (*madhyam*) means devoid of both purity and impurity. Thus, "equality" (*samatā*) is the state of having a single flavor (*samarasatā*). The meaning is that there should be only the vision of that. Alternatively, "pure" (*śuci*) means sanctified; "impure" is the other. The remainder is as before. And this is the explanation of the phrase "purity and impurity" (1d). "To be cultivated," and so forth: "to be cultivated" (*sevya*) means approachable; "not to be cultivated" (*asevitam*) means unapproachable. "Intermediate" is devoid of those two.

"In this way, the arising of equal gnosis" means that the equality of gnosis and mind arises. "Of those whose bodies are situated in equilibrium": the meaning is that by the very logic previously stated, there would be equilibrium of the body. "Like speech situated in equilibrium": the meaning is that there is also equilibrium of speech. This is the sense: just as the mind is mere self-awareness (*svasaṃvinmātra*), so too is the body; and just as the body, when analyzed down to its atoms, is nothing at all, so too is the mind.

Just as with the mind and the body, so too is speech; for, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), sound is not expressive of an external object. In this way, there is the equality (*samatā*) of the body and the other [faculties]. And thus it is said: "May you generate the mind in the form of the body, the body in the form of the mind, and the mind through the utterance of speech. To the question, "What would result from this?", he says: "From equality," and so forth. The meaning is that through the vision of equality, the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*) arises.

“O Blessed One,” and so forth; “the vision of equality” (*samatādṛṣṭi*) refers to the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*). “Of what kind? means: in what manner does it arise? The underlying sense is: how are phenomena, which are non-dual in nature, to be directly realized in the form of oneself and the deity?

[2.3.6] He speaks in order to pose a question: "Listen," and so forth. "According to reality" means non-erroneously. Regarding "the characteristic of non-dual gnosis": the sense is, "listen to how non-dual gnosis arises. The passage beginning with "free from" is easy to understand. Regarding "by three," and so forth: the meaning is that one should recite the mantra beginning with "purified by the three," namely, the three natures (*svabhāva*) and so on. When? He says: "at the beginning of all yogas. The meaning is that one should recite the aforementioned triad of mantras at the commencement of all yogas.

[2.3.7] He says those very things: "by intrinsic nature," and so forth. They are pure, empty, and void by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), characterized as existent and non-existent, permanent and impermanent, being and non-being, that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted, the grasped and the grasper, and so on. To the question "Which ones?", he says: "all phenomena" (*sarvadharmāḥ*). They are called "phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) because they bear (*dhāraṇāt*) their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as arising, abiding, and ceasing; these are the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. And they are pure by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and primordial essence (*prakṛti*). He says, "I too am likewise": "I am pure by intrinsic nature. The sense is that although one is already pure by nature, one is purified for the sake of removing adventitious stains.
[2.3.8] "Vajra," and so forth: *vajra* is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), because it is indivisible (*abhedyatva*). They are pure in that same manner.

[2.3.9] Yoga has the deity as its object; by means of that, they are purified, having abandoned their ordinary forms. Having visualized one's own seed-syllable in one's own heart, and having caused the appearance of the Guru and one’s chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) through the stream of rays emanating from it, and having performed the gestures of offering flowers and so forth with flowers and other items, one should then perform the contemplation of the confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, the dedication of merit, going for the three refuges, the surrender of oneself, the making of vows, taking recourse to the path, loving-kindness (maitrī), and so on. After that, one should recite the "Threefold Purity. This is the intended meaning.

[2.3.10] Having recited these, one should cause the *añjali* (palms joined) to be made for the Unsurpassed One alone; the meaning is that, having placed the *añjali* at the heart for the sake of unsurpassed gnosis (*anuttarajñāna*) and having performed the confession of sins and so forth, one should recite the threefold purity. He states the perfection of the place: "favorable to the mind," and so on. The sense is that if any particular location is favorable to the mind, one should begin meditation there; or else, on a mountain and the like. [2.3.11] "Patākā" means devoid of symbols. A "dhvaja" is a banner marked with symbols such as fish or birds.

[2.3.12] "In the same way, with ten places on all sides beginning with the fragrance-mandala": the meaning is that in such a location, one should, during the time of meditation and so forth, create a single mandala of fragrance pervading the ten directions on all sides. The pervasion of the ten directions occurs by scattering showers of fragrance upwards and by smearing it in the center. Immediately after the worship and so forth, having meditated upon oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī, one should perform what is about to be described; thus he says, "Instantly," and so forth. "Instantly" means that one should be visualized as the solitary Jñānaḍākinī.

[2.3.13] "Performing worship for oneself" means having performed the worship and so forth by oneself. He states what is to be done: "the hand turned upward," and so on. Having meditated upon a five-pronged vajra in the form of a flame in the upturned right hand...

[2.3.14] One should perform the clapping of hands in the center; then, in the eastern direction, and subsequently by turning counter-clockwise toward the north and so on—thus, having visualized a vajra-made enclosure extending down to the subterranean realm (rasātala) while reciting the mantra *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should visualize the ramparts and other features according to the previously mentioned method. The instruction is that the visualization must first be commenced while facing westward. One recites this very mantra: "by the syllable *hūṃ*" and so forth. The "blow" (*ghāta*) at the end refers to the syllable *phaṭ*, which is the blow.

Then, having meditated upon a golden palace—transformed by the mantra *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, situated atop Mount Sumeru composed of the four jewels, inlaid with the seven precious gems, and expanding according to one's desire—one should meditate upon the Bhagavatī therein; this is the remainder of the sense.
He says this very thing in the verse beginning with "the summit of Meru" (2.3.16).

Regarding the mudrā, he says "having bound," etc. Among all mudrās, having first bound the *samaya-mudrā*, one should display it; this is the remainder. The intended meaning is that, having meditated upon the Bhagavatī in the golden palace, one should display the mudrā to her.

[2.3.17] How one should form the mudrā is stated: "The vajra-fist," and so forth. The meaning is that, having placed the left fist at the heart and raised the right arm, one should display the *samaya-mudrā*.

[2.3.18] He states its mantra: "Just as," and so forth. "Just as" (*yathā*) means "of which" (*yasyāḥ*). The seed-syllable consisting of vajra is the syllable *hūṃ*. Regarding "at the end" (*ante*), it means that the word *svāhā* should be placed at the end. The complete formula is *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. Regarding "of this," and so forth: it means that the mantra of this *samaya-mudrā* has been shown.
[2.3.19] Now he describes the seat: "the lion throne," and so forth. One should visualize five lion thrones in five locations, and upon those, five solar disks.

[2.3.20] Jñānaḍākinī is in the central seat; in the remaining seats are Vajraḍākinī and the others. He will describe other seats as well. The sense is that one should meditate on the deity preceded by the meditation on the seats. Regarding "having emerged by means of one's own breath": the sense is that, having meditated on the *samayasattva*, one should cause the *jñānasattva* to emerge from one's own body and enter the *samayasattva*. Regarding "Jñānaḍākinī in the center": the sense is that Jñānaḍākinī is to be meditated upon in the central lion-throne.
He describes her form with the words "three-faced," and so forth.

[2.3.21] “Having spread out the hair, adorned by the five Buddhas”: having extended the hair, she is adorned by the five Buddhas; the meaning is that they are radiating forth. [2.3.22] “With laughter, wrath, and passion”: the root face is passionate (*śṛṅgāra*), the left is laughing, and the right is wrathful.
[2.3.23] “And the *khaṭvāṅga* is upward”: one should visualize the *khaṭvāṅga* pointing upward.
[2.3.24] "The middle one is wise": the meaning is that one should meditate on such a Blessed Lady, Jñānaḍākinī, in the central seat through the purification of space.

[2.3.25–34] "The self enters" (*ātma āpeti*): the word *ātman* denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Enters" (*āpeti*) means water; thus, the meaning is "having the nature of water. In this way, Ghorāḍākinī and the others, who possess the natures of fire and so forth, are to be visualized in the northern and subsequent directions by moving counter-clockwise.

[2.3.35] “Ātmapañce” (the fivefold self): the meaning is that these five ḍākinīs have the nature of the five elements; this is the sense of the summary. “Pañcapañca” (five times five): the meaning is that these five are purified by the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*); they are to be meditated upon upon the lion-thrones previously mentioned. Alternatively, each individual yoginī is purified by the five gnoses. [2.3.36] “In the northeast,” and so forth: in the northeast is Siṃhī, who bears a lion’s face and has a dual color of white and yellow. The lord of nāgas is the elephant, which serves as her seat.
[2.3.37] "With a vajra-hook and the threatening finger": on the right arm is a hook marked with a vajra; on the left is the threatening finger (*tarjanī*).
[2.3.38] In the southeast is Vyāghrī, seated upon a throne fashioned from the seven jewels, her body colored white and blue according to the two parts of the ground.

[2.3.39] "With a hand resplendent with a hook" means that the right hand is adorned with a hook. "The threatening finger like a noose" means that the left thumb (or index finger) is joined with a noose.

[2.3.40] “The color of red and black”: the color of both the red and black grounds. [2.3.41] “With a goad, a noose, and a threatening finger”: the goad is in the right hand; the threatening finger (tarjanī) marked with a noose is in the left.
[2.3.42] “In the northwest is the goddess Lūkikā”: Ulūkī has the color of both yellow and red ground.

[2.3.43] ... She sits upon a serpent and is adorned with serpent ornaments. This is precisely what is meant by: "having stepped upon a serpent seat, she is decorated with serpent ornaments. The [mudrās] of the goad, the noose, and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) are as before. These, beginning with Siṃhī, have faces well-known by their own names. [2.3.44] "But eight Ḍākinīs in the middle": the meaning is that these eight Yoginīs are situated in the middle enclosure (*puṭa*). "But of the outer ones, four each": the intention is that four Ḍākinīs are to be mentioned in the outer enclosure.

[2.3.45] He states those very [deities]: "In the eastern [gate]," and so forth. The connection is that she is named Raudrī at the eastern gate. "O King of Kings" (*rājendra*) is an address to Vajrapāṇi. [2.3.46] "Having cast her hands into her mouth":

the meaning is that she stands having placed both hands in the form of an *añjali* into her mouth. "The loud-laughter woman" (*aṭṭahāsī*): the meaning is that she stands laughing with a loud laugh while her *añjali* is cast into her mouth.

[2.3.47] “Dīpinī in the north” means Dīpinī is at the northern gate. “With two hands in the *añjali* gesture, the head raised like a lamp”: the sense is that she stands having formed the *añjali* and displaying it above her head in the shape of a lamp. [2.3.48–50] “She should drink blood from the hands with the red thread in the *añjali* gesture. Regarding “with the thread”: the meaning is that she should hold it in the form of a thread. The meaning is that, having taken the *añjali* of blood and raised it, she should drink it as a stream.

Regarding "those with the threatening finger and the mace in their hands": the mace is in the right hand and the threatening finger is in the left. "Deluding" means bringing [others] under one's control.

[2.3.53] "All, all-knowing": the meaning is that the yogin should thus meditate upon the entire mandala. Regarding the "heroic posture" (*sattvaparyaṅka*): one should place the left foot in the form of a cross-legged posture upon one's own seat and extend the right foot slightly; this is the heroic posture. The yoginīs are situated in the heroic posture. Like the lion throne, the thrones of the lords of nāgas and so forth, as well as the thrones of the *pretas*, should first be visualized as being stepped upon by the sun. Upon those thrones, the yoginīs are manifested from the transformation of their respective seed-syllables.

"One should also show the pledge (*samaya*) of the foremost [deity] by means of these [mudrās], such as the *bimba*": the meaning is that one should show each of their respective pledge-mudrās (*samayamudrā*) in the presence of these yoginīs.

[2.3.54] Regarding the mantra and the mudrā, he first states the mantra: "anila," and so forth. By the word *sapta* (seven), the seventh [letter] is intended; that is the meaning. The seventh letter of *anila* (wind) is *sa* (s); and the [seventh] of *anala* (fire) is *ha*. That itself is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vajrī, because it is a constituent part of the seed-syllable. And because it has the nature of nectar (*amṛta*), it shares the same quality as the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). Consequently, by the term "seed-syllable of Vajrī," the half-moon is meant. With that, one should "pierce" the seventh of *anala*; the meaning is that one should place it upon the head of *ha*. By this, the following is stated:

"Between the seventh of the wind and the seventh of the fire": the seventh of the wind is the seed-syllable of Vajrī. "With that, one should pierce the seventh of the fire. "Overcome by *bindu* and *nāda*" means: the *bindu* is above the half-moon of the letter *ha*; the *nāda* is the letter *ū* below it. Thus, the mantra would be *hūṃ*. "Showering a stream" (*dhārāvarṣa*) means: it showers a stream of nectar; thus, "showering a stream" is the conventional name for the syllable *hūṃ*.

[2.3.55] "Praṇama" and so forth is easy to understand. "Oṃ hūṃ svāhā" is the mantra; this belongs to Jñānaḍākinī. By means of this, the mudrā should be displayed. Jñānaḍākinī arises from the seed-syllable *hūṃ* alone. Likewise, in subsequent cases as well, the mudrā should be employed with the seed-syllable beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*. From the mere seed-syllables, the respective Yoginīs arise. Regarding the phrase "of the seed-syllable preceded by a vowel": the vowel is the initial *a*; it is the "first" (*ādi*) of the seed-syllables—this is the intended meaning.

The meaning is: excluding the seed-syllable of Jñānaḍākinī, among the seed-syllables of the others, it is the first. This has been explained as "the *praṇava* at the beginning and the *huta* at the end. At the beginning is the syllable *oṃ*, and at the end, upon the completion of the extraction of the mantra, is the syllable *svāhā*.

Regarding the phrase "the name of Vajrī is the preceding one": the intention is that the letter *a* is the seed-syllable of Vajraḍākinī, who resides in the eastern direction. Thus, the complete collection is *oṃ a svāhā*. Regarding the phrase "of the second in the group of vowels": the second of the vowel-letters is the letter *ā*.

[2.3.57] In the northern direction, this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Ghorī, namely the letter *Ā*. The complete mantra is *Oṃ Ā Svāhā*. Regarding the phrase "of this" and so forth: the meaning is that next to this employed seed-syllable *Ā*, there is another *Ā* in the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*). Thus, the seed-syllable is *Ā³*. [2.3.58] In the western direction, this is the seed-syllable of Vettālī. The complete mantra is *Oṃ Ā³ Svāhā*. Regarding the phrase "of this" and so forth: a nasal drop (*bindu*) should be placed above the seed-syllable *Ā*. Thus, the seed-syllable is *Āṃ*. The complete mantra is *Oṃ Āṃ Svāhā*.
[2.3.59] *napuṃsā pūrva bījasya*: The neuter vowels are four—*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. Among these, the first vowel is the *ṛ*-seed (*ṛ-bīja*). The aggregate *oṃ ṛ svāhā* is the mantra.

[2.3.60] *napuṃsaka* etc.: The second seed of the neuters is *ṝ*. The mantra is *oṃ ṝ svāhā*. [2.3.61] *napuṃsaka* etc.: The third seed of the neuters is *ḷ*. The aggregate *oṃ ḷ svāhā* is the mantra.
[2.3.62] Regarding "the fourth of the neuter seeds": the fourth seed of the neuter [vowels] is *ḷ*. The mantra is the aggregate: *oṃ ḷ svāhā*.

[2.3.63] Regarding "in *lū* there is the sound *hūṃ*": *ulūkī* is the sound primarily consisting of the syllable *hūṃ*. The meaning is that this is its seed-syllable (*bīja*) and this is its mantra. Regarding "of the fifth," etc.: the second letter of the fifth class (*varga*) is *pha*. [2.3.64] Regarding "but the root-sound among the seeds": the root (*mūla*) is the bindu (*bindu*); the sound (*nāda*) is the vowel *u*. The letter *pha* joined with that [becomes] *phuṃ*. This *phuṃ* is the seed-syllable of the *Ḍākinī*; the mantra is *oṃ phuṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.65] Regarding "of the fifth group": the word "the second syllable" is to be supplied as the remainder. "The letter *e* joined with a *bindu*" means the seed-syllable (*bīja*) *pheṃ*. The complete mantra is *oṃ pheṃ svāhā*. [2.3.66] Regarding "of the fifth seed-syllable": the phrase "the second syllable of the fifth group" is understood to carry over. The seed-syllable is *phoṃ*. The complete mantra is *oṃ phoṃ svāhā*. [2.3.67] "With the letter *ra*, the elephant-goad (*aṅkuśa*), and the *bindu*" means the seed-syllable *phriṃ*. The complete mantra is *oṃ phriṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.68] Now he describes the mudrā: "Both," and so forth. Having formed two vajra-fists, one should extend the two middle fingers and, having made those two fingers kiss each other at their tips, the mudrā should be performed. One should show this to Jñānaḍākinī. *Oṃ hūṃ svāhā* is its mantra. [2.3.69] "The hands," and so forth: Having formed the vajrāñjali, one should repeatedly touch and move the pair of middle fingers with the two *vṛddhāṅguṣṭha* (thumb-like) fingers; this is the mudrā of Vajraḍākinī. *Oṃ a svāhā* is its mantra.

[2.3.70] "Equal," and so forth: having bound two fists equally, one should extend the two thumbs; this is the *ghorī* mudrā. Its mantra is *oṃ ā svāhā*. [2.3.71] "In this," and so forth: having bound this very same mudrā, one should extend the two little fingers; this is the *vettālī* mudrā. Its mantra is *oṃ ā³ svāhā*.

[2.3.72] "Atretyādi" (beginning with "here"): having bound this very mudrā, one should extend the two middle fingers; this is the mudrā of Caṇḍālī. "Oṃ āṃ svāhā" is its mantra. "The right mudrā has been explained": the meaning is that the mudrā of Caṇḍālī is on the right. "This set of four mudrās": the sense is that this is the set of four mudrās belonging to the four Yoginīs.

[2.3.73] “Vajra” and so forth: having formed two *vajra*-fists (*vajramuṣṭi*) and extended the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), one should cause the tips of each to touch the tips of the other. This is the single mudrā for the four deities beginning with Siṃhī who reside in the corners; however, their mantras are distinct. One should display the mudrā to Siṃhī with the mantra *oṃ ṛ svāhā*, to Vyāghrī with *oṃ ṝ svāhā*, to Jambukī with *oṃ ḷ svāhā*, and to Ulūkī with *oṃ ḹ svāhā*.

[2.3.74] "Two hands," and so forth: having extended both hands and placed them over the mouth, one should utter the mantra *oṃ phuṃ svāhā*; thereafter, while pronouncing the syllable *phaḥ* in successive order, one should release the mudrā. This is the mudrā of the guardian of the eastern gate. [2.3.75] "On the head," and so forth: having formed the *sampuṭa-añjali* (the hollowed-cupped palms) upon the head, one should hold it there. This is the *dīpinī-mudrā*. The mantra is *oṃ pheṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.76] *Praṇāma* and so forth: Just as the *añjali* is performed for the purpose of salutation, so should it be done. Furthermore, it should be placed at the mouth preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*; this is the *cūṣiṇī-mudrā*. Its mantra is *oṃ phoṃ svāhā*. [2.3.77] *Āvarta* and so forth: Having performed the turning of a lotus with both hands and again forming the *añjali*, one should place it at the location of the *bhaga*; this is the *kāmbojikā-mudrā*. Its mantra is *oṃ phriṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.78] Now, showing the mantras and mudrās for fragrance (*gandha*) and the other [offerings], he says: "Having prostrated," and so forth. Extending the right hand and holding it in the gesture of anointing with fragrance is the *gandhamudrā*. The mantra is: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. [2.3.79] "Amṛta," and so forth: "Amṛta" is the letter *sa*. Regarding "of the *repha* and the *bindu*": a *repha* is placed below the *sa* and a *bindu* above it; thus, it becomes *sraṃ*. The complete mantra is: *oṃ sraṃ svāhā*. By joining the thumb and index finger of the very same *gandhamudrā*, one obtains the *puṣpamudrā*.

[2.3.80] Regarding the rule *vargapūrvakapūrvasya*: the "group preceded by a class" (*vargapūrvaka*) is the *ka*-class (*kavarga*). Its "preceding" member is the letter *ka*. Below this is the vowel *u* and above it is the nasal dot (*bindu*), according to the statement to be made later in verse 83b: *nādabinduṃ tu*. Thus, it becomes *kuṃ*. The complete mantra is *oṃ kuṃ svāhā*.
[2.3.81] The incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrā*) is formed simply by raising the middle finger of the very same flower mudrā (*puṣpamudrā*).

[2.3.82] *Navāntabīja* means "the ninth and the final seed-syllable"; thus, *navāntabīja* is the letter *kṣa*. It is the ninth because it is counted starting from the letter *ya*. Below this [letter *kṣa*] is the vowel *u*, and above it is the nasal dot (*bindu*). Therefore, it becomes *kṣuṃ*. Forming a fist with the right hand and extending the thumb constitutes the *dīpamudrā* (lamp gesture). The mantra is: *oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.83] “Taking the third of the first group”: the first group is the *ka*-group (*kavarga*); its third is the letter *ga*. From the oral instruction, the short vowel *u* represents the *nāda*. The *bindu* is the *anusvāra*. With the *u* and the *bindu* above and below the *ga*, it becomes *guṃ*. [2.3.84] “Two,” etc.: having extended both hands, one should move the two thumbs and the two middle fingers; this is the *balimudrā*. The mantra is *oṃ guṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.85] One should perform the worship with perfumes and so forth according to the appropriate application by means of the yoga of mantra and mudrā. "One should worship with these through reality" means: one should worship with this *bali*-reality; "all deities" is the ellipsis. He describes the *bali*: "The *adaityābali* is as before. That in which there are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the five goads (*pañcāṅkuśa*), raw fish, meat, onions, and so forth, is the *adaityābali*. The sense is that the deity-yogi should offer the *bali* with those substances—such as flowers, incense, and so on—along with the previously mentioned mantras and mudrās.

He says this very thing: "five," and so forth. "The former" refers to those well-known as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). The "cow-products" (*gokudahanāḥ*) are called the "five goads" (*pañcāṅkuśāḥ*); they are called "goads" because they pull one toward the desired accomplishment (*abhimatāṃ siddhim*). The rest is easily understood. Regarding "the mudrā and mantra": these are the previously mentioned *bali*-mudrā and mantra. He describes the twenty-fold worship to be performed at the time of the *bali* offering and so forth, beginning with the words "afterwards," etc.

[2.3.87] “In the form of a song of the syllable *hūṃ*”: the meaning is that one should perform what is about to be described simultaneously with the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. “The delighter of the previous Yoginīs”: the meaning is that this is primarily for the purpose of pleasing the Yoginīs. With the words “the two vajra-fists,” etc., he demonstrates the twentyfold worship. Having placed the two vajra-fists on the two hips by means of the gesture of holding the vajra and bell, one should move the hips, limbs, and head while preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*.
[2.3.88] He says this very thing: “with the syllable *hūṃ*,” and so forth. [2.3.89–91] “With the form of *phoṃ*”: by means of the gesture of the *kāhalā* (trumpet).
[2.3.92] "In the form of a musical instrument" means in the form of a bronze cymbal (*kaṃsatāla*) and so forth.
[2.3.93–96] "In the form of a banner": having raised the left hand upward, one should extend the right arm over it.
[2.3.97–98] "In the form of a flag": one should extend only the right arm.

[2.3.99] "In the shape of an umbrella": the meaning is that one should perform the mimetic gesture (*abhinaya*) of holding an umbrella with both hands. [2.3.100] "In the shape of a *mauñjī* (girdle)": by means of the mimetic gesture of playing an upright drum (*ūrdhvamardala*).
[2.3.101–106] "In the shape of a *mardala*": the meaning is that one should perform the mimetic gesture of playing a horizontal drum (*tiryaṅmardala*).

[2.3.107] "One should worship all things as the eight yoginīs in reality": by means of these objects consisting of the symbolic gestures (*abhinaya*) of the vajra, vajra-bell, and so forth, one should worship the eight yoginīs primarily in their true nature (*tattvataḥ*). That very thing is the form of the song, the *hūṃ* syllable manifested from oneself: the song has the *hūṃ* syllable as its primary element, which is: "Pay homage to the one whose form is causeless, who is full of desire, and who is the savior of beings! Hūṃ for that, hūṃ for that, hūṃ for that, hūṃ for you! (4.4.93)
And so forth. "That very thing" refers to what is well-known. "Created by oneself" means that it is to be sung by oneself. By this, the worship through song is shown.

[2.3.108] Showing the worship through praise, he says: *vajja hu*, etc. This is a praise common to both male and female deities. *Vajja hu* means: O Vajra, because you consist of the indestructible *dharmakāya*.

*Surata* means the performance of the welfare of sentient beings; the five eyes—namely, the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye—are capable in that regard. He whose vision of the world consists in the perception of the welfare [of beings] by means of those [eyes] is *suratasamarthalocanadarśana*. The vocative form of that is *suraasamatthaloaṇadaṃsaṇae*.

It does not decay, thus it is the "imperishable" (*akṣara*), which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*). Its state is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such as the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth. That which has this as its intrinsic nature is "one whose intrinsic nature is the state of the imperishable" (*akṣarabhāvasvabhāva*); the vocative of that is *akkharabhāvasahāvu*. In a world empty of intrinsic nature, one causes one's own mind to sport—that is, to play—thus [one is] "the sporter in emptiness" (*śūnyavilāsana*); the vocative of that is *suṇṇuvilāsaṇae*.

[2.3.109] "The marrow (*majjā*) is the reality (*tattva*) that is liberated from both the existence and non-existence of phenomena (*dharmas*); because it is known through that specific distinction, one is called 'one who has realized the marrow liberated from existence and non-existence' (*bhāvābhāvavimuttamajjavijāṇia*). Regarding the phrase *bhañjia akkharu savva*: the meaning is having broken—that is, having abandoned—all expressive forms of words. To the question of what was done after that, he says: *sesuvicintiae*;
this is an address to one who has been contemplated by means of the remainder, which is the ineffable form; thus, 'one who has contemplated the remainder' (*sesuvicintiae*)."

[2.3.110] *Dvandvāliṅganayogasalilakāryaka*: "embracing" (*āliṅgana*) refers to the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*); "yoga" is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by means of that; "water" (*salila*) is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), which is itself the "effect" (*kārya*); one who acts through that is "one for whom embracing, yoga, water, and effect are the work" (*dvandvāliṅganayogasalilakāryaka*). The vocative address to him is *dondāliṅgaṇajouśalilākajjiae*. *Mokkhavipāviae*: he who has thoroughly attained (*susthu prāpya*) the non-dual Dharma, which is selflessness (*nairātmya*), and has specifically reached liberation (*mokṣa*). The vocative address to him is *mokkhavipāviae*.

[2.3.111] For the sake of sentient beings who are deluded by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) as being pleasant, he is free from attachment even to liberation (*mokṣa*) through that liberation; his address is *suhasaṃsāravimohia-mokkhavivajjie*.
By means of wisdom (*prajñā*), there is no remaining in existence (*bhava*); by means of compassion (*karuṇā*), there is no abiding in quiescence (*śama*).

Because of this statement: by the words "embracing" (*dondāliṅgaṇa*) and so forth, the perfection of the means for one's own and others' welfare is expressed; by "the Dharma is imperishable" (*dhammu adaia*) and so forth, the perfection of one's own welfare; and by "in the blissful saṃsāra" (*suhasaṃsāra*) and so forth, the perfection of others' welfare. Having thus addressed the Blessed One who is distinguished by these qualities, someone praising him says: "savva... and so forth. "By the nature of all" (*savvasahāveṇa*) means in every way, that is, by body, speech, and mind; and "the yoginīs were made to dance by you in intoxication" (*joiṇi mattaviṇacciae*) is the meaning of that [phrase]. *savvasahāveṃ joiṇi mattaviṇacciae* is its sense.

[2.3.112] Regarding "pañca vī" and so forth: the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*) is the reality (*tattva*) of the Buddhas; it should be understood that you have specifically characterized even the five yoginīs as the reality of the Buddha. This is the meaning of the phrase *pañca vi yoiṇi buddhatattvavilakkhiae*. By this, the Dharmakāya of the Blessed One is indicated. The remainder of the sense is: "By means of manifold illusory forms (*māyā*), sentient beings have been matured by you. From this, the Nirmāṇakāya is also shown.

[2.3.112] By means of the *vajra* of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), that by which the task characterized by non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*) has been thoroughly accomplished (*susārita*)—that is, realized—he is one whose task is thoroughly accomplished by the *vajra* (*vajrasusāritakārya*). This is an address to him: "O *vajrasusāritakāja*! Having thus addressed him, he states what was said: "Dhamma," and so forth.

Because they uphold characteristics such as life, death, pleasure, and pain, sentient beings are "dharmas"; the meaning of *dhammavimohiae* is that you have, by means of a distinguished sequence in the form of teaching the Dharma, turned back their afflicted delusion—the word "by you" being understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, the Saṃbhogakāya has been revealed. Now, having awakened the sentient beings, he says: *ṇamate*, etc. O sentient beings! Pay homage to that Blessed One who has become thus! And pay homage to that Blessed One who is the Essential Dharma (*sāradharma*); this is to be connected with what precedes.

"Sārudhammu jjo" has been explained as "and together with the Dharma. It should be construed as: "Bow down to him by whom the Yoginīs were liberated. "Joiṇimokkhiae" is well-established [as meaning "by whom the Yoginīs were liberated"].

[2.3.114] He speaks the *Saṃskṛtastava* (Praise of the Perfected), beginning with "Homage be... and so forth. Yoga is the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and skillful means; that itself is the Lord (*adhipa*) because of its excellence. One who liberates sentient beings by means of that is the "Liberator of Sentient Beings through Yoga" (*yogādhipasattvamocaka*). Alternatively, "O Lord of Yoga" (*yogādhipa*) is a separate word; the sense is: "Homage to you, O Blessed One, who are thus distinguished. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the *dharmadhātu*. Those born from that are "sons of the Self" (*ātmaja*). He whose sons are all [beings] is the "Father of All" (*sarvātmaja*). "With single-mindedness" (*ekabhāvataḥ*) means with a unified mind.

[2.3.115] Saṃsāra itself is an ocean because it is difficult for the foolish to fathom. Delusion (moha) is the obscuration of the knowable. Homage be to the one who cuts through delusion for those situated in the ocean of saṃsāra; "to him" is the ellipsis. He is "the one in truth" (tattvaika) because he is supreme by virtue of his reality; since there is no other like you who knows reality, this is an address as "O Tattvaika."

[2.3.116] Regarding *iti viśeṣataḥ*: the meaning is "specifically. By the words *stava*, *gīta*, and *stotra*, one means "praise-song" (*stutigīta*). With that, one should perform an offering (*upahāra*), that is, worship (*pūjā*). Praise (*stuti*) is the proclamation of true qualities (*sadguṇa*) through the declaration of reality (*tattvākhyāna*). A song in the form of praise is a "praise-song" (*stutigīta*). In the case of songs such as *praṇamāma* (4.4.93), there is merely a song because of the brevity of the reality described; therefore, there is a distinction between these two.

[2.3.117] Immediately after the praise, one should ring the bell. This very point is stated with the words beginning with "hūṃkāra. Regarding the phrase "and by that which is interspersed with the syllable hūṃ": one should ring the bell as distinguished by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. The meaning is that the ringing of the bell is preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. [2.3.118] The word "atha" (then) means immediately after the sound of the bell. The word "akārṣīt" (he performed) means "one should perform.
[2.3.119] He states the threefold aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) with the words beginning with "vajrāñjali. Having placed the vajra-gesture of joined palms at the heart...

[2.3.120–122] ... One should recite the three mantras beginning with *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ*. [2.3.123] "Having performed the *kamalāvarta* [gesture], one should visualize a lotus in the right hand; having released the vajra in the left, one should display the *mahāmudrā*. This means that after performing the *kamalāvarta*, one should visualize a lotus vessel in the right hand, and by pressing the little finger with the thumb of the left hand, one should apply the left hand to the lotus vessel—thus one should display the *mahāmudrā*. [2.3.124] Its mantra is: *oṃ ha ho hrīḥ svāhā*.

[2.3.125] Therefore, he says: "the mantra of Mahāmudrā. [2.3.126] Even in the tasting of *madana* elsewhere, these two alone are the mudrā and the mantra. For this very reason, he says: "And at the same time, the yogins should contemplate all the deities. "At the same time" (*samam*) means simultaneously. "And at that time" (*tāpi ca*) refers to that purification of *madana*. "All the deities" (*sarvadevābhi*) means that the yoga of all the deities must be performed instantaneously by the yogin; this is the intended meaning. As for the worldly [practices] and so forth, for the wise, the external maṇḍala is merely imagined.

The worldly and supreme knowers who are guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla)—for the purpose of offering oblations (bali) to them—the outer mandala is prepared. It is called "outer" because it is situated outside of oneself. There, having drawn a triangular mandala with red sandalwood or saffron, one draws a circle in its center, and within that, a mandala of nine squares by the intersection of four lines.

There, in the eastern and other compartments, respectively, are these Kṣetrapālas: Kṛṣṇarudra, Mahārudra, Devadatta, Kṛṣṇakarāla, Bībhatsa, Nanda, Atīta, and Vināyaka; each is surrounded by four of the thirty-two Yoginīs, beginning with Cāmuṇḍī and Ghorī, their hands raised holding their own weapons. And in the central compartment is Jñānaḍākinī, consisting of thirteen aspects. Thus the outer maṇḍala is to be visualized.

[2.3.127] "Smeared separately with perfume," and so forth: "separately" means by means of perfume and other substances that have not been used elsewhere. "One should cause the separate union to be meditated upon": the intended meaning is that at the time of offering the *bali*, one should become the essence of the maṇḍala of the Jñānaḍākinīs. "Separateness" refers to the distinction from the maṇḍala of the Jñānaḍākinīs situated within the external maṇḍala.

[2.3.128] Regarding the phrase "resting upon the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛtasamāśritam*): the meaning is that one should offer the five nectars contained within a vessel such as a conch shell (*śukti*). Therefore, he says: "one should meditate upon the conch shell and so forth. By the word *śukta*, he means *śukti*. Regarding the syllable *ha* and so forth: one should meditate on the syllable *ha* within the five nectars, and it removes their natural color. And when the syllable *ho* is meditated upon, it destroys their natural odor.

[2.3.129] Furthermore, the syllable *hrīḥ*, when meditated upon here, destroys ordinary vigor (*prākṛtavīrya*). The meaning is that one should meditate upon the three Lords of the World and so forth, in their proper order, by pronouncing these three syllables—which are of three kinds according to their phonemes and so on. The sense is that one should meditate upon Lokeśvara with the syllable *ha*, Vairocana with *ho*, and Akṣobhya with *hrīḥ* within the *pañcāmṛta*.

[2.3.130] Therefore, he says "Padmeśvara," and so forth, in order to show that the color and other qualities will become completely pure. Padmeśvara is Amitābha; he himself is Lokeśvara. He produces a golden-colored radiance of form. The phrase "of the five nectars" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And Lokeśvara, possessing a golden luster, is to be meditated upon. Regarding the phrase "one should contemplate the scented water": he brings about—that is, he produces—the nature or essence of a state that is fragrant like scented water. Who is this? He says: "and Surocana. This means Vairocana.

And this [deity] is white. Regarding "Vajreśvara, Vajrapāṇi, the Taste": he produces the taste, which is the pure essence; "Vajreśvara" refers to Akṣobhya, and he is Vajrapāṇi, the one with the vajra in his hand. And this [deity] is black. Having destroyed ordinary color and so forth, Speech and the others produce something else entirely that is purified. Concluding this very point, he says: "One should make known through the three deities by means of the threefold [colors]. The meaning is that one should meditate upon the three deities by means of the three colors, such as yellow and so forth.

[2.3.131] Now he shows the purification of *madana* (intoxicant) for the purpose of worshipping the *yoginīs*: "On the left, the moon, the hand," and so forth. Having visualized the moon on the palm of the left hand, one should visualize within its center the syllable of nectar, the letter *sa*. One should visualize it joined with the *praṇava*, which is the measure of all-knowingness; that is, *soṃ*. And "the thumb is indeed earth": the thumb has the nature of earth.

[2.3.132] “The nameless one is Sumeru”: the nameless one has the nature of Mount Sumeru. “Nectar” (amṛtā): the meaning is that nectar is intoxication (*madana*). “With the two strengths” (*balinā*): by means of the two strengths—the thumb and the ring finger—which have the nature of Wisdom and Means and the nature of the earth and Sumeru respectively—one churns; thus, “by churning. And their status as strength is for the sake of producing nectar. When this is done, the intoxication attains the state of nectar; therefore, the meaning is that this is “strength,” which is the inherent power of this substance. “One should make known the *m-ambhaḥ* in three ways.”

The meaning is that one should meditate upon that water as nectar (*amṛta*) by means of the mantra *ha-ho-hrīḥ* according to the previously mentioned sequence. Having placed the *madana* [substance] on the palm of the left hand and visualized the syllable *soṃ* above it, one should rub it with the thumb and ring finger. Then, having visualized the forms of the World-Lords (*lokeśvara*) and others by means of the syllable *ha* and so forth, one should offer the *madanachiḍriṅga* separately to each of the Yoginīs individually from those [substances] using the thumb and ring finger, while reciting their names.

[2.3.133] Therefore he says: "separately," and so forth. *Chidriṅgā* is the scattering of fluids. Regarding "with the thumb": with the thumb and the ring finger. Regarding "afterwards," and so forth: thereafter, one should make one's own mind into the nature of the Knowledge-Ḍākinī by means of one's own being.

[2.3.134] Regarding "the five-fold *sphoṭa* of the *stūpa*": *Sphuṭāḥ* means they burst forth or perish; thus, the *skandhas* are the *sphoṭas*. The meaning is that the *stūpa*, which is the body, consists of five *sphoṭas*. One should bathe that with the three types of *chidriṅgas*. The sense is that, having worshipped the *yoginīs* with the *madanachidriṅgas* held in the hands, one who possesses the yoga of the *Jñānaḍākinī* should also worship oneself with the three *chidriṅgas*. He states the location of the *chidriṅgas* within oneself as "on the tip of the tongue," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should worship oneself by placing a single *chiḍriṅga* in each of these three locations: at the tip of the tongue (*bindu*), in the middle of the *ūrṇā*, and on the crown of the head (*ūrdhvānāma*).

[2.3.135] In the circle of the Gaṇas, he utters a verse on the gift of passion (*madanadāna*): "Having seen," and so forth. "The dharmas have been purified and seen" (*pecchia sohia dhammu*)—this is the meaning of this phrase. Because there is no dogmatic adherence (*anabhiniviṣṭatvāt*). To the question "What by this?", he says: "Abandon the notion of nihilism" (*ṇahisaṃbhāvaṇu mellu*). Abandon the conception of non-existence (*nāstika-saṃbhāvanā*), for all dharmas do indeed exist; however, the point is that they are utterly pure. Consequently, the distinction between Brahmins and others is merely unreal. He states this very point in the verse beginning with "Brahmin" (*bamhaṇu*).

Brahmins, dogs, and outcasts are eaten with a single nature; that is to say, they are grasped by a single nature. This is because the semen, blood, and so forth, as well as passion, hatred, and so forth, are entirely indistinguishable among Brahmins and the others; thus, there is no real distinction. What then? It is merely conceptual. By the word *brāhmaṇa*, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are meant. By the word *kukkura*, animals in general are meant. By the word *caṇḍāla*, all those born of low status are meant. Although the Śūdra is not explicitly mentioned, he should be understood [to be included].

Since even that is established as being of the nature of color (*varṇatva*), there is nothing whatsoever that is either pure or impure; therefore, the intended meaning is "drink all conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). [2.3.136] Regarding the passage beginning with "by these": the meaning is that by reciting this verse, the vessel of intoxication (*madana*) should be given to the male and female practitioners (*yogi-yoginī*).

[2.3.137] Regarding the passage beginning with "the *kamalāvarta* however," he speaks while explaining what was previously mentioned: "the *kamalāvarta*, however, is of the former. Regarding "with the mind like a crystal" (*cittasphaṭikacetasā*): it means with a mind free from the stains of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), like a crystal. The passage beginning with "the triple-needle" (*trisūcī*) is easy to understand.

[2.3.138] Immediately after the section on giving (*dāna*), he states the verse concerning the apprehension of passion (*madana*): "Welcome," and so forth. It has come by itself, that is, it is realized through its own nature, because it is self-cognizable. He asks: "What is this? and answers: "Dhamma" (*dharma*). *Dharma* is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) of entities such as the aggregates (*skandha*). Furthermore, that is suchness (*tathatā*). And this is non-dual knowledge (*advayajñāna*). And that is the Tathāgata. He asks: "What is the qualification of this *dharma*? and answers: "Priceless," and so forth. That for which no price (*argha*)—that is, worship—is found anywhere is "priceless" (*anargha*).

The meaning is that there is no object in the three worlds worthy of his worship. The sense is that awakening itself is his true worship. Regarding the phrase *rāamalāgatae*: *rāga* is craving; that itself is the stain (*mala*) because it defiles the mind. "Come from that" means having slightly departed from it or fallen away from it. Because of the presence of pure passion (*viśuddharāga*), he has not fallen away from it entirely. Now, one might ask: why is only passion mentioned, setting aside afflictions such as hatred and the rest? True; pleasant sensation is the primary cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and the cause of that is passion.

"Through the purification of passion (*rāga*), cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—along with its members and in its entirety—becomes purified. Regarding the words "grasping," and so forth: since [the mind] is free from the stain of passion, there is "grasping" (*grāha*), which is attachment (*abhiniveśa*); "non-grasping" (*agrāha*) is the opposite of that; the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is devoid of both. The sense is that it is even devoid of the attachment [expressed by the thoughts] "I am attached" or "I am unattached. The connection is: "Bow down to that Dharma characterized in such a way. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "For the sake of reality" (*tattvārtha*). That is, for the sake of reflecting upon reality. The sense is: "By means of this prostration, may the mind abide in reality."

[2.3.139] "With this verse, the recipient should receive"—this is the intoxication (*madana*). Therefore, he says: "with this verse," and so forth. He states the reason for giving and receiving the gift: "for the sake of the cause of the accomplishment of yoga. Yoga is the non-perverted state; the meaning is "equality of time" (*samasamayatva*). Its accomplishment is that by which there is the purpose characterized by eating, drinking, and so on; that itself is the cause. Regarding the giving and receiving of the vessel of intoxication with the verse: "just as," and so forth: "just as one acts," and so on.

The sense is that the yogi should practice with whatever is obtained; all of this is pure and holy for yogis. Regarding the statement "as one pleases": after giving the *madana*, the yogi should say, "as one pleases."

[2.3.141] He provides the detailed explanation for what was indicated by the statement "the outer mandala is fashioned" (126d): "with a red mandala," and so forth. The sense is that, having drawn a square mandala with saffron or red sandalwood, one should then draw a triangular mandala outside of it. He also states the mudrā and mantra for the invocation of the external deities: "with the two vajra-fists," and so forth. Having formed two vajra-fists, one should join their backs together...

[2.3.142] ... Having encircled the left little finger with the right little finger, having raised both index fingers, and having bent the right index finger and placed the left index finger upon its back, one should form the mudrā.
[2.3.143] Its mantra is: *oṃ* and so forth.
[2.3.144] Therefore, it says: "the invocation mudrā and mantra."

[2.3.145] The passage beginning with *rakta* is easy to understand. He states the sacrificial substances (*balidravya*) with the words beginning with *ohāra*. Raw meat and so forth are designated by the term *ohārabali*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), onions, garlic, and the like are included. A great abundance of items such as raw meat, fish, onions, and so on, should be placed in the vessel for the offering. [2.3.146] All of this is edible. He says exactly that with the word *khādya*. "All substances" refers to *madana*. And all of that should be offered according to what is available. For that is of many kinds. Thus he says: "The preparation of grains, bark, and so forth, is to be known from worldly convention."
Surā is considered to be maireya, which is a fermented infusion of the juices of sugarcane and other such substances.

Thus. Regarding "well-conjoined with the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛtasuyuñjitam*): therein the five nectars are to be offered. And that is "well-conjoined" because their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been placed [upon them]. Regarding "on the left side," and so forth: having placed the left hand on the left side of the vessel for the offering (*balibhāṇḍa*), having raised the right arm, and having formed the vajra-fist (*vajramuṣṭi*), one should display it by extending the index finger (*tarjanī*). This very point he states: "One should display the wrathful giver. The wrathful one is the index finger.

Alternatively, having conceived the *bali* offering as consisting of two portions, one should present the left portion to the maṇḍala-cakra and the right to the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*). In this context, by the word "vessel" (*bhāṇḍa*) the maṇḍala-cakra is meant, and by the word "wrathful ones" (*krodha*) the guardians of the directions are meant.

[2.3.147] One should invoke the world-protectors with the mantra beginning with *oṃ ekavṛkṣe* and ending with *dhanus tathā* (152d). The term "vessel" (*bhājana*) refers to a water-receptacle. The phrase "mātaṅgāṃ tu" means in the house of a *caṇḍāla*. Those who dwell in solitary trees and so forth—such as Kṛṣṇarudra and others—should be invoked and ushered in into the previously mentioned squares that have been consecrated, together with their retinues.

[2.3.148] Among them, Kṛṣṇarudra is in the east; Mahārudra is in the north; Devadatta is in the west; Kṛṣṇa is in the south; Karāla is in the northeast (aiśānī); Bībhatsa is in the southeast (āgneyī); Nandātīta is in the southwest (nairṛtī); and Vināyaka is in the northwest (vāyavī). These are three-eyed and four-armed, equipped with the aforementioned weapons, adorned with garments and ornaments, and located in the directions starting from the east, having colors—black, yellow, white, and red—respectively. Those situated in the northeast and so forth have the colors black, yellow, black, red, red, white, white, and yellow.

[2.3.149] In front of Kṛṣṇarudra is Cāmuṇḍī, on the left is Ghorī, behind is Bībhatsā, and on the right is Umādevī. These have the colors of Ḍākinī and the others in their respective order. To the east, north, west, and south of Mahārudra are Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā, who have the colors of Dīpinī and the others.

[2.3.150] To the east, north, west, and south of Devadatta are Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, Sthūlakālī, and Indrī; their colors are those of Cūṣiṇī and the others. To the east, north, west, and south of Kṛṣṇa are Candrī, Ghorī, Duṣṭī, and Lambakī; their colors are those of Kāmbojī and the others. To the east, north, west, and south of Karāla are Tridaśeśvarī—[2.3.151]—Kāmbojī, Dīpinī, and Cūṣiṇī; their colors are those of Cāmuṇḍī and the others. To the east, north, west, and south of Bībhatsa are Ghorarūpā, Mahārūpā, Daṃṣṭrārūpā, and Karālinī; their colors are those of Candrī and the others.

[2.3.152] To the east, north, west, and south of Nanda are Kapālamālāmālinī, Khaṭvāṅgāyī, Maharddhikā, and Bhadrakālī, possessing the colors [of their respective directions]. To the east, north, west, and south of Vināyaka are Jayā and others, possessing the colors [of their respective directions], with swords in hand, axes in hand, vajras in hand, and bows in hand. These, from Cāmuṇḍī up to Maharddhikā, are playful goddesses, holding flowers and other items for the fivefold offerings in their hands. The four beginning with Khaḍgahastā have symbols corresponding to their names.

[2.3.153] "The five Yoginīs in the Great Reality (mahātattva) are the accomplishers of all desires": Dīpinī and the others are thus described. "Yogamaṇḍalamahārājñī Vajreśvarī" refers to the mandala of Jñānaḍākinī. "And likewise the Lord" refers to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas).

[2.3.154] Regarding "the great body of the Tathāgata" (*tathāgatamahākāya*): the meaning is that these are the forms of the Tathāgatas. To the question "How so?", he says: "created by the stainless yoga" (*nirañjayogasṛṣṭika*). *Añja* means "stain," which is to say, affliction (*kleśa*). That in which stain has departed is "stainless" (*nirañja*). *Yoga* is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). *Sṛṣṭikāḥ* means "created" or "produced. Thus, the meaning of the term *nirañjayogasṛṣṭika* is "those created—that is, accomplished—by means of stainless yoga. "By this command of Vajreśvarī, she summons all who possess all things."

By this [phrase] "idam" (this), the command of Vajreśvarī—the mistress of the maṇḍala, the Knowledge-Ḍākinī—is meant. By this command of the Knowledge-Ḍākinī, characterized by the previously mentioned mantra, one should invoke the external deities in every way and perform what is about to be described; such is the intended meaning.
[2.3.155] He states that very point: "Oṃ ka kka," and so forth.

[2.3.156] “Having filled the mouth with nectar” (*amṛtamukham āpūrya*): “Nectar” (*amṛta*) refers to the *bali* offering. Having invoked all the deities into the mandala by means of the previously mentioned mantra and having visualized them, one should fill the mouths of the deities with the mantra beginning with *oṃ ka kka*, etc.; this is the intended meaning. “The ritual of the feet (*padakarman*) and so forth has been contemplated”: that which has been thus contemplated is designated by the term “ritual of the feet. And that is the most excellent. Alternatively: having filled one’s own mouth with nectar—that is, with *madana*—one should cast that *madana* into the *bali* offering in the form of a *pīkā*.

This very thing is the "foot-rite" (*padakarma*); such is the instruction. Some say that by the term "foot-rite" dance (*nṛtya*) is meant. The sense is that one should subsequently perform the dance with the "vajra-step. Regarding the phrase "one should visualize," and so forth: the conclusion is that the offering (*bali*) should be given by a yogin or a yoginī through such a visualization. To the question, "What would result from that? he says: "All rites are accomplished. This means rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), and so on. [2.3.157] Now he states the mudrā for the offering: "The vajra-fists," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

[2.3.158] *Oṃ bhakṣa*, etc., is its mantra. These two, the mudrā and the mantra, have been shown according to the detailed method (*vistarapakṣa*); previously, they were shown in an abbreviated form (*saṃkṣipta*). [2.3.159] “One should join them according to the rite”: wherever there is a connection with a particular rite, the offering (*bali*) should be given at that very place by means of this procedure. [2.3.160] The passage beginning with “for pacification” (*śānti*) is easy to understand. “The offering through the reality of the external”: the meaning is that this is the reality of the external offering. By means of this reality, the offering should be given to the external deities. And by that, all rites are accomplished. Therefore, he says: “One should accomplish the offering, the rites, and so forth.”

[2.3.161] Now he speaks of the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*): "Now," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "but the special worship" (*pūjāviśeṣaṃ tu*): "special" (*viśeṣa*) means distinguished (*viśiṣṭā*) worship. For it is distinguished because it is performed by Vairocana and the others. To the question, "In what way is it distinguished even thus?", he says: "free from ritual and non-ritual" (*kalpākalpavivarjitam*). That which is conceptualized is "ritual" (*kalpa*), meaning a procedure such as purity and so on; its opposite is "non-ritual" (*akalpa*), meaning the absence of such a procedure. Since the yogin is free from both of these, [the worship is distinguished].

Indeed, the practice of Vairocana and the others is for the purpose of abandoning ordinary conceptual constructions. He speaks of worship: "By means of the hook and so forth. These hooks are five; they are the five principles (*tattva*), because they consist of the deities in the form of the five [Buddhas] such as Vairocana, being the very nature of reality. One should cause [them] to act, that is, one should purify.

[2.3.162] As to what those "hooks" (aṅkuśa) are, he says: "The great hook," and so forth. "Named Mahāṅkuśa" means that the primordial source (ādi) is named Mahāṅkuśa. "Worshipped the deity of gnosis" means that the deity of gnosis is Vairocana; the meaning is that Vairocana, who is the Great Hook, was worshipped. "Vajrāṅkuśa is the primordial source" means that he is Akṣobhya. "In the Hook of the Abode is the Jewel-Bearer" means that the Hook of the Abode is the primordial source, and he is Ratnasaṃbhava.

[2.3.163] Regarding *amogharājamahāṅkuśa*: *rājamahāṅkuśa* means *rājāṅkuśa*. And here, that begins with *hā*, having the form of Amoghasiddhi. Regarding *amitābhaṃ calamaṅkuśaiḥ*: *calāṅkuśa* ends with *śvaḥ*, and that is Amitābha. These hooks (*aṅkuśa*) are to be employed in the form of Vairocana and the others, transformed from their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) which will be described later. This very point he states: "One should apply the *sarvatattva* to the five hooks and so forth.
One should meditate upon the *sarvatattva*—that is, the reality (*tattva*) of the respective deity—within the five hooks.

[2.3.164] Regarding the passage beginning with *yad īpsita*: because that which is desired—such as the great goad (*mahāṅkuśa*) and so forth—becomes empowered by reality (*tattva*). To the question "By whom is it desired?", he says: "Of all the gods. This means "of all the yoginīs. Therefore, one should please all the yoginīs with that; the meaning is that one should satisfy them. He says "without distinction" regarding how one should observe the pledge (*samaya*): "but not," and so forth. And "those who delight in desire": "desire" (*kāma*) means wish; they are "attached" (*raktāḥ*) to that. The meaning is "as much as one wishes" or "according to one's desire. One should not act in such a manner.
This is the intended meaning. For the conduct of the *samaya* is conducive to the highest good only when practiced without differentiation. Thus it has been said:
"In brief, everything should be performed in such a way that no differentiation arises;
for through the differentiation of the *samayas*, there is neither accomplishment nor a practitioner."

Thus it is said.
