But it is not "dependent upon enjoyment" (*bhogāśrita*); for "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) refers to a conditioned object (*saṃskṛta-viṣaya*), in the sense that it is enjoyed or specifically tasted. The meaning is that one who is dependent on enjoyment—that is, one who is attached to enjoyment—should not observe the *samaya*. For when [the object] is being conditioned, differentiation arises. Furthermore, the practice of the *samaya* is for the sake of non-attachment to worldly things; if there is attachment to the *samaya*, that itself is a fault.

[2.3.165] "Pure in every way": the meaning is that even regarding other things such as forms, sounds, and so forth, one should engage with them in every respect by means of non-attachment to the seen, the seer, the seeing, and so on. Even while this is the case, he says "worship" and so forth, because there would be a particularly distinguished worship of the Tathāgata. Regarding "of him" and so forth: the meaning is that in the midst of that *gaṇamaṇḍala*, the heroes—the yogins of perfectly pure conduct and unimpeded mind—should perform the union of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya-samāpatti*) through the *āli* and *kāli*.

[2.3.166] He says "alikālī" etc., meaning that by this all the *yoginīs* shall be gratified. Likewise, "tathoddhṛta" etc.: having thus produced through union the nectar—the fluid of sexual bliss—within the center of the lotus, one should taste it all oneself and offer it to the assembly (*gaṇa*). Having purified it oneself, one should taste what resides in the lotus with the tongue. Having placed it in the vessel of the lotus, one should give it to others.

[2.3.167] Therefore he says: "From the remainder," and so forth. One should give the nectar and wisdom—the flowers and so on that remain after one has personally consumed them. To whom? He says: "One should arrange the outer maṇḍala. This means one should arrange and offer them to those who have entered the outer maṇḍala, the circle of the assembly (*gaṇamaṇḍala*), and who are bound by the commitments (*sāmayika*). Afterwards, one should have them sing a song primarily consisting of the syllable *dhūṃ*. In this regard, the song is as follows: "Prostrate to the causeless form," and so on (4.4.93). He states this very point: "In the form of a song of the syllable *hūṃ*."
This is not all; rather, it is "filled with auspicious sounds. The intention is that one should also have auspicious songs sung afterwards.

[2.3.168] He states the auspicious song, beginning with *paṇamaha*. Regarding *bhāvavivajjia*: "bhāva" means arising (*utpāda*); the connection is "bow down to that which is devoid of that. The point is that arising does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), though it exists conventionally (*saṃvṛti*). Having stated the qualification by way of its own meaning (*svārtha*), he speaks by way of its meaning for others (*parārtha*), beginning with *ṇāhia*. "Nāthita" means requested or sought after. "Aṅga" refers to sentient beings (*sattva*), so called because they go to various states of existence (*gati*) under the power of karma.

That by which the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārtha*) is accomplished is a limb (*aṅga*), namely, arising (*utpāda*). Because one seeks (*nāthita*) the purpose of the limbs, it is a limb; thus [in Prakrit] it becomes *ṇāhia*, *aṅgam*, or *uaṅgu*. If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no arising at all, how can there be [arising] even for the sake of sentient beings? To this he says: "The embrace of the couple," and so forth. The union of the embrace of the couple is arising and cessation. That itself is an illusion (*māyā*), not the ultimate reality—this is the meaning. It is adorned with the illusion of the union of the embrace of the couple.

The meaning is that he abides through various emanations (*nirmāṇa*); the meaning is that he has become such for the sake of sentient beings. For his arising, too, is indeed non-arising because it does not perform the function of arising, since it arises without attachment.

[2.3.169] Immediately after the auspicious song, one should ring the bell. This very point is stated: "The auspicious song is performed at will with the resonance of the vajra-bell. Then, one should make the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*); thus he says: "With the vajra-añjali," and so forth. Having placed the vajra-añjali at the heart... [2.3.170] ... "All sentient beings," and so forth.
[2.3.171] The meaning is that after reciting up to the words "I shall compose the Yogaśāstra," one should perform the formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*).

[2.3.172] He states the dismissal of the deity (*devatāvisarjana*): having formed two *vajramuṣṭi* fists, placing the left *vajramuṣṭi* at the heart, extending the right *vajramuṣṭi*, and resting it upon the ground, one should then recite the mantra: *oṃ ātmani tiṣṭha hūṃ svāhā* (173), and dismiss Jñānaḍākinī together with her retinue, who resides in the central ninth square.
[2.3.173] He states the mantra: *oṃ ātmani tiṣṭha hūṃ svāhā*.

[2.3.174] After the dismissal of the Jñāna-Ḍākinī together with her retinue who has been summoned, one should cause the Samaya-Jñāna-Ḍākinī together with her retinue to enter into oneself by means of one's own breath; thus he says: "Afterwards," and so forth.
[2.3.175] He states the dismissal of the World Protectors (Lokapālas) and others: "Oṃ sarvaduṣṭa... and so forth.
[2.3.176] Having performed three snaps of the fingers at the same time as the recitation of the mantra, while embracing with both arms, one should dismiss the external World Protectors.

Thus, a "chapter" (*prakaraṇa*) is that in which the procedure is carried out according to the stated sequence, beginning with the yoga of the deity and ending with the *bali* offering. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Parapīṭha*, the compendium of the four seats (*catuṣpīṭha*).

[2.4.1] Now, in order to explain the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth in detail, he says: "O Blessed One," and so on. Regarding "the five nectars specifically": previously they were understood without distinction; the intention here is that one now wishes to hear about the five nectars according to their various forms and types. Regarding "by what are the five hooks?": the connection with the preceding is that one wishes to hear specifically which those five hooks mentioned before are. "By what" means "which are they? Regarding "how would the *alikāli* come to be?": this means how would the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) come to be?

[2.4.2] Regarding the phrase "of the non-dual and dual-free phenomenon" (*advayādvayadharmasya*): non-duality is suchness (*tathatā*), which is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Phenomenon" (*dharma*) means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The "non-dual phenomenon" of that which is non-dual is characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) and so forth. How could there be a conceptualization of existence or non-existence regarding that? This is the question, as before. "Conceptualization of existence and non-existence" refers to an imagination that is dissimilar to both existence and non-existence. Regarding the phrase "seals of speech, etc. (*vākyamudrādīti*): the seal of speech (*vākyamudrā*) is a verbal sign (*vākchommaka*). Regarding "of the mind" (*cittasya*): it is the seal of signs (*cihnāmudrā*).

Regarding the reading *cihnasya*, the meaning is the same: the mind-seal (*cittamudrā*) is indeed the sign-seal (*cihnamudrā*). As for the phrase "the method of the Yoga-treatise" (*yogaśāstranaya*): "Yoga" refers to the means for accomplishing feats such as medicinal elixirs (*bhaiṣajya*). A "treatise" (*śāstra*) is that by which sentient beings are taught and established in the True Dharma (*saddharma*). A "method" (*naya*) is that by which perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*) is led to or attained. It is a "Yoga-treatise" (*yogaśāstra*) because it is both yoga and a treatise; and it is the "method of the Yoga-treatise" (*yogaśāstranaya*) because it is both that Yoga-treatise and a method.

Through the accomplishment of medicines and other such means, sentient beings are led toward the path to Buddhahood by these conditions. Having entered that path, they attain perfect enlightenment through practice. Since enlightenment is attained through this very yoga in a gradual succession, that too is its method (*naya*). Alternatively, for those performing recitations and so forth for this purpose, there is first the accumulation of merit; from that, the entry onto the path; and from that, through practice, perfect enlightenment. Thus, the yoga in a gradual succession is the "method of perfect enlightenment" (*saṃbodhinaya*). The question is: how might this come to be? [2.4.3] Releasing the question, he says: "The Blessed One said," and so forth.

[2.4.4] The connection is that, first of all, "the vajra-water is presented. Regarding "the nectar-vajra-water": the nectar-vajra-water is the *bodhicitta*, which has the nature of nectar. Regarding "consisting of five": it consists of five, having the nature of the five [elements] beginning with fire. "Let it be attained" means "let it be presented. He states its fivefold nature with the words "fire," and so forth. "It becomes warm to the touch": the sense is that it is fire because of its association with the sensation of heat. "Wind is seen as smoke": the meaning is that it is wind because of the appearance of vapor like smoke.

[2.4.5] “The waters have the portion of fluidity (*dravabhāga*): that which flows downward is *drava*; it is moisture (*sneha*). A “portion” (*bhāga*) is a part. Thus, the waters consist of a portion of moisture. The word “waters” (*apaḥ*) denotes water. “The form of earth is perceived”: because the quality of solidity (*kakkhaṭatva*) is perceived, it is known as earth. “By the vajra presided over by gnosis (*jñāna*): these four elements are known, thus they are “gnoses” (*jñānāni*). Their “presiding” (*adhiṣṭhita*) is their abiding. By means of that abiding of the four elements, it is understood that space exists within the bodhicitta. “By the vajra”: [as follows].

The vajra is space because it is indivisible. Since it consists of five [elements], one should meditate upon the five deities; the meaning is that one should perform meditation—that is, conceptualization—of the five deities, namely Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, Akṣobhya, Vairocana, and Ratnasaṃbhava, within the single bodhicitta itself.

[2.4.6] He states the meditation on the five Tathāgatas, beginning with "sakala" and so forth. Regarding "apasaṃsthāna": that which has the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) or connection of water (*ap*) is "apasaṃsthāna," namely the letter *sa*. That very [letter], existing together with its parts (*kalā*), is the "sakala" moon, because the letter *sa* is the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛta*). "And likewise, *kṣaya* is fire": it destroys or burns, thus it is *kṣaya*, namely the letter *kṣa*. That very [letter] is fire, due to its similarity to fire. "And as for wind among the eternal [elements]... [and so forth].

To the question, "How then is that the seed-syllable of wind? the response is, "In the manner [of the following] illustration. Wind is the letter *ya*. Why? He says: "Of the eternal," meaning eternally. The sense is: because its nature is that of wind. Regarding "Haṃ is the witness of the earth": *haṃ* is the letter *ha*. "Earth" refers to the seed-syllable of earth. And that letter *ha* is the witness of the past and so forth. Under what condition? He says: "In the company" (*sārthe*). In a common object—that is, in a class of entities such as emptiness and the like—it is the letter *ha* that is the witness, just like the earth, and because it is the seed-syllable for the arising of the earth.

[2.4.7] "By joining with the *bindu* and the *nāda*": the sense is that these four seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*. Thus, they become *suṃ*, *yuṃ*, *kṣuṃ*, and *huṃ*. "Knowledge is the fivefold syllable": knowledge is the syllable *hūṃ*. And that is the "syllable" (*akṣara*). It is called a "syllable" because it does not perish (*na kṣarati*); it is space (*ākāśa*). The meaning is that it is the seed-syllable of space. "Fivefold" means five seed-syllables. Regarding "there, in the center, of the moon":
In that regard, within the bodhicitta is the lunar disc; and upon that lunar disc is the syllable of nectar, the letter *a*, situated in the center—that is, located in the middle of the lunar disc.

[2.4.8] Regarding the statement "five, five" should be said: the meaning is that each individual [nectar] consists of five nectars. Just as in the case of the *bodhicitta*, one performs the consecration by means of the seed-syllables of the five elements whose nature is the five Buddhas—namely *suṃ*, *yuṃ*, *kṣuṃ*, *huṃ*, and *hūṃ*—which have the essential nature of Akṣobhya, Amoghasiddhi, Amitābha, Vairocana, and Ratnasaṃbhava; having done so, one should contemplate a moon-maṇḍala above that, and upon that, the syllable *a*. The same applies to the other four nectars as well.

Since each individual nectar (*amṛta*) consists of five aspects, the five nectars together consist of twenty-five aspects. That in which the five nectars arise is [called] the "five nectars. Regarding the phrase "the purification of oneself by the vajra-water": it should be understood that when there is such purification by the vajra-water, the yogi becomes liberated from existence and non-existence through enjoyment. Since the vajra-water is illustrative, it is established that by partaking of the other nectars as well, one is liberated from existence and non-existence.

Existence (*bhāva*) is arising, non-existence (*abhāva*) is non-arising; it is devoid of both because it has existed for a long time. Therefore, "delusion is far away": since it is thus, the meaning is that delusion—the cognition of impurity—should be abandoned from afar. Alternatively, when the *bodhicitta* is consumed by such a sequence, delusion remains far away. In this same way, it should be understood regarding the other [nectars] as well.

[2.4.9] Regarding "external nectar" and so forth: just as an external substance, when processed by the cooking of fire, becomes a fine substance like nectar, so too are Vairocana and the others located in the belly and other parts. Because they are produced within the belly, the belly is Vairocana; by the word "and so forth," Akṣobhya and the others are included. To the question of what kind of things these become nectar, he says: "The leftovers are the fire of gnosis. This means they are attended by the fire of purifying gnosis—that is, they are cooked by the fire of gnosis.

The meaning is that just as an external object becomes excellent when cooked, so too Vairocana and the others, being cooked by the fire of gnosis, become excellent, having their natures liberated. Nevertheless, he asks "Who are they? and answers: "Viṭ and Drava. Viṭ is Vairocana; Drava is Akṣobhya.

[2.4.10] Regarding "the fire-cooking of the fires": the sense is that first they were cooked by the fire of the body, and now they are cooked by the fire of gnosis (*jñānāgni*). One should consume the *bodhicitta*, Vairocana, and Akṣobhya, which have been cooked by the fire of purification. This very point is stated as: "But in its center, the oblation. The oblation is to be offered into the center of that body. Regarding "with the seed-syllable of whose water of the vajra, the recitation is with seed": one should recite that very seed-syllable by which the water of the vajra was purified.

It should be understood that this is for the sake of purification during the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of wisdom and means. Therefore, it says: "possessing seed" (*sabījatā*). That which exists together with the seed—the syllable of the mantra—is "possessing seed"; the state of being such is "possessing seed-ness" during the absorption. The purification of the vajra and the lotus will be explained in various places. Alternatively, the meaning of the text is that by whichever seed-syllable the purification of the vajra-water is performed, by that very same one the consumption [of the substances] is performed.

[2.4.11] Therefore he says: "In its center. The meaning is that one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the syllable *a* in the center of that *bodhicitta*. He asks: Is it only the syllable *a*, or rather the syllable *kṣuṃ* as well? To this he replies: "But the blazing sun," and so forth. *Ciccākṣara* refers to the syllable *kṣuṃ*. The meaning is that one should recite the syllable *kṣuṃ*, which is filled with garlands of flames and possesses a radiance equal to the sun. The meaning is that one should recite "a kṣuṃ. [2.4.12] "The Lord of the Lotus," and so forth... [2.4.13] ...has already been explained.

[2.4.14] "The one named Amṛtodaka is proclaimed by three deities. The meaning is that these, beginning with Bodhicitta, who take the forms of Lokeśvara and others, are those named Amṛta, and they are three.

[2.4.15] Immediately after the response to the question concerning the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he states the response to the question concerning *ali* and *kali*: "Ali," and so forth. The response to the question is given out of sequence (*akrama*) in order to indicate the absence of dogmatic attachment (*anabhiniveśa*). In the sense that "one takes (*lāti*) or receives (*ādatte*) the incomparable essence of bliss (*sukharasa*) by means of this," the word *ali* is used in this meaning. There is no concern for correct or incorrect words (*śabdāpaśabda*), because they are merely conceptual constructs (*kalpita*). Therefore, this *ali* is called the "means" (*upāya*); its meaning is "vajra. However, in the *Hevajratantra*, the vowel of the word *āli* is indeed long (*dīrgha*).

That word *ali* denotes wisdom (*prajñā*), whereas this word *ali* expresses skillful means (*upāya*). Regarding "bee" (*bhramara*): it is called a bee because by means of it one leaves behind wandering (*bhrama*). Regarding "Vajrabhairava the bee": it is a vajra because many delight (*ramante*) by means of it. Bhairava is the giver of fear to the immature, because he is the cause for the realization of non-duality (*advaya*). Thus, "bee," "bumblebee," and "Vajrabhairava" are synonyms for skillful means. He states the designation of the bodhicitta: "The bee [is] the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), extending as far as space."

It is called *ali* (space) because beings find room (*avakāśante*) and arise within it; thus, *ali* means space (*ākāśa*). It is called *paryanta* (limit) because it binds (*antati*) happiness all around (*pari-samantāt*); the verbal root is *ati-adi*, meaning "to bind. It is called the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) because it holds (*dadhati*) and nourishes (*puṣṇāti*) those phenomena (*dharmas*)—beings—by virtue of their maintaining their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇadhāraṇāt*). It is called *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) because it exists in itself (*svasmin bhavati*). The phrase "by way of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) is used in the sense of the first case. Thus, *ali* (space), *dharmadhātu*, and *svabhāva* are synonyms for the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).

[2.4.16] To explain how this term is derived, he says: "sakala... and so forth. "Caras" are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), who constantly and excessively move toward what is not to be done—that is, they transmigrate. "Acaras" are those who act with prior reflection; they do not constantly and excessively move toward what is not to be done. "Of bodies" means of embodied beings. "Sakalas" refers to all embodied beings. Those that exist together with the moving (*cara*) and the non-moving (*acara*) are "sacarācaras," and they arise from the very *dharmadhātu*.

It is not only these [ordinary beings] who arise; rather, those of secret wisdom (*guhyadhī*) also do so. Thus he says: "those of secret wisdom" (*guhyadhī*). That which is hidden is the secret reality—the gnosis consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Those whose wisdom (*dhī*) is directed toward that are "those of secret wisdom," namely the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The meaning is that they too, being free from attachment, arise from the *dharmadhātu* itself for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. Incidentally, he provides the designation for the *bodhicitta*: "eighteen," and so forth.

The nectar previously mentioned, which is the *bodhicitta*, exists in eighteen locations beginning with the breasts; because it flows and drips (*sarati*), it is called "all" (*sarva*). Being of such a nature, it exercises sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over the bestowing of bliss, and thus it is an "organ" (*indriya*).

[2.4.17] Regarding "but in its center, having drawn up" (*tasya madhye tu m-ākṛṣya*): "of that" (*tasya*) refers to that [lotus]. "But in its center" (*madhye tu*) means that because it rests in the center, the center is drawn up. "Ālī" means *ali* (the bee). By this, the *bodhicitta* itself is turned upward. "But it dissolves in the center" (*madhye tu līyate*) means it dissolves in the center of the pistil (*varaṭaka*) of the lotus and the vajra. The meaning is that the effect (*kārya*) is joined there. The collective sense is: that *bodhicitta* which resides in the eighteen parts is drawn up and should be made to enter the center of the pistil of the lotus and the vajra.

To explain how it is to be drawn forth, he says: "By the terrifying vajra-sound. The intended meaning is "by the striking of the thunderbolt. Regarding the phrase "arisen through the union with substances": that nectar becomes a substance arisen from the union of the two organs.

[2.4.18] How so? He says: "In the wind," and so forth. Alternatively, "by means of yoga" (17d) refers to the yoga with the deity. The bodhicitta that has arisen through yoga becomes the most excellent substance. He states "in the wind," and so forth, to show that its excellence exists even by way of another method: "the wind" (*anila*) is the letter *ya*; "fire" (*anala*) is the letter *ra*. It is called "object" (*artha*) because it is sought after (*arthyate*), that is, it is something to be acquired. One seeks the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) only until the object is obtained; therefore, the object of the search for the means comes to an end.

Therefore, *artha* and *anta* are synonyms. The meaning of "the seventh horse" (*sapty-anta*) is the seventh steed among the seven horses of the Sun; thus, by the term *sapty-artha*, the seventh horse of the Sun is intended. Because of their common property of being the seventh, the syllables *sa* and *ha* are called *sapty-artha*, since they are respectively the seventh [letters] following the *ya* and *ra*. The seed-syllable of Vajrī is *sa*; and because its nature is nectar (*amṛta*), it is a synonym for the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

Furthermore, *vajrībīja*, *sakāra*, and *ardhacandra* are synonyms. One should join the letter *ha* with that; the meaning is that one should place the *ardhacandra* upon the head of the letter *ha*. Regarding "surpassing the *bindu* and *nāda*": the *bindu* is above the *ardhacandra*, and below it is the *nāda*, which is the letter *ū*. The letter *ha* is "surpassed" or pervaded by those two. Thus, it becomes *hūṃ*. This should be meditated upon in the center of the hub of the vajra.

[2.4.19] Regarding that, concerning the statement "in the middle of the moon, situated within the syllable of nectar" (7cd), he explains by means of extraction, indicating the letter *a*: "The vowel," and so forth. The seed-syllable preceded by the vowel is the letter *a*. And that is the first because of its excellence. The rest is easily understood.

[2.4.20] He speaks of the answering of the question regarding wisdom (*prajñā*): "Kālī," and so forth. She is called *Kālī* because in her one licks (*āleḍhi*) or tastes (*samāsvādayati*) bliss (*ka*). Her femininity is due to her being the nature of wisdom. This is a designation for the *dharmodayā*. It is called *puṣpa* because it blossoms (*puṣpati*), i.e., expands through the striking of the *vajra*. Thus, *Kālī* and *puṣpa* are synonyms. Regarding the phrase "the Vajra-holders have ascended the form of the *puṣpa*": therein, upon the white *dharmodayā*—which is triangular, designated as *puṣpa*, and contains within it the universal lotus and *vajra*—the Vajra-holder, whose nature is great bliss, ascends and dwells. And thus he said:
It is called "Sukhāvatī" precisely because of the protection of bliss.

Thus, it is said that he is not merely of the nature of great bliss: "He whose body is a flower. "Flower" (puṣpa) is also a designation for the *bodhicitta*. He whose body (*vigraha*)—that is, his physical form—is this flower of *bodhicitta* is "he whose body is a flower" (*puṣpavigraha*). And so it is said in the *Hevajra*:
"The Blessed One exists in the form of semen (*śukra*)."

Thus: "She is the mother of all in the arising of saṃsāra across all planes. And she is Kālī, the cause of the arising of saṃsāra for everyone; therefore, she is the mother. "Across all planes" means in all states of existence (gatis).

[2.4.21] "This is an ocean of the water of gnosis": this refers to Kālī. Because she is the substratum for the various forms of gnosis—such as the mirror-like cognition and so forth—which resemble water in that they cause the subsiding of the afflictions (*tāpa*), she is an ocean. For this very reason, she is *prajñā*. She is called *prajñā* because within her gnosis free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is known. Indeed, through the cultivation of gnosis free from proliferation, all cognitions such as the mirror-cognition arise. Regarding the phrase "by the crocodiles and fish": the Buddhas, whose nature consists of completely purified passion and so forth, are themselves the crocodiles and fish. Thus it has been said: "Through the union of the *bola* and *kakkola*, by means of touch, the latent impression of solidity [is removed]."
Because the *kaṭhina* is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), Vairocana is considered to be delusion.
And so forth. *Kālī* is characterized by crocodiles and fish. Thus it is said: "The jewel-casket of the Buddha.

Regarding "the non-dual one in the midst of the mud": the non-dual one is external wisdom (*prajñā*); its "midst of the mud" means the midst of *kālī*. To the question "What is there?", it says: "by the sprout which is the skillful means (*upāya*). Therein, the sprout is that which constitutes the skillful means; and that is the channel (*nāḍī*) called *khagamukhā*.

[2.4.22] He states the nature of the sprout: "resembling a blooming *bandhūka* flower. It is like a blossoming *bandhūka* blossom. Regarding "the abode of honey and nectar": honey is *rajas*, and nectar is *bodhicitta*; it is the abode of these two. Regarding "Kālī" and so forth: this sprout also receives the name Kālī, as it is the locus for the tasting of nectar. Its "unfolding" (*vivarta*) is the blossoming of that sprout which has the luster of a *bandhūka* flower. When that occurs, what happens? He says: "the flower is *ambuṣa*. The flower is *rajas*.

That very thing is the form of water; the sense is that it flows. The channel whose mouth is in the sky (*khagamukhā*)—which is designated as *aṅkura* and *kāli*—when it has blossomed, flows simultaneously or sequentially with the "flower-water" or the *bodhicitta*. First, the *bodhicitta* was mentioned by the passage beginning with "the nectar-vajra water" (4a) and "the channel is space" etc. (15c). By the phrase "feces and fluids" (9d), Vairocana and Akṣobhya are indicated. And by the phrase "the flower is the water-seed" (22d), *rajas* is mentioned.

And according to the oral instruction (*upadeśa*), there is the inclusion of *kheṭa* (saliva). By this, these five nectars (*amṛta*) are established. For each of the remaining nectars, their fivefold nature must be proven in the same way as that of the *bodhicitta*. Furthermore, wherever the "five nectars" are mentioned, it is the flower alone that is to be understood, and not merely blood, because the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) is its designator.

[2.4.23] He states the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the syllable *kṣuṃ*: "twofold," and so forth. The twofold syllable is *kṣa*, because it is a composite form of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*. One should join the letter *kṣa* with the bindu at its head and the *nāda* at its base. Thus it becomes *kṣuṃ*. That syllable, being the seed-syllable (*bīja*), is the Mother of the Family (*kulamātā*) of the deities and the *yoginīs*. Alternatively, the deity is the Fire-deity (*vahnidevatā*), and she is the Mother of its Family. Therefore, one should meditate upon that within the *bodhicitta*.

[2.4.24] Having meditated on the letter *A* situated within the moon at the center of the *bodhicitta*, one should meditate on the syllable *KṢŪM* with the brilliance of the sun; thus he says, "In the moon," and so forth. In that regard, the concluding statement is: "But in the middle of the moon, [one should meditate on] the nectar-syllable situated in the center" (7cd). It should be understood that at the time of the ritual procedure (*pravṛtti*), one should meditate on the letter *A* in the pericarp of the lotus. The passage beginning with "bhāva" and so forth is easy to understand.

[2.4.25] He states "Ali," and so forth, meaning that even he who is the external means (*bahirupāya*) is *ali*, and external wisdom (*bahiḥprajñā*) is *kāli*. Regarding "tathāgatī": she is called *tathāgatī* because one goes to—that is, knows—the "thus" (*tathā*), which is non-erroneous, by means of her; thus, she is wisdom itself. The essential point is that the bodhicitta, which is nectar produced from the union of these two external ones, *ali* and *kāli*, becomes supreme when practiced according to the ritual procedure.

[2.4.26] Now he extracts the form by means of its manifestation (*vyakti*): "Just as... and so forth. This is to be understood according to the previous explanation. Furthermore, one should extract the mantra by placing a staff (*daṇḍa*) beneath the letter *ḍa*. Just as *a* is the seed-syllable (*mantrabīja*) of the mantra, and not *a* as the combination of the letters *ḍa* and *ṣa*. In this tantra, the manifestation of the letter *a* is the combination of the letter *ḍa* and the staff. The pronunciation, however, is exactly the same; only the manifestation differs.

[2.4.27] "By these," and so forth: this is the reality of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); by means of this, there is the cleansing of the body of embodied beings. Regarding "the nectar-born" (*amṛtā*) and so forth: those who specifically know the five nectars in this way—that is, through this particular method of purification—and consume them, are "the nectar-born"; the sense is that they are not dead (*na mṛtā*). That is to say, death does not come to them.

[2.4.28] Now, death may occur; then, for those who have attained immortality (*amṛta*), the gateways to rebirth—the destinies of gods and humans—become purified. "Having observed" means "it should be seen. In which destiny? He says: "In whichever body. The sense is: in whichever [destiny] there is the arising of the body, or the physical frame.

Alternatively, the meaning of the half-verse beginning with "by yoga" is as follows: those who, having mastered and empowered the *bodhicitta* alone—which is the immortality born of yoga—experience its taste according to their own will, they too become immortal.

[2.4.29] He speaks the response to the question regarding the hooks (*aṅkuśa*): "Listen," and so forth. The connection is: "O Vajrapāṇi, listen to the five things to be consumed (*bhakṣya*) and the five hooks. "According to reality" means without error. "Specifically" means by way of distinction from the sequence previously mentioned. Regarding "by which," and so forth: the meaning is that one should listen to those hooks by whose consumption preceded by knowledge liberation (*gati*) is swiftly seen—because liberation is possible in this very life, whereas elsewhere it is difficult to attain even in incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). This is the intended sense.

[2.4.30] Regarding the goads (*aṅkuśa*), he says: "Mahāmati," and so forth. *Mahāmati* refers to an elephant. Regarding *vākya*: *vākya* refers to a cow. *Sajāti* refers to a dog. *Cchṛṣṭavīraka* refers to a horse. Regarding "one should eat with crystal": the meaning is that one should eat after purification. Regarding "with the great goad" (*mahāṅkuśa*): it means the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*). Regarding "of the yogins": it means by the yogin.

[2.4.31] By the term "seed-syllable of consciousness" (*vijñānabīja*), *hūṃ* is meant; its recitation (*japa*) is to be performed there upon the Great Hook (*mahāṅkuśa*). This very point he states with the words "of the recitations. The meaning is that the syllable *hūṃ* is to be meditated upon there in the center. Regarding "consume with a crystal-like mind": the sense is that one should consume [the object] with a mind free from the stains of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). [2.4.32] "The single hook of the obstacle": the obstacle-hook is an elephant. The Great Hook and the obstacle-hook have one and the same basis because they possess a single seed-syllable. Therefore he says "of that," and so forth. The meaning is that one should also meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ* upon the obstacle-hook.

[2.4.33] "The goad is the mastery over the place" means that the dog is the master of its own place because of its strength therein. "In that regard, there is an application for a reason" means that an application must be performed there. To the question "By what?", he says: "By the seed-syllable *ghriṃ*. The meaning is that one should preside over it with the seed-syllable *ghriṃ*.

[2.4.34] "One should preside over the form of the horse-goad, which is all-encompassing and all-knowing": one who is all-knowing in every respect should preside over the form of the horse-goad. By what means? He says: "by the syllable *jriṃ*. The sense is that the seed-syllable *jriṃ* is to be meditated upon as the horse-goad.

[2.4.35] The "vajra-hook" is the cow. It is to be empowered by means of the seed-syllable *sriṃ*. To the question, "What would result from that? he says: By consuming the pledge-substance (*samaya*) beginning with the cow, preceded by the empowerment of the syllable *sriṃ*, the yogin becomes a vajra-body. Through all these hooks, there is also the cleansing of evil. For these are called "hooks" (*aṅkuśāḥ*) because they thoroughly sever (*kuṣṇanti*) the attainment of perfection.

[2.4.36] He states the time for the offering: "On the eighth day," and so forth. By the practitioner of deity-yoga, on these lunar days, an offering (*bali*) should be given according to the ritual procedure with these substances and others. To the question, "How? he says: "With effort. That is, with constancy.

[2.4.37] He says "nityam" and so forth, meaning that accomplishment (*siddhi*) shall always arise through worship. Regarding the phrase "whatever one desires, like enjoyment and liberation": "enjoyment" (*bhukti*) is experience characterized by heaven and the like; "liberation" (*mukti*) is release, which is Buddhahood.

[2.4.38] To demonstrate what was stated—that "all rites are accomplished"—he says: "In the royal court," and so forth. If one who possesses the yoga of the Jñānaḍākinī enters the royal court after tasting a pill made of the ten substances, then he very quickly becomes endowed with glory (*śrī*). Regarding "the unpleasant becomes most dear": by this very sequence, that which is most unpleasant becomes dear. "And he may desire even the sight [of the deity], and it is accomplished": the sight of the desired object is accomplished.

[2.4.39] If a poor person seeking wealth finds that his prosperity becomes abundant, and houses for those seeking houses—this is the intended meaning. The passage beginning with *cyuti* is easy to understand. [2.4.40] Regarding "ten substances": the five nectars are Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya. Amoghasiddhi is semen (*kheṭa*). And there are the five products of cow dung (*gokudahanāḥ*). By means of these, when combined with fragrance, the yogin becomes one who deludes both himself and the world through incense. To explain how this is done, he says: "With ten syllables," and so forth.

The seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and Akṣobhya are to be seen in their respective order as *huṃ*, *hūṃ*, *kṣuṃ*, *yuṃ*, and *suṃ*. The seed-syllables of Gokudahanas are *sriṃ*, *ghriṃ*, *hūṃ*, *jriṃ*, and *hūṃ*. The mantra is: *oṃ huṃ hūṃ kṣuṃ yuṃ suṃ sriṃ ghriṃ hūṃ jriṃ hūṃ svāhā*.

[2.4.41] Having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) by reciting this ten-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times preceded by the offering of a *bali*, one should then take incense consecrated with that same mantra one hundred and eight times. This very mantra is used for what follows as well; therefore, it says "one hundred thousand," etc., meaning that the preliminary service should be performed in exactly that manner.

[2.4.42–45] Regarding the statement "these are to be joined with the ritual action": there is no doubt that sandalwood and other substances joined with these [mantras] are effective as described. This very point he states: "My word, there is no doubt. The meaning is: "This is my word."

[2.4.46] Now he explains the practice for accomplishing the *yoginīs*, beginning with "O Blessed One," and so forth. This is the practice for the four *yoginīs* beginning with Dīpinī. He asks: for what purpose is the practice of the female messengers (*dūtī*)? He replies: "The messenger," and so forth. The meaning is: for the sake of bringing the *yoginīs* under one's own control. He asks: for what purpose is this very act of bringing them under one's control? He replies: "What is this accomplishment, the *yoginī*? For what purpose is this bringing under one's control? Because when the *yoginīs* have been accomplished, the practitioner becomes a master of all rites.

[2.4.47] Therefore he says: "All," and so forth. The intention is that all ritual action (*karma*) has its primary focus on the *abhisāra* (the rite of summoning), and one becomes capable for the sake of accomplishing it. Consequently, one should accomplish the female messengers (*dūtī*) with effort.

[2.4.48] He states the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*): "At the foot of a single tree," and so forth. The meaning is that at the root of a single tree, the practitioner of mantras (*mantrī*), intent upon the worship of the *samaya*, should first offer a bali-oblation and then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) before accomplishing the *dūtī* who is about to be described. He explains the recitation itself: "A *pauruṣa* plus a quarter," and so forth. A *pauruṣa* is the measure of a cubit (*hasta*). A quarter (*pāda*) is a fourth part of a cubit. The connection is that having spread out a cloth measuring one cubit and a quarter, one should accomplish the *dūtī*. Regarding the phrase "form and so forth are visualized":
The meaning is that the form of the *dīpinī* should be drawn exactly as conceived. The instruction is that it should be written upon a cloth such as one from an ascetic (*avadhūta*).

[2.4.49] He describes the form of the *dīpinī*: "twelve," and so forth. The *dīpinī* is to be drawn with the specific attributes of being twelve finger-breadths in measure, yellow in color, and so on. It should be understood that the cloth is pervaded by her. Having spread out such a cloth before him, the practitioner should accomplish the *dīpinī*; this is how it should be known. [2.4.50] Regarding "rites, worship, and so forth": [this refers to] red flowers, perfumes, and the like. (51a)
[2.4.51] "One should fumigate with dried meat and so forth": having performed worship before the cloth painting (*paṭa*), one should offer incense of dried meat.

[2.4.52] Then, having offered the *bali* and performed worship with the ten substances, one who has previously completed the service with the *lakṣamantra* should again recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. The five substances are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). The five materials are the cow-products (*gokudahanāḥ*).
[2.4.53] He says, "When the messenger (*dūtī*) has arrived, one should show her the mudrā," beginning with the words "samaya" and so forth.
[2.4.54] The mantra beginning with *oṃ* is to be recited.

[2.4.55–56] "With two hands," and so forth, refers to the *samaya-mudrā*. Regarding the word "should utter": the meaning is that one should utter this very mantra even at the time of displaying the *mudrā*.

[2.4.57] Having filled the skull-cup (*kapāla*) with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should offer the *samaya-water*; thus he says, "with the five," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the *samaya* being given when the rite is performed": once the offering of the *samaya-water* has been performed, having taken hold of her with the left hand...

[2.4.58] ... Having said "Siddhāsī" (Be successful), one should empower both; this means that one should perform the union of the two organs—this is the collective meaning. The rest is easily understood. She should give food and other such things to the practitioner.

[2.4.59] She should be enjoyed with her for one watch (*ekayāma*), that is, for one *prahara*. Why? He says: "Because she is a yoginī who delights in sexual union. Since she is fond of sexual union, and because she does not become fond of sexual union after that watch has passed, she should not be desired beyond that time. If this is not accomplished in this way, then one should interlace the *dīpinī* mantra with the seed-syllable *kṣuṃ*, which is the seed of the terrible *ḍākinī*. The interlacing is as follows: *kṣuṃ oṃ dīpeśvarī hūṃ sriṃ pheṃ kṣuṃ*. One should recite it in that same manner one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*).

By means of that seed-syllable, when being pressed, Dīpinī is accomplished. If she is not accomplished, then her head bursts asunder. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "yadi" and so forth.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhāryā": by this procedure, Dīpinī shall become an accomplished wife. Regarding the phrase "intent upon acting for the benefit of sentient beings": the sense is that the welfare of sentient beings must be performed through the giving of food, drink, and other such things.

[2.4.61] With the words beginning "Listen," etc., he teaches the *sādhana* of Ḍākinī. "By others" means another *sādhana*. "A cloth of two cubits" means a cloth measuring one and a half cubits should be made. One should accomplish Ḍākinī—who will be described below—in the form to be explained, preceded by the offering of bali, worship, and so forth.

[2.4.62–66] “Mounted upon the vessel of the earth”: the earth is the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*); therein, the vessel is the funeral pyre (*cit*). “Mounted” means having placed [it] there. The sense is that, having gone to the cremation ground and spread out the cloth of the aforementioned form upon the pyre, one should accomplish the *ḍākinī*. He asks what kind of vessel of the earth it is, and says: “all around,” etc., which is easy to understand. Here too, during the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), the recitation is one hundred thousand (*lākṣika*), and the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is likewise from one hundred thousand.
[2.4.67] With the mantra “Oṃ ḍākinī hūṃ aiṃ phur,” one should display the pledge-seal (*samayamudrā*). This very [mantra] is also to be recited.

[2.4.68–96] The seed-syllable of Vajrī is *suṃ*. The interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) is: *suṃ oṃ ḍākinī hūṃ aiṃ phuḥ suṃ*. Alternatively: *suṃ oṃ caṇḍālī hūṃ ghrūṃ phuḥ suṃ*. One should likewise recite this one hundred thousand times. [2.4.97] Regarding those who have not achieved success through the aforementioned rite, one should cause them to perform another rite: having visualized oneself in the form of Jñānaḍākinī...
[2.4.98] ...one should step upon a Kāmbojī cloth with the left foot and perform five hundred recitations of the Kāmbojī mantra. Thereby, success is attained.

[2.4.99] "In the midst of the heroes" means in the midst of the circle of yoginīs; "he should bring" means he should cause [the victim] to be brought. If, even by this method, one does not achieve success, then it should be understood that one should quickly bring a piece of cloth from Kāmboja into the midst of the heroes and, while uttering "jriṃ phaṭ," cut it into pieces. "Striking" (ghāta) refers to the sound *phaṭ*. Regarding "with forceful shouts" (*deḍḍhakair*): the meaning is that one should cut it into pieces while shouting loudly. *Uccakair* is an alternative reading.

[2.4.100] He says that one should meditate on the syllable *hūṃ* upon a cloth divided into all its parts and then consume it; the phrase "one should consume" and so forth is easy to understand. That Kāmbojī dies due to her previous karma. Even in this way, she—the yoginī to be accomplished—is the sovereign and leader among all yoginīs. If she should remain unaccomplished, then by this very procedure one should offer oblations into the midst of the fire. He states this very point: "the yoginī to be accomplished," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

[2.4.101] The *kālavṛkṣa* is the *riṣṭikāvṛkṣa*. Having kindled a fire with the wood of the *bhallātaka* and *kālavṛkṣa*, one should stir it with mustard seeds, blood, and pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), divide it into pieces, and offer it as an oblation one hundred and eight times into a cloth [already prepared] with *rājikā*, poison, and *nimba*, preceded by the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*. This very point is stated in the verse beginning with "In the midst of the fire," and so forth. (102ab)

[2.4.102] If it is not accomplished in this manner, then she certainly dies. It is not only the Kāmbojī who does so, but other ḍākinīs as well. If they have not been accomplished through their own previously mentioned respective rites, then they are accomplished by means of this rite; he states all of this in the passage beginning with "they die," and so forth. Regarding "ḍākinīs": these are the yoginīs. Regarding "cried out with a cry of distress": the meaning is that they wail with a sound of agony. Regarding "the ritual act is necessarily accomplished":
the meaning is that in this way the ritual act characterized by the accomplishment of the messenger (dūtī) is necessarily successful.

The response to the question, "Is the non-dual and dual-free reality conceptualized as existence or non-existence? (2ab), is indicated by the passage beginning with "Therefore, one is free from existence and non-existence; hence, delusions are far away" (8cd). Furthermore, the response to the question concerning the system of the Yogaśāstra (2d) is stated by the passages beginning with "The ten substances" (40c) and "O Blessed One, I wish to hear the sādhana of the four yoginīs" (46ab).

[2.4.103] Now, at the time of entering the maṇḍala of the assembly, he recites the verse for requesting the gatekeeper, beginning with *sohaï* and so forth. "O Nīladaṇḍa Krodha, your ritual activity (*samayaceṣṭā*) shines. Nīladaṇḍa is called simply "Nīla" because a whole is understood even through a part, just as Amoghasiddhi is called "Amogha" and Avalokiteśvara is called "Avalokita. This is the meaning of the sentence: "O Nīla, O Krodha, your ritual activity shines. To the question "How does it shine?", he says:

"He holds a staff in his hand, bound with rubies. Regarding "pāṇihi," it means he holds a staff (*daṇḍa*) in his hand (*pāṇau*); this refers to his action. What kind of staff? He says: "bound with rubies" (*māṇikkehiṃ baddhu*). It is bound with rubies, that is, with gems (*maṇi*). In some versions, the reading is *pāṇehiṃ*; in that case, it is an adjective qualifying the rubies. Because they are rare and beloved, the meaning is that they are like life-breaths (*prāṇa*), resembling one's very life. To the question "What would happen in this way? he says: "pecchavi," and so forth.

The connection is: "I shall behold [her] in the midst of the *yoginīs*. O Hero, conqueror of the afflictions (*kleśa*), "mellu" means abandon. What is that? He says: "duvāra," meaning the door. To the question, "What would come of entering the midst of the *yoginīs*? he says: "saṃsāra-uttāra jāmīti. I go—that is, I attain—the crossing over the ocean of *saṃsāra*. And therefore, abandon me. He says this very thing: "mella mahuṃ" (abandon me). By this verse, the disciple is made to enter the mandala.

[2.4.104] The limb-seal (*aṅgamudrā*) has been explained in its various places, as well as the sign-seal (*cihnāmudrā*). Consequently, the answering of questions regarding these two is established. Now he speaks of the answering of questions concerning the sentence-seal (*vākyamudrā*) and the limb-seal, beginning with "O Blessed One," which is easy to understand. Regarding "the secret," etc.: that which is the secret to be hidden from yogins and yoginīs—that most secret of secrets—one should make it known; the sense is that it is understood by means of the characteristics of the sentence-seal. [2.4.105] Regarding "of the yogins," etc.: the meaning is that the seal should be shown by the yogin with the right hand, and by the yoginī with the left.
[2.4.106] By the phrase "having cast into the mouth," and so forth, the *aṅgamudrā* (limb-seal) of the *yoginīs* is indicated; the meaning is that it is the *cihnamudrā* (symbolic seal).
[2.4.107–109] "Gho ghu," and so forth, is the *vākyamudrā* (sentence-seal).
[2.4.110–153] "The thumb of the Guru" refers to the middle finger.

In this manner, according to the sequence stated, that which begins with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and ends with the *mudrās* for the practice of the *ḍākinīs* is what is practiced herein; thus, it is called the "section" (*itiprakaraṇa*). This is the fourth chapter of the *Parapīṭha*. Within that section, because it extends from the fire-oblation (*homa*) up to the practice of the *yoginīs*, and because it pertains to the supreme state of the self, it is "supreme" (*para*). That itself is the seat (*pīṭha*) of accomplishment. And since that is completed, he says: "The *Parapīṭha* is finished. Thus, in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*, the *Parapīṭha* is concluded.

[3.1.1] Now, referring to the *yogapīṭha*, he says: "O Blessed One," and so forth. "By others" means something else. What is that? He says: "The characterized and the characteristic. The connection is: "I wish to hear the characteristics—the essential nature and reality—of those four, beginning with the *vajra*. Asking by way of differentiation, he says: "The four realities," and so forth. These four are: the *vajra*, the bell, the rosary, and the knowledge of the *saṃsāra* of the five destinies; [he asks about] their reality.
"How should one apply it after knowing? means: having known the reality (*tattva*), how should one perform the ritual actions such as the vajra-holding (*vajradhāraṇā*)?

[3.1.2] Regarding "the characteristic of crossing over saṃsāra": the connection is that one should listen to the "characteristic," which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the vajra and so forth. And that is called "crossing over saṃsāra" because by means of it one crosses over from saṃsāra. He says that very thing: "O Vajra, of the reality," and so on. First is the vajra, second is the bell...

[3.1.3] ...the third is the rosary (*akṣasūtra*), and the fourth is the characteristic of gnosis (*jñānalakṣaṇa*), meaning the characteristic of gnosis regarding the saṃsāra of the five destinies. He explains what was indicated by the phrase "crossing over saṃsāra" (*saṃsārottāra*) with the words beginning with "fourth": by means of the reality (*tattva*) of the four—vajra and so forth—the multitude of sentient beings is led across the waves of conceptual construction to the further shore of saṃsāra, which is liberation; this is the meaning. "As desired" (*īpsita*) means according to one's wish.

[3.1.4] Regarding that, he first states the reality (*tattva*) of the vajra, beginning with "in the middle" and so forth. Having meditated upon Vairocana—the nature of the earth, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), and the others—within the central spoke of the vajra, one should meditate upon the four [Buddhas], Akṣobhya and the rest, who are the nature of the wisdoms such as the perfectly pure water and so forth, within the eastern and other spokes in due order. "Sarvapūrva" means: the time that is entirely prior, the very first time, is "sarvapūrva. Its status as "prior to all" (*sarvapūrva*) is in relation to Ratnasaṃbhava and the others.

[3.1.5] Below the prongs of the vajra, at the limit of the fist, is an eight-petaled lotus; there, one should visualize Padmapāṇi and the others. This very point is stated in the passage beginning with "on the lotus, eight," and so forth. "On the lotus, eight" means on an eight-petaled lotus. "Factor of enlightenment" (saṃbodhyaṅga) means the means (upāya) for enlightenment. "According to the ground" means according to their respective positions. The intended meaning is that one should visualize Padmapāṇi and the others, who constitute the means for enlightenment, in the petals starting from the east.

[3.1.6] "Padmapāṇi" refers to Lokeśvara. "Gagana" means Gaganagañja, that is, Ākāśagarbha. "Yakṣādhipati" refers to Vajrapāṇi. "Kṣiti" refers to Kṣitigarbha. The sense is that one should "establish," meaning one should visualize them.

[3.1.7] "One should establish these eight" is the conclusion. Regarding "in the center, the egg of the thirty-three": in the fist of the vajra, the "egg" (aṇḍa) is the place of the gods; there, one should visualize the "Knowledge God," namely Jñānaḍākinī.

[3.1.8] At the end of the other fist, on an eight-petaled lotus, the goddesses beginning with Vajrāṅkuśī are to be visualized in the petals of the cardinal directions (east and so forth), and Cundā and the others in the petals of the intermediate directions; thus it is said, "eight deities on the lotus," and so on.

[3.1.9–11] On the needles at the other end, Jñānaḍākinī and the others are to be seen according to their division starting from the center. This very point he states with the words "on the needle," etc.
[3.1.12] Regarding "the diamond-reality (*vajratattva*) of the deity": the meaning is that the wise one should understand the diamond-reality in the form of the deity.
[3.1.13] The passage beginning with "tribhāga" and so forth is easy to understand. Regarding "the lotus bud": it refers to a cluster of filaments (*śūka*) having the shape of a lotus bud.

[3.1.14] By the phrase beginning with "diśādi" and so forth, he explains the reality (*tattva*) of the nine-filamented vajra. On the nine filaments starting from the east, there are Padmapāṇi and the others; likewise on the filaments at the western end. The remainder is as before.

[3.1.15] Regarding "the needle emerging from the mouth of a makara": the needles in the east and other directions should be made as if emerging from the mouths of makaras, excluding the central needle. Furthermore, they should be seen as being joined with rays, moons, and so forth; this is the general characteristic. The specific characteristics of the vajra and the bell should be understood from other sources. Regarding "nine needles": it should be understood that there are nine prongs through the purification of the ninefold True Dharma (*saddharma*), and five prongs through the purification of the five gnoses (*pañcajñāna*). Therefore, he says: "gnosis," etc.
The meaning is that there are five prongs due to the purification of the five cognitions, such as the mirror-like cognition and so forth. The world itself is the vajra, being supremely pure.

[3.1.16] Why? He says: "Because of the reality (*tattva*) of things," and so forth. Because the reality of the *vajra* is its own nature (*svarūpa*). What is that? He says: "The *vajra*-self is the self, which is consciousness (*cetanā*). The self of the *vajra* is its own nature; that is the self as it is conceptually constructed by others. Since the so-called "self" is established as a mere name and is in ultimate reality nothing but the form of non-dual suchness (*advaya-tathatā*), the meaning is that it should be understood as the *vajra*-consciousness. Regarding "of the essence of the *vajra*": the sense is that the *vajra*, being the very essence of the mind, is perceived within the mind of the yogi.
"Because of the cause," and so forth: since the vajra, which is the essence of the yogi’s mind, consists of all things...

[3.1.17] ...therefore, one should make firm the purity of the vajra, thinking: "All phenomena are pure as the vajra; I am pure as the vajra. Why is this so? He says: "The vajra," and so forth. All phenomena are indeed the vajra. How is that so? He says: "The vajra," and so forth. Because they are produced from non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*), all phenomena are indivisible and thus like the vajra. The ritual actions such as pacification (*śāntika*) are the vajra. "By way of convergence" (*abhisārataḥ*): because, by virtue of being the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, they are omnipresent.
[3.1.18] By means of the radiation of the form of the deity, the *vajra* is that which delivers one from *saṃsāra*. The remainder is easily understood.

[3.1.19] Just as a lamp would destroy darkness and bring about its end, so too does the distinguished knowledge whose nature is the *vajra* destroy the darkness of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Consequently, by means of the *jñānavajra*, which has become like a lamp, the directions attain illumination. The sense is that through knowledge, everything is seen without obscuration.

[3.1.20] He states that even the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) is of the nature of the *vajra*: "O *vajra*, accomplished," and so forth. He also states that liberation from the bonds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is the *vajra*: "O *vajra* of the Dharma," and so forth.

[3.1.21] He states that one should accomplish the world through wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*): "By the *vajra*," and so forth. Since when the *vajra* is held, the entire world—both mundane and supramundane—is held, the *vajra* is held by the master. Alternatively, one should meditate solely upon the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].

[3.1.22] Now he speaks of the reality of the bell (*ghaṇṭātattva*): "Listen, O Vajradhara," and so forth. "Vajradhara" is used in the sense of "O Vajrapāṇi. "Rāja" is used in the sense of "O King. Regarding "of those whose reality is impelled by wisdom": the reality of the bell is through the purification of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). "Listen to that, O Bhava, for the sake of crossing over"—the meaning is: listen to that bell, and from that, there is a crossing over from existence (*bhava*).

[3.1.23] All phenomena are empty; all phenomena are unconditioned; all phenomena are by nature in a state of nirvāṇa—thus, with such sounds pervading the element of space and continuing to pervade until the time of being established at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), the bell resounds and reveals the reality of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). Thus he says: "the element of space," and so forth. Indicating that it extends as far as the element of space, he says: "the ten directions," and so forth.
[3.1.24] One should visualize eight goddesses or their seed-syllables on the eight sides. Thus he says: "the directions," and so forth.
[3.1.25–26] Vasudhārā is golden; Cundā is sweet; Bhṛkuṭī is lovely; Vajramālā is so named according to her actual meaning.

[3.1.27–29] Within the filaments (*śūka*), Vairocana and the others are to be visualized like vajras: the filaments are those above the vajras, which are lotuses. "As before" means as in the case of the vajra. The center has the form of a knowledge-staff (*jñānadaṇḍa*).

[3.1.30] “One should shake it in the eight directions”: having taken up the bell and grasped it with the thumb and ring finger, one should shake it in the eight directions, beginning with the east. The meaning is that having produced eight sounds in the eight directions, one should set the bell down; it should be understood that one does not make more than this sound. As for how one should shake it, he says: “employed with the *āli* and *kāli*. *Āli* is the vajra; *kāli* is the bell. The sense is that, having taken up the vajra with the right hand using the thumb and ring finger, one should cause the bell to resound.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Āli," and so forth. For it is by means of the union of wisdom and skillful means that one cuts through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

[3.1.31] A bell marked with a vajra is a *vajraghaṇṭā*. And that is the method (*upāya*). It approaches the vajra, which is the method; thus it is the method. It approaches the bell, which is wisdom (*prajñā*); thus the method is the vajra. At the time of offering the *bali* and so forth, there is neither the bell alone nor the vajra alone; rather, there is the simultaneous holding of both. In this way, they follow one another. "And in the middle" indicates holding them in the fist. He speaks of the purification of holding: "Two in the hand," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

[3.1.32] By means of the word "upāya" (skillful means), through the production of the bell, one should hold it upon one's own body. Regarding "svecchā" and so forth: the intended meaning is that having visualized the sun on the right hand and the moon on the left, one should hold the vajra and the bell respectively.
[3.1.33] He states two verses concerning the holding [of the implements]: "hūṃkāra... and so forth. Preceded by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*...

[3.1.34] One should recite the verse beginning with “...sohia” by means of the *vajrollāla*. What is this *vajrollāla* like? It is that by which sentient beings have been delivered; thus, the term “one who has delivered sentient beings” (*tāritasattva*) demonstrates its purpose for others. Regarding “*vimokkha*”: it is called *vimokṣa* because it liberates from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); such is the *vajrollāla*. For this very reason, it is established that it delivers sentient beings. Why is this so? He says: “In the liberation through the Dharma (*dhammavimokkhe kajju*). The Dharma of the *vajra* is its intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*), from which comes the liberation from conceptual construction.

The verbal root *ā-dā* is used here in the sense of "liberation" (*mokṣa*). Therefore, the phrase "vajra-susāra-varam" means that the vajra is superior because of its essence; furthermore, it is superior due to its firm limb, which has emptiness as its intrinsic nature (*śūnyatā-svabhāvatva*). The verse beginning with "Oṃ," etc., is to be recited when holding the bell.

[3.1.36] “He proclaims by means of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*): Wisdom is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); skillful means is existence (*bhāva*). The sense is that he proclaims by means of the intrinsic nature of both. It should be understood that he proclaims in order to bring about the form of the deity—the state of being wisdom and skillful means—in others. Why is this so? He says: “Wisdom,” and so forth. He declared that all phenomena are awakened by way of the nature of wisdom and skillful means. From the word “or” (*vā*), it follows that he proclaims (*gadati*) and will proclaim (*gadiṣyati*). “Ignorance,” and so forth: †...†.

[3.1.37] Reality (*tattva*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). By virtue of the purity of the ultimate truth, the vajra should be held. By virtue of the purity of the sound [expressing] that "all phenomena are empty" and so forth, the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) should be sounded. Pure mind is the vajra; the bell is the body (*kāya*); its sound is speech (*vāk*). Thus, the grasping of the vajra and vajra-bell should be understood as occurring through the purification of mind, body, and speech, even at the time of the vajra-bell initiation.
[3.1.38] He who sounds the bell without knowing reality holds the bell like an elephant.
[3.1.39–41] It has been established by the passage beginning with "yanmadhye" that the Vajrācārya, while observing the vajra-vow, must carry the vajra.
[3.1.42] He states the reality (*tattva*) of the rosary: "Listen," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
[3.1.43–46] The seed-syllable of time (*kālabīja*) is the seed-syllable of the *riṣṭikā*.

[3.1.47–49] There are eight threads for the purification of the cardinal and intermediate directions, and upon them, Padmapāṇi and the others are to be visualized. The ninth thread is for the purification of the center; therein, all the Buddhas or Vajradhara are to be seen. This very point he states with the words "diśāhi" and so forth. [3.1.50] He says that the rosary should be strung with a thread spun by a maiden, beginning with the words "saṃpūrṇa" and so forth. [3.1.51] The sense is that through recitation with a rosary strung with such a thread spun by a maiden, the accomplishments of pacification and so forth, as well as liberation, are attained. The remainder is easily understood.

[3.1.52–63] He states the mantra for purifying the rosary: *akkharu* and so forth. Regarding *akkharu kāraṇu rūvu*: that form whose causes are the syllables (*akṣara*), such as *a* and *ka*, is "that which has syllables as its cause" (*akṣarakāraṇa*). That mantra which has as its own nature (*svarūpa*) a form whose cause is the syllables is "the mantra whose form is caused by syllables. *Sohia* means purified. *Manta vīti* means the mantra itself. The purified mantra itself is the essence (*sāra*). And purification is by means of selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth. He says this very thing: *gaṇiasaṃkhu alikku*.

That which has a calculable number is a "mantra of calculable number" (*gaṇitasaṃkhya*). It is also false (*alīka*); its purification is the determination of it as being false. A mantra characterized in this way is accomplished; it is the essence, the heart, of the *yoginīs*. The passage beginning with "brāhmaṇa" and so forth is easy to understand. Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇa is the body, the Śūdra is speech, and the Kṣatriya is the mind. Through the unification of these, the mantra—the net of *yoginīs*—is accomplished. The remainder is easy to understand. The mantra begins with "akkharu" and ends with "svāhā."

[3.1.64] By this, there is the purification of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). Because it strings together (*sūtraṇāt*) and enumerates (*saṃkhyākaraṇāt*) the syllables (*akṣara*) of the mantras, it is called a "rosary" (*akṣasūtra*). Therefore, the meaning is that a mantra being recited with it will accomplish the desired deity, and not otherwise.

[3.1.65] Now he states the reality of the saṃsāra of the five destinies, beginning with "Listen" (*śṛṇu*), and so forth. Sentient beings situated at a distance from one another are divided by differences in knowledge and differences in karma. But what else? He says: "by way of common knowledge and speech" (*sāmānyajñānavākyataḥ*). The meaning is "by way of common ignorance" (*sāmānyājñānatvena*), according to the principle that "the world is nothing but consciousness" (*jñānamātraṃ jagat*).

[3.1.66] Regarding "the supreme Daitya among the Daityas": the sense is that they are called *daityāḥ*. The *yakṣas* are well-known. The *asuras* are the *rākṣasas*. By "accomplished ones" (*siddhakaiḥ*), the gods are meant.

[3.1.67] Regarding "of one kind in form, like those in the Avīci hell": "like those in Avīci" means beings who have gone to the Avīci hell. "Subtle" means subtle living beings. "Eggs" means egg-born creatures. "Retention" (*dhāraṇā*) means: let it be understood. [3.1.68–70] Regarding "common," etc.: because the worlds consist of nothing but cognition, "common cognition" means the world itself. What, then, is the distinction? The sense is that it is by way of the five destinies (*pañcagatikatvena*).

[3.1.71–72] He states the divisions of the gods: "twenty," and so forth. "Twenty" means twenty. "Threefold" (*triketā*): there are twenty-three abodes of the gods. "Twofold above, however, successively": the lifespan of the gods doubles at each higher level. The sequence therein is as follows. There are six belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*): the Four Great Kings (*caturmahārājakāyika*), the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*), the Yāmas, the Tuṣitas, the Nirmāṇaratis, and the Paranirmitavaśavartins. These six belong to the realm of desire. Above this is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

There are seventeen distinct locations. For the first dhyāna, there are two locations and two levels: the Brahmakāyikas and the Brahmapurohitas. In the second dhyāna, there are three distinct locations and three levels: the Parīttābhas, the Apramāṇābhas, and the Ābhāsvaras. In the third dhyāna, there are three distinct locations: the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, and the Śubhakṛtsnas. In the fourth dhyāna, there are eight distinct locations:

The Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Abṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas; and the Mahābrahmans and the Asaṃjñisattvas constitute the ninth level. By the term "place" (sthāna), the levels (bhūmi) are meant. Thus, there are twenty-three divine places, which are the divine levels. Six days and nights of the gods belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) equal fifty human years. In this manner, months and years are calculated by means of such days and nights.

By this calculation, the lifespan of the gods of the Great Kings (*mahārājika*) is five hundred years. By doubling the sequence of days and so forth from that point, the lifespan of the gods of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśa*) is one thousand years. By doubling the sequence of days and so forth from that point, the lifespan of the Yāma gods is two thousand years. In this manner, the measure of the lifespan for the remaining three classes should also be understood by doubling the days and so forth. Thus is the determination of the lifespan for the six [classes] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Furthermore, for the gods residing in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no reckoning of days and nights. Their lifespan increases according to the sequence of *kalpas*. "In ascending order" (*ūrdhvaśas*) means that the lifespan of the gods increases in this manner, moving higher and higher through the twenty-three classes of gods; such is the sense. The remainder is easily understood.

Thus, because the reality (*tattva*) of the vajra-bell and so forth is practiced herein according to the stated sequence, it is called the "Yoga-pīṭha Section. This concludes the first chapter in the Yoga-pīṭha of the *Catuṣpīṭha-nibandha*.

[3.2.1] Now he speaks the chapter on the accomplishment of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth by means of the wheel (*cakra*) and other implements: "Listen," and so on. Regarding "that which is to be accomplished specifically by the wheel": that ritual action such as pacification which is to be accomplished by means of the wheel is "that which is to be accomplished by the wheel. "Specifically" (*viśeṣataḥ*) means: specifically compared to the previously mentioned rituals of pacification and so forth; this is the sense. He states what is to be accomplished itself: "Pacification," and so on.

[3.2.2] Regarding "of the wheel with nine squares and so forth": a wheel consisting of nine squares is indeed an eight-spoked wheel provided with eight spokes and a hub (*varaṭaka*). "One should make the exterior depressed" means that the rim (*nemi*) should be formed on the outside. "The ritual colors and so forth of the wheel" means that one should visualize the colors in accordance with the specific ritual action. [3.2.3] He states the mantra: *Oṃ*, etc.

[3.2.4] "But the seed of this [mantra] belongs to all": these seeds are to be visualized in the central and other compartments. In the eight compartments starting from the east, there are the eight syllables beginning with *tā*, while the *oṃ* and *hā* syllables are in the center. Therefore it is said: "The *praṇama* at the end and the middle. Here, *praṇama* means the *praṇava*, which is the *oṃ* syllable; *anta* means the end of the mantra, which is the *hā* syllable; and *madhyaka* means that those two are to be contemplated as being in the middle. As for the phrase "one should join the name in the middle":

The meaning is that the name of the person to be protected (*sādhyanāman*) is placed between the syllable *oṃ* and the syllable *hā*. Regarding the phrase "the protective formula," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) should be understood here. Therefore, it should be known that the name of the person to be protected, joined with the protective formula and so forth, is to be visualized between the *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and the syllable *hā*. The application is as follows: *oṃ devadattaṃ rakṣa hā*, and so on.

[3.2.5] To explain how this wheel is to be cultivated, he says: "By means of equality," and so forth. The meaning of "the gnosis of emptiness through equality" (*samatājñānaśūnyeṣu*) is that emptiness is not merely partial; such is the intended sense. One should wash away one's own ordinary form with the water of the gnosis of emptiness. Regarding "equality, omniscience, and the abodes": the meaning is that the gnosis of emptiness is the knowledge of all-knowingness (*sarvajñajñāna*), which is the cognition of everything by means of equality. "By the abodes" refers to the state of being an abode.

The intended meaning is that the cultivation of the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*) itself constitutes the protection of the place of practice. The sense is that protection is achieved through the cultivation of the protection wheel (*rakṣācakra*) preceded by the cultivation of emptiness. Regarding the phrase "one should color" (*rañjayet*): the meaning is that at the time of the cultivation for subjugation (*vaśya*), one should color both one's own and others' mental continuums. This is the same meaning even in the reading *raktayet*. Alternatively, regarding the passage beginning with "Samatā is the All-Knowing One," the meaning is as follows: immediately after the cultivation of emptiness, the protection of the place must be performed by means of the protection wheel, such as the diamond cage (*vajrapañjara*).

[3.2.6] “One should meditate,” and so forth: the meaning is that when the wheel has been meditated upon in this manner by the yogin, all fears and calamities become distant. “But by the non-existence of beings” means that after one has contemplated the non-existence—that is, the emptiness—of beings (sattvas), which are here [figuratively] called entities (bhāvas), the meditation on yoga follows. He says this very thing: “the meditation on yoga. Yoga is the yoga with the deity; its state (bhāva) is its cultivation (bhāvanā). To the question “How is it thus?”, he says: “but by fear. That is, by fear of disease and so forth.

The meaning is that for the sake of achieving pacification and other results from the fear of disease and so forth, one should perform the yoga with a deity endowed with colors and other attributes appropriate to that end.

[3.2.7] He speaks of the yoga with the deity: "In the moon," and so forth. The meaning is that one should meditate on oneself in the form of Tārā upon a moon-maṇḍala above a lotus. Following the meditation on emptiness, the collective sense is that one should meditate on Tārā—arisen from the transformation of the seed-syllable *tāṃ* situated upon a moon-disk above a lotus, which itself has arisen from the transformation of the central pericarp (*varaṭaka*) of that lotus. [3.2.8] Immediately after the generation, he describes the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*): "Oṃ," and so forth. "Oṃ tāre svāhā" ... [3.2.9] ... [is placed] on the head.
[3.2.10] Oṃ tuttāre svāhā... [3.2.11] ...on the two eyes. [3.2.12] Oṃ ture svāhā...
[3.2.13] ... in the two nostrils.
[3.2.14] Oṃ tu svāhā ... [3.2.15] ... in the two ears.
[3.2.16] Oṃ re svāhā ...
[3.2.17] ... on the tongue.
[3.2.18] Oṃ tāriṇī svāhā ...
[3.2.19] ... in the heart.
[3.2.20] Now he states the rule for the arms and so forth: "two-armed," and so on. For protection, the Blessed Lady is indeed dark blue, and the mantra is also dark blue.

[3.2.21] One should meditate on her as granting fearlessness with her right hand, while with her left she holds a blue lotus by its stalk, its petals touching her ear. Regarding the phrase "by the rays of all": one should contemplate the body of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) as being pervaded by the rays of one's own body, by the dark-colored rays of the wheel, and likewise by the rays of the mantra; while contemplating the *sādhya* being thus pervaded, one should recite the mantra—thus he says: "the recitation of the mantra especially. [3.2.22] The recitation is: *Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture devadattaṃ rakṣa svāhā*.

[3.2.23] Thus, regarding the mantra for the rite of protection (*rakṣākarmika*): "protection" (*rakṣā*) refers to [guarding against] future bondage and so forth, while "pacification" (*śānti*) is the quelling of present bondage and so forth. The rest is clear. However, in the previously mentioned wheel, the placement of the mantra is counter-clockwise; furthermore, on the rim (*nemī*), there are the vowels beginning with *a*. [3.2.24–25] Regarding "the wise person for one of dull intellect": through the meditation on this wheel and the recitation of the mantra, one of dull intelligence becomes wise. Regarding "one should wear it written": by wearing the eight-spoked wheel written on birch bark or similar material, protection will be attained.

[3.2.26] He explains this very point with the words "of the Goddess," and so forth. "One should accomplish the principles of yoga for the protection of all" means that for the sake of protecting everyone, one should accomplish the principles of yoga, the deity-yoga, and the *cakra*, according to the sequence already stated. The meaning is that the practitioner of Tārā (*tārāyogī*) should meditate upon and recite the *cakra* and the mantra for the sake of protection.

[3.2.27] Now he speaks of the wheel of wisdom (*prajñācakra*): "This wheel has eight petals. This means a wheel with eight spokes. "One should encircle the outer rim" means that one should encircle or visualize two lines on the outer rim. "The end, beginning, and middle of the former" means that for this wheel, just as for the previous wheel, the letters at the middle, the end, and the beginning are the syllable *hā* and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). "One should establish all by means of recitation" means that the remaining syllables of the mantra should be visualized upon all the spokes.

[3.2.28] "White-colored, etc., of the wheel": the meaning is that the wheel is white. He says, "one should contemplate the vowels on the rim," beginning with "vowels," etc. The seed-syllables *pra*, *jñe*, *ma*, *hā*, *pra*, *jñe*, *hūṃ*, *svā* are on all the spokes; *oṃ* and *hā* are the seeds in the center; and the vowels are on the rim—this is the collective meaning. Here too, he shows that the practitioner of deity-yoga, contemplating the wheel preceded by the meditation on emptiness, attains the benefits to be described, beginning with "equality," etc.
