[3.4.44] "May they go by that path through which they attain Buddhahood. "Kuru" (do): this is an authorization for the activity of one's own mind; "O Mind, you too must do that by which sentient beings are happy and free from affliction"—the meaning is "you should practice. He says "jhaṭitākāre" and so forth, stating that in the meditative union of wisdom and means, the yoga of the deity must be performed instantaneously.

[3.4.45] This very point is stated: "The bell belongs to the God of the yogins. When the yoga of wisdom (prajñā) belongs to the God Vajradhara, then one should immediately perform the ritual actions such as the deity, the mudrā, and the mantra. "The wise one should meditate" means that in this manner, the wise yogin should meditate upon himself in the form of Vajrasattva and upon wisdom (prajñā) in the form of the Goddess; such is the intended meaning.

[3.4.46] He describes the placement of the eight syllables (*aṣṭākṣaranyāsa*) upon the body of the Goddess, beginning with "of the eight syllables" (*aṣṭākṣarasya*), and so forth. The sense is that the eight syllables, which are the very nature of the deities, are to be placed upon the body of the Goddess just as they are on the body of the Lord (*bhagavat*). This is the specification of the "calculation" (*kalana*) previously mentioned. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "of the Goddess" (*devyāḥ*): the sense is that one should effect consciousness (*cetanā*) and the mind (*citta*) within the body of the Goddess by means of this calculation. Regarding the phrase "once again": although the calculation has already been described, it is stated once more for the purpose of recollection; such is the sense.

Others, however, describe it thus: "If there should be a yogin who, for the sake of elevating his waned passion, would direct his own mind toward the Goddess, then there is 're-calculation' (*kalanam*). Regarding the passage beginning with "from that" (*tataḥ*): "from that" means immediately after the calculation. "Of the Vajra" refers to Vajrasattva. "Embracing" means: having himself embraced the Goddess, he should generate a mind that is itself impassioned toward the Goddess. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "of the Vajra": while generating the mind in this manner...

[3.4.48] ... One should form the ego-identity within oneself, thinking, "I am Vajrasattva. This very point is stated as "I," and so forth. Alternatively, *tataḥ* means immediately after the state of the ritual action (*karaṇa*). *Vajrasya* refers to Vajrasattva. *Āliṅgya* refers to the act of embracing and so on. *Svena* means by oneself. Regarding *anuraktasya ceto na*: *anuraktasya* means "of the one who is impassioned"; *cetaḥ* means "mind" (*citta*); *na* is used in the sense of negation. This is what is meant:

Even during the stage of the instrument (*karaṇāvasthā*), it is observed that the mind of the consort (*prajñā*) does not become impassioned; at that time, the Vajrasattva-yogin himself should perform the embracing and so forth of her—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the word *atha* (47c), it means "below. In some versions, the reading is *adhaḥ*. The yogin should place himself below the consort. To the question of how he should do this, he says: *cetana sahā* (47d). That is, together with the mind. The intended meaning is that when her mind is observed to be impassioned, then this too should be performed.

By this, even the inverted union (*viparītarata*) is shown. It is said that "the pride of Vajrasattva and so forth belongs to the Vajra" so that, in that state, the mind may not otherwise lose its identity as Vajrasattva. This is the explanation of what was previously indicated by the phrase "I shall recite Vajrasattva."

[3.4.49] Now he describes the nature of the *khagamukhā* channel, beginning with the words "of the water-born" (*ambhodbhavasya*). "Of the flowers of the water-born" means of the lotus flower, that is, of the *dharmodayā*. To the question "What of it?", he says: "the characteristic of that which is hidden within. That which is hidden—that is, concealed—within that lotus is the *khagamukhā* itself, for it is by that alone that it is characterized; thus it is the "characteristic. The meaning is that the *khagamukhā* channel is hidden within the *dharmodayā*. To the question "Like what?", he says:
"Sprouts of roots and flowers": just as a sprout is the root of flowers, so too the channel (*nāḍī*) is the root of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). The remainder is easily understood.

[3.4.50] Now, making clear that very same previously mentioned *kalana* by means of its placement (*sthāpana*), he says: "of the two thighs," and so forth. "The two thighs" refers to the two shoulders. Regarding "of the seeds": because of the use of the plural number, the base of the throat, the heart, and the base of the navel are also included. Due to the abundance of items to be placed, there is an abundance of placement locations. By the word "seed" (*bīja*), the *kūṭabījas* are intended. Consequently, one places *smryuṃ* on the two shoulders, *hmryuṃ* at the base of the throat, *ymryuṃ* at the heart, and *kṣmryuṃ* at the base of the navel.

"Earth" is the syllable *hūṃ*, and it is located in the two eyes. "Wind" is the syllable *yuṃ*, and it is located in the ears and nose. "In the low place, the nature of water": in the low place, which is the tongue, is the syllable *suṃ*, the nature of water. "A sprout, like the seed of fire": in the sprout, which is the palate, is *kṣuṃ*; this is the seed of fire.
[3.4.51] The passage beginning with "just as" and so forth is easy to understand.

[3.4.52] "Having contemplated the form of the Goddess": having produced the form of the Goddess by means of that extracted syllable *aṃ*, [it is said] "it dissolves into the center of the Earth. The Earth is the *dharmodayā*; into its center, that *hūṃ* syllable dissolves—that is, it merges. This recalls what was already stated previously: the sense is that the syllable *aṃ* is to be placed within the "beak of the sky-goer" (*khagamukha*). "Of the fire of Kālāgni and the fire of the Pretas": the fire of Kālāgni is said to be on the right, and the fire of the Pretas is on the left.

And thus, the meaning is that first the Means (upāya) embraces with the right hand, which is the Fire of Time (kālāgni), and afterwards with the left hand. Now he describes the embrace of Wisdom (prajñā): "The Fire of Pretas is like the Fire of Time. The meaning is that first Wisdom embraces with the left hand, which is the Fire of Pretas, and afterwards with the right hand. By this it is indicated that the right side is primary for the Means, while the left side is primary for Wisdom.

[3.4.53] Regarding "of the hands in the union of the two": as to what kind of hands are these in the union (*saṃpuṭa*) of the two—wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)—he says: "the vajra raised with three needles. The meaning is that the hands of those two are raised in the form of a three-pronged vajra. To explain how they indeed take the form of a three-pronged vajra, he says: "one should encircle the little finger and the thumb with the two."

Pressing the little finger with the thumb of the [same] hand, the remaining three fingers should be raised; the intention is that it should thus take the form of a three-pronged vajra (*triśūka-vajra*). Even so, he states where those hands should be held: "The two mudrās and so forth on the sides. The intention is that they should be held on both sides through the application of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). And thus, it is the meaning of "mudrā" that it should be the three-pronged vajra mudrā.

[3.4.54] “Having firmly pressed the lower lip with sharp [teeth], the nectar-eater, the conscious one”: the sense is that, having bitten the lower lip with sharp teeth, one should drink the honey of the lower lip. “Nectar” refers to the honey of the lower lip. “Eater” means one should take; the meaning is “one should consume. “The conscious one” refers to the yogin. With the words beginning “with the eighteen,” he causes one to remember the exhortation regarding the *bodhicitta*. “The bell is the exhortation”: the meaning is that one should urge forth the nectar of wisdom (*prajñā*).

[3.4.55] Regarding "the left side of the *bandhūka*": the channel (*nāḍī*) shaped like a bird's beak is similar to the *bandhūka* flower, and it is located on the left side of the *dharmodayā*. Therefore, he says: "the form of *kharatāpa-m*. *Kharatāpa* refers to the bird-beak. "*M-ākṛti*" means manifested or made manifest. He asks again: "of what kind? and replies: "the shape of a bird's beak. This means it resembles the beak of a bird. By this, the form is described; "*kharatāpa*" is the description of its essential nature. "One should impel with its seal" means:
One should stimulate that channel with the index finger, which has been empowered by the *kṛṃ* syllable through mudrā, or else with the "elephant-trunk" [mudrā] and so forth.

[3.4.56] “The thunderbolt of the waters is to be given”: the meaning is that at the time of union (*samāpatti*), one should perform the friction of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) with the thunderbolt turned to the right and the lotus (*padma*) turned to the left. “Of the waters” means the water-born lotus, which is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*). By virtue of the thunderbolt being on the right, the lotus is logically on the left. “Like a corresponding equal form” means the friction of wisdom and method is equal. “One should give a thrill (*pulaka*) upon the breast; it is established everywhere.”

One should apply the *pulaka* with the index finger; the meaning is that this is done on the chest and the breasts. By means of that, the action should be understood as the bodhicitta residing in all parts of the body flowing forth. Since "on the chest" is merely an illustration, one should also apply the *pulaka* to the generative organ and other such places.

[3.4.57] "One should apply the position of the side for the *vajrasūcī* and other mudrās. Regarding "from this" (*ata*): the meaning is "therefore. The sense is that, therefore, for the purpose of impelling the *bodhicitta*, the *vajrasūcī* mudrā was previously shown in the context of the embrace of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Regarding the rubbing, he says while making it fleshy: "The two joined forms, the lotus and the vajra, should impel one another.

The sense is that the two—wisdom and means—in the form of being joined, should impel one another by performing a rubbing: the lotus with the vajra turned to the right, and the vajra with the lotus turned to the left.

[3.4.58] Recalling the recitation (*japa*), he says: "The sound *hūṃ*, etc. Making the sound of the syllable *hūṃ*, the Vajra-holder should recite the non-dual seed-syllable, which is non-dual gnosis itself. The sense is that one should satisfy all deities within one's own body with true bliss. [3.4.59] He says, "The bell also should recite the syllable *aṃ*, etc.": "But the gnosis-seed at the tip of the vajra" means that having visualized the syllable *hūṃ* at the tip of the vajra, one should satisfy oneself. The meaning is that at the time of union, the syllable *hūṃ* is to be meditated upon at the tip of the vajra. Furthermore, the syllable *aṃ* is also to be meditated upon in the lotus of the Wisdom consort (*prajñā*).

[3.4.60] Regarding "vajra" and so forth: *vajra* is the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*). The bell (*ghaṇṭā*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, the meaning is that the union of these two within one's own body is the *mudrā*. Demonstrating that the holding of the *vajra* and the bell-mudrā occurs through such realization of reality (*tattva*), he says: "the vajra and the bell," and so forth. The sense is that the yogin should hold the external vajra, the bell, and the *mudrā* precisely as the purification of those [internal ones].

[3.4.61] "The vajra," and so forth. "By means of reality" (tattvena) means by means of the syllable *hūṃ*. The meaning is: by the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. The sense is that while uttering the syllable *hūṃ*, one should rub with the vajra. Having thus raised the lotus and displayed it, she says: "Uttering the syllable *aṃ*, she should receive the vajra"; "she should cause the bell to resound according to her own will. Having thus gratified oneself through the ultimate gnosis of the union of the vajra and the bell, one should satisfy the deities residing within the body; this very point is expressed in the verse beginning with "vajra-bell," which is easy to understand.

[3.4.62] “One should preside over,” and so forth: the meaning is that one should consume. What is that? He says: “of its *m* and *ambu*. That is the *bodhicitta* produced from the union of those two. And that has the nature of one’s own mind. “By means of the two natures”: the sense is that it is born from both natures. Furthermore, this *bodhicitta* of both should be understood as something to be tasted by both.

[3.4.63] Previously, the instrument (*karaṇa*) was shown primarily as wisdom (*prajñā*). Now, he explains the instrument as the leader (*nāyaka*), namely the means (*upāya*): "The erotic attraction," and so forth. A yogin endowed with the posture of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), considering himself the primary self, sits upon a comfortable seat, assumes the form of Vajrasattva, and asks: what should he do? He says: "Graceful," and so forth. "Graceful feet" means the contraction of the right foot. "On the left thigh, the bell": the meaning is the contraction of the left foot of the Wisdom (*prajñā*).

By this it is said: Vajradhara, having contracted his right foot, should extend his left; Prajñā, having contracted her left foot, should extend her right. Regarding "the left is embraced by the breast and hand": the meaning is that one should embrace with the left hand and press the breast. Regarding "the right vajra is caressed": the meaning is that with the right hand, the vajra—acting as the means (*upāya*)—should be inserted into the lotus. Having performed everything in this manner, while performing actions such as laughing and so forth, he should kiss her again and again.

[3.4.65] Now he states another method: "The bell," and so forth. The meaning of this is that the contraction of the right foot of the Prajñā is the *lalita* posture; it should be understood that the contraction of the left foot belongs to the Upāya. Regarding "the thigh, the seat, the sitting": the meaning is that the Prajñā sits upon the thigh of the Upāya. With her right foot, the Prajñā should encircle and hold the region of the [Upāya’s] hip.

[3.4.66] "Embracing the neck with one" means: having embraced the neck of the Wisdom Consort (prajñā) with the single right hand, one should encircle it. "The left resounding with bells" means: the intention is that one should extend the lotus of the Wisdom Consort with the left hand; or rather, the sense is that one should cause it to move. The remainder is easily understood. Thus far, two methods have been shown; others should likewise be inferred.

[3.4.67] Regarding "the vajra-song" and so forth: *vajra* means the non-dual secret; the sense is that one should sing the song endowed with that, immediately after the performance of the ritual actions and so on. He says "after drinking the *madana*" and so forth, meaning one should sing after drinking. *Amṛtodaka* (nectar-water) is *madana*. This singing and drinking should be performed for the purpose of removing fatigue and for the sake of satisfying the *prajñā* (wisdom-consort). For indeed, both [the practitioner and the consort] drink.

[3.4.68] He speaks the *Vajragīta*: "The essence," and so forth. Regarding "the essence is gathered": the essence is non-abiding nirvāṇa; that which gathers or accomplishes this is the *Sārasamuccaya*. Even such a thing is empty—this is the ornament of contradiction (*viruddhālaṅkāra*). In reality, it is empty of the grasped and so forth, like a jar is empty of water and the like. To the question "What is it that is thus?", he says: "saṃsāra. Saṃsāra refers to the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

For the pentad of aggregates (*skandhapañcaka*), when meditated upon as having the nature of a deity and as being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), accomplishes non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa*) through non-attachment. Regarding the term "insubstantial" (*asāra*): that which lacks a core—that is, a stable limb characterized by permanence—is "insubstantial," namely, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). If cyclic existence is devoid of the apprehended object and so forth, then how could there even be non-abiding nirvāṇa? To this he says: "existence," and so on. "Existence" (*bhāva*) refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by the apprehended object and so forth.

Alternatively, "bhāva" refers to that in which existence, non-existence, permanence, impermanence, and so forth, occur—that is, appear; thus, it is the mind possessing a dual aspect. Accomplishment (siddhi) is also liberated from that; the meaning is that even the realization of non-abiding nirvāṇa is liberated. The principle is that like produces like. He states the explanation of the meaning by means of a synonym: "mokṣa. The meaning is that "non-abiding nirvāṇa" and "liberation" (mokṣa) are synonyms. To the question "For what purpose is that?", he says: "tāraṇena. The meaning is: for the sake of delivering sentient beings.

[3.4.69] This very point he states: "The union of the couple (*dvandvāliṅgana*) for the sake of all the tasks. The deity-yoga, whose nature is emptiness and compassion, is the yoga of the union of the couple; it is for the purpose of accomplishing the welfare of all beings. Regarding the phrase "therefore, saṃsāra is not essence-less": for those practicing the yoga of the union of the couple, there is no essence-less saṃsāra, because through its utter purity it is of the nature of *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the meaning is that even the yoginīs are indeed immersed [in this state] and are utterly pure.
At the end of every word, those *nā* syllables should be seen as *hūṃ te nā hūṃ te nā te te hūṃ*. For this very reason it was said: "The *hūṃ* syllable is considered manifold" (67b).

[3.4.70] Having sounded the bell, one should sing again. He says that very thing: "With the vajra-bell," and so forth. Showing that the yogi succeeds by reciting and meditating in this manner, he says: "In a state of meditative equipoise," and so forth. Showing that whatever task is conceived by such a yogi, all of that is accomplished, he says: "Whatever is unconceived," and so forth.

[3.4.71] Now he states the yoga for the purpose of bringing [others] under control, beginning with "ākṣepa" and so forth. That by which one is drawn in—that is, brought under one's own control—is "ākṣepa," such as medicinal herbs and the like. Regarding the phrase "it should be joined with that": the sense is that, primarily, the medicine should first be joined with wisdom (*prajñā*). The remainder is easily understood.

[3.4.72] "The place of yoga is taken" means that the portion is equal for all. "One should consecrate them with its substance" means that those substances are to be consecrated by means of that *bodhicitta*. And *bodhicitta* is to be understood as that which arises from the union of the two organs. Some maintain that by the term "place of yoga," *bodhicitta* itself is meant.

[3.4.73] With the words “*indrahasta* and so forth,” he states another formulation. That which has a root shaped like an *indrahasta* is called *indrahasta*. *Mohanī* is *vaṭaparṇikā*. *Stambhanī* is *śālaparṇī*. *Ātmapañcika* refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). Regarding *pañcāṅga*: the impurities of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and vajra are called *pañcāṅga*. “One should make them equal portions” means that equal quantities of *indrahasta* and the others should be taken; for the others, they are to be taken as available.

[3.4.74] Regarding "drinking": this refers to the drinking of intoxicants such as wine. Regarding "the consumption of betel": the sense is that it should be given with lime-powder when eating the areca nut (*guvāka*). [3.4.75] Regarding "by means of the conjunction with the rising dust, rites of subjugation and so forth are accomplished": the connection is that the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) is accomplished through female menses (*strīrajas*) and by means of the application of the blood of a deity. He says "mantra... and so forth to state that it is also accomplished by means of the characteristic of the mantra.

[3.4.76] "Having emitted" means having emitted that *bodhicitta* from one's own body; the meaning is that it has become mixed with both the previously mentioned *rajas* produced from one's own body and the *bodhicitta*. The intention is that the practitioner of the union with the Red Deity brings everything under control. Therefore, he says: "One should cause it to be performed according to one's wish. The intention is that whoever is given the *rajas* and the *bodhicitta* by one who has recited the mantra one hundred thousand times and is a practitioner of the union with the Red-colored Deity, that person shall be brought under control.

[3.4.77] He states the application of the mudrās at times such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, beginning with "the one who observes vows" (*vratī*). "The one who observes vows" (*vratī*) means a female ascetic (*vratinī*), specifically a *kāpālikī*. "Of the kinswomen" (*jñātīnām*) means "of the wise women" (*jñāninī*); it means a woman who performs the ritual of piercing the *kāṇḍa* (a type of spear) or an astrologer (*daivajñā*). This is also the case in the reading "of the wise ones" (*jñānīnām*). "The queen" (*rājñī*) means a *kṣatriya* woman. "The venerable secret one" (*guravaguhyā*) means a *brāhmaṇī*. Some say "the venerable one" (*guravā*) means a *brāhmaṇī*, while "the secret one" (*guhyā*) means an actress (*naṭī*). [3.4.78] "The leather-worker" (*cirmikā*) means a female shoemaker (*carmakārī*). "The meat-seller" (*māṃsikā*) means a woman who sells meat; it means the daughter of a butcher (*khaṭṭikā*) and others. "The fisherwoman" (*mīnā*) means a *kaivartī*.

[3.4.79] *Rajakī* is well known [as a specific type of woman]. Even when the reading is *rajanī*, it refers to the same *rajakī*. Regarding the phrase "from that" and so forth: *yoga* refers to rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and the like. *Śāstreṇa* means by the scripture, namely the scripture of mantras (*mantraśāstra*). *Dhīyatām* means let it be accomplished. The sense is: since the entire collection of mudrās has been taught in the Mantra system, let that be diligently accomplished for the sake of achieving pacification and other such results.

[3.4.80] Now he explains the manner of binding: "By another... and so forth. It should be understood that another *ākṣepa* (projection) is being described. Regarding "the state (*pada*) by which beings are delivered through binding": the *pada* for the sake of delivering beings consists of the *samapada* and others. "The two joined together, the *ākṣepa*, emerges as reality; one should bind them": when two *padas* are joined in equality, it becomes a *samapada*; this is the definition of *samapada*. That very thing is called *ākṣepa* because it projects obstacles. "Emerges as reality" (*tattvamudra*): [this refers to the emergence of the true nature].

The meaning is that the *mudrātattva* (the reality of the seal) is the *samapadabandha* (the binding of equal feet). Others, however, explain it as "the drawing together (*ākṣepa*) of the two": the union, contact, and so forth of the two—wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). That very [union] is the "drawing together" as before. Its reality (*tattva*) is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) free from error; this is the meaning. Since its form is the seal (*mudrā*) consisting of the *samapada* and so forth, one should therefore bind it; thus, this is not a definition of the *samapada* itself. The *samapada*, however, is already well known.

[3.4.81] *Samapada* (equal-foot stance) consists of two feet being equal. Some say that *samapada* means one should hold one foot with its tip pointing south and the other with its tip pointing north. However, according to the system of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*), *samapada* is the equal contact of the toes of each other's feet. [3.4.82] In that very same state, when one foot of the woman is contracted, it is *bhinna-pada* (separated-foot stance).
[3.4.83] Having assumed the *samapada*, one should spread the knees equally; this is *maṇḍala-pada* (circle-foot stance).
[3.4.84] In the case of a full attainment (*samāpatti*), it is the *trivikramapada* because one noble being raises a single foot upward.
[3.4.85] It is the *kūrmapada* because the left foot is stepped upon by the right foot.
[3.4.86] It is the *ālīḍhapada* because of the contraction of the left foot and the extension of the right foot.
[3.4.87] By means of the extension and contraction of the left and right feet, one assumes the *pratyālīḍha* stance.

[3.4.88] Having lifted one foot and standing on the other, one should cause [the body] to revolve in the form of a wheel; this is the *ekasthāna* (single-stance) posture. This is a variegated execution within the state of meditative union (*samāpatti*). [3.4.89] Regarding "seated" (*niṣadya*), it refers precisely to the *lalitākṣepa* and other such postures. It is called *niṣadya* because wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*) rest comfortably (*sukhena*) within it.
[3.4.90] *Pādavikṣepa* (the foot-stretch) consists of moving the feet as one desires.

[3.4.91] *Yūpākāra* (the sacrificial-post form) is the union of the two sleeping wisdom and means, having straightened the shanks by alternating their upper and lower positions in order to remove fatigue.
[3.4.92] *Añcupīḍana* (the knee-press) is so called because, after sitting down and contracting one knee, one proceeds by supporting the neck; the meaning is the contraction of the knee.

[3.4.93] Having placed a second thigh upon one thigh, it is made *saṃyamī* because it proceeds between the two hips by means of wisdom (*prajñā*). Others, however, explain *saṃyamī* as follows: one should perform the union after placing the legs of wisdom under the armpits, wrapping them with both arms, and holding the neck. [3.4.94] It is *samasthāna* because it proceeds by sitting with both thighs extended not too far apart.
[3.4.95] It is *kālāgni* because it proceeds by pressing the right foot of wisdom against one’s own heart.

[3.4.96] Having placed the two thighs of Prajñā between her own two shanks and having set her two feet upon one’s own heart, the mudrā of the Heart-Bursting of Pravṛtti is designated by the word "Heart" (hṛdaya).
[3.4.97] Sitting upon the two thighs of Prajñā, Pravṛtti is called the Nandāsana. [3.4.98] Contracting one foot, it is the Ekasaṃyata of Pravṛtti.

[3.4.99] These eighteen modes of objection (*ākṣepaprakāra*) are to be employed during the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Regarding the statement "the possibility of qualities should be distinguished by yogins everywhere": the meaning is that those specific bonds (*bandhaviśeṣa*) should be applied only to that [attainment] in which there is the possibility of these qualities.

[3.4.100] Now he describes the specific types of physical gestures (*abhinaya*): "In the heart," and so forth. Having entwined wisdom (*prajñā*) with both arms behind her back and pressed against the heart with one's own heart, the "pressing of the heart" (*hṛdayapīḍana*) occurs through the process of engagement.

[3.4.101] Having placed the two feet of Prajñā upon his own heart, he is joined to the feet of Pravṛtti; or else, having joined his own two feet to the two feet of Prajñā, he is joined to the feet of Pravṛtti.
[3.4.102] An embrace preceded by the gesture of a garland is the "garland-gesture" (*sragdāmābhinaya*).
[3.4.103] From the touching of the breasts comes the "breast-gesture" (*kucābhinaya*).

[3.4.104] Wisdom (prajñā) licks the lotus (kamala), which is the means (upāya), and the means licks the vajra, which is wisdom. This should be understood as being in a relationship of lower and upper; this is the meaning of "the tasting of the two joined" (*lagnadvibhakṣaṇa*). The sense is "the tasting of the two joined. [3.4.105] Because of embracing with half the body, it is called "half-embrace" (*ardhāliṅgana*).

[3.4.106] From the touching of each other's secret parts with both hands—this is the meaning of "the two hands below touching the secret parts. This is also the meaning of the reading *ardha-dvau pāṇī guhyasparśanam*.
[3.4.107] Lifting the chin with the index and middle fingers is *cibutolanam*.
[3.4.108] Touching the limbs following from touching the body is *aṅgasparśanam*.
[3.4.109] "One should have a smiling face through *śṛṅgāra*" means that *śṛṅgāra* is the cause of the smiling face; the meaning is that the performance (*abhinaya*) is *śṛṅgāra-hasita*.

[3.4.110] Not only are these ten dramatic gestures (*abhinaya*) to be performed; rather, showing that the biting of the teeth and so forth are also to be performed, he says: "various," and so on. Concluding the rule regarding the wearing of the vajra and other implements, he says: "vajra," and so on. The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā, as previously described, must always be held by the yogin who is devoted to yoga.

[3.4.111] He says "devoid," etc., because there can be no accomplishment through wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) being devoid of one another. The "vajra-secret" is the means; "of the bell" refers to wisdom. What kind of fruit would there be for a means devoid of the bell? The implication is that there is no fruit at all. The implication is also that for a bell devoid of the means, the goal to be accomplished is as far away as possible.

[3.4.112] Having stated the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), he states the positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "Having taken hold of the vajra, the bell, and the mudrās, one goes to the further shore. The meaning is that accomplishment occurs only when wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are united. He provides an example, beginning with "on the night," and so forth. What is a night devoid of the moon like? It is like a lack of moonlight; the meaning is that it is incapable of accomplishing its own purpose or the purpose of others. What is a day for the moon like?

What would even the moon be like during the day, due to the absence of night? The meaning is that, being devoid of moonlight, it is incapable of accomplishing any purpose, whether for itself or for others.

[3.4.113] Concluding the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*), he says: "From that," and so forth. Just as the simultaneous occurrence of night and the moon is capable of serving both its own purpose and the purpose of others, so too the equality—the simultaneous occurrence—of the vajra and the bell is what is meant by "attainment" (*samāpatti*). "He makes the reality shine" (*tattvaṃ jyotih karoti*): "reality" (*tattva*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*); "he makes it shine" (*jyotih karoti*) means he endows it with light, that is, he illuminates it. And this essential nature is precisely the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*). Illumination is the means of realization (*sādhana*).

In some places, the reading is *sarvajyotsnayā*; in that case, the meaning is "by means of everything. Regarding the passage beginning with *ālī-kālī*: having first meditated on the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*) as the "city" (the body), the practitioner—the yogin—should accomplish all activities by means of the "great yoga" through the previously described sequence of the generation of emptiness, mantras, signs, and so forth; this is the connection. [3.4.114] He explains the meaning of *ālī* and *kālī*: the passage beginning with *ālī* is easy to understand.

[3.4.115] He says, "For the sake of sentient beings," and so forth, meaning that one should accomplish the entire welfare of sentient beings through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) in the form of the deity. He says, "Even nirvāṇa through the union of wisdom and skillful means," and so forth; for those who are outside of wisdom and skillful means, by what means could they cross over from *saṃsāra*? The sense is that apart from this very means which is the nature of wisdom and skillful means, there is no other means for crossing over from *saṃsāra*.

[3.4.116] He states that the *samaya*, which takes the form of a deity and so forth, is not to be spoken of as one pleases: "The *samaya* has been shown to the fool, whose mind is fixed on external objects. Since the *samaya* has been shown to the fool who is attached to external things, the *samaya* is not to be spoken of. What does it mean that "the *samaya* has been shown"? It is understood from the shaking of the head that it has "not been shown. The passage beginning with "guhya" is easy to understand.

[3.4.117] Regarding the passage beginning with "from whom the scripture," etc.: the meaning is that he who indeed desires to know the scripture—that very person is a yogin. "One should teach the dharmas to him whose mind is like pure crystal" means: one should teach the Dharma to him whose mind is as stainless as pure crystal.

[3.4.118] Why is this so? He says: "If," and so forth. If "mind" (*manas*) refers to doubt—the uncertainty as to whether "this is so" or "it is not"—then that is the meaning of the word *maṇavicikitsā*. If one should have doubt even regarding the words of the Blessed One, the Guru, then he falls into the Avīci hell and other such realms because of his rejection of the Guru’s scriptural teachings. Therefore, the intention is that only those possessing faith and wisdom, by virtue of having a mind like pure crystal, are qualified to hear this Dharma. He states "But not," and so forth, to show that the Dharma is not to be taught to one who is attached to sensual desires and the like.

[3.4.119] "Taking reality as the support" (*tattvam ālambya*): this means that reality is the limb of selflessness and emptiness. The intention is that this tantra should be taught to one who, having understood the method of the perfections (*pāramitānaya*), desires to act for the benefit of sentient beings. He states the enjoyment of sense objects for the yogin: "If," and so forth. If the yogin, being devoted to desire, wishes for the enjoyment of desire, then there is only a single means for him; this is the meaning of the phrase "the means has a single characteristic."

[3.4.120] He states the very means: "arising," and so forth. "Clear" refers to the sense objects (*viṣaya*). "Momentary" means they have reached their proper occasion. It should be understood specifically as "female sense objects. When there is the arising of sense objects—that is, when their attainment is established—if desire is enjoyed, then it is by means of the union of the bell and the vajra; the intended meaning is that one should enjoy through the union of the vajra and the lotus (*vajrapadmayoga*). To explain how that very union of the vajra and the lotus is accomplished, he says: "instantaneously manifested," and so forth. One should assume the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*), thinking, "I am the Vajradhara instantaneously perfected."

[3.4.121] By the passage beginning with "antardhā," it was reminded that the syllable *aṃ* is to be meditated upon in the mouth of the bird-faced goddess (*khagamukhā*). Regarding "the *hūṃ*-utterance of those who are momentarily united with the self": the momentary is the vajra; the meaning is that one should join the syllable *hūṃ* to the vajra of the self. Regarding "that which follows is to be recited": the recitation of both is thus reminded.

[3.4.122] All of this—beginning with wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*)—has been shown in the conclusion. It is the mental activity characterized by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Demonstrating that within that state the activities of body and speech dissolve, he says: "If," and so forth. Whatever activity there may be of body and speech, it goes to dissolution (*laya*) in the yoga of the deity. And this is the intended meaning (*bhāva*): if one is a practitioner of deity yoga who is devoted, uninterrupted, and long-term, why would such a person perform recitations of hymns, prostrations to *caityas*, and the like?

Demonstrating the greatness of the teaching, he says: "With palms joined," and so forth. Those yogas and yogins residing in all directions, such as Vajrapāṇi and others; and the "mistresses of yoga" (yogīśvarī), meaning the yoginīs and ḍākinīs—having heard [it], that is, having heard the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena)—they join their palms in reverence...

[3.4.123] It should be understood that they praise the Blessed One with hearts filled with joy and refreshment. He states the hymn of praise beginning with "Today" (*adya*), etc. By this very means taught by the Blessed One, one may go to liberation (*mokṣa*) right here in this very birth; by saying "the world" (*jagat*), he shows the absence of restriction regarding caste (*jāti*) and so forth. "Aho! expresses wonder. "The supreme path of Dharma": [this refers to the teaching].

Since this path is supreme, excellent, and the Dharma—and "Dharma" here means natural emptiness—this path is the Dharma because it has that very nature; therefore, there is wonder. To the question "How can it be such?", he says: "O, the cutter of cyclic existence! The sense is that it invariably cuts through cyclic existence.

[3.4.124] "O, the state of liberation!"—why is it the cutter of saṃsāra? Because it is the state (*pada*), that is, the means (*upāya*) to liberation. Therefore, one should apply oneself (*yuñjīta*) through yoga even for yogins and Buddhas. "In wonder" (*vismaye*) means with wonder. The path is the agent. He states the ease of attaining the path: "No lunar day," and so forth. The remainder is easily understood.

[3.4.125] He states the expansion of ritual activity (*karmaprasara*): "The arrangement of the wheel of ritual activity," and so forth. Due to the various dispositions of practitioners, the arrangement of the wheel of ritual activity will be explained. The "wheel of ritual activity" (*karmacakra*) is the expansion of ritual activity. "In the moon," and so forth. Having visualized Vetālī as thus distinguished... [3.4.126] ...one should recite "three hundred thousand times": that is, three hundred thousand.

[3.4.127] He states the mantra: "With double the number of syllables," and so forth; this is easy to understand. Although the syllable *kṣuṃ* is the seed-syllable of Ghorī, nevertheless, this mantra belongs to Vettālī and is joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and other elements. Regarding the phrase "one should accomplish the action of reality" (*tattvakarma sādhyetīti*): the intended meaning is that one should fully achieve the reality of the ritual action (*karmatattva*). [3.4.128] Regarding "on a corpse-cloth," and so forth: one should paint Siṃhinī on a cloth from a corpse, a cloth from a great warrior, or a cloth from a woman who has recently given birth. "Two-armed," and so forth, is easy to understand. [3.4.129–132] Regarding "in the middle of the earth," and so forth: this refers to the middle of a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). Having offered the aforementioned oblation to the Daityas, one should perform the ritual action.

[3.4.133] Having kindled either the fire of a corpse (*pretāgni*) or the fire of a *caṇḍāla* in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should perform the *homa*—this is the ellipsis. "Kindling with *devadāru*" refers to fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *devadāru*. "The five beginning with milk" refers to the five fuel-sticks produced from the milky trees, such as the *aśvattha* and others. [3.4.134] Having performed a grand worship and offering (*bali*) as prescribed, one should offer oblations with the meat as described. "Having mixed blood and honey": "honey" (*madhu*) here means great oil (*mahātaila*). Having smeared human flesh with blood and honey, one should offer it into the fire eight hundred times. [3.4.135] *Oṃ*, etc. ...
[3.4.136] ... the *homamantra*.

[3.4.137] "All [mantras] beginning with *yukta* are as before": the meaning is that the oblation (*hotavya*) is to be offered according to the previous sequence. [3.4.138] He states the cause: "first," and so forth.

[3.4.139] “With the fifth [mantra], there is the entry of the companion as a lion-form”: in the case of the *uttarasādhaka*, a lion-form is seen. The meaning is that he appears like a lion, due to the entry (*āveśa*) of the lioness.
[3.4.140] “Accept [it]; take your seat in the proper place”: when it is said, “May the Blessed Lady take her seat in her own place,” the meaning is that she should sit down upon the seat.

[3.4.141–142] When it is said, "O Goddess, perform the vision, setting aside the subsequent means of accomplishment," then that Blessed Lady says, "Child, what must I do?"—that is to say, "For what purpose have I been accomplished? The remainder is easy to understand.
[3.4.143] Having recited the mantra beginning with *oṃ*... [3.4.144] ...one should place the hand upon the head.

[3.4.145] “By means of the vehicle of the deceased” means by way of counter-clockwise rotation (*vāmāvarta*). The remainder is easily understood. [3.4.146–149] “But one should accomplish the tiger, the *śivī*, and the owl through its ritual action”: the meaning is that the accomplishment of the tiger and so forth is like that of the lioness. However, the mantra for the tiger is *oṃ hmyruṃ svāhā*. *Śivī* refers to the female jackal; her mantra is *oṃ ymyruṃ svāhā*. The mantra for the female owl is *oṃ kṣmryuṃ svāhā*.
[3.4.150] Showing that in all cases success comes through the union of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāyayoga*), he says: “And the vajra and bell,” etc.; this is easily understood.

In this chapter, the means for accomplishing the practice of the non-dual union of wisdom and method according to the sequence described above—including the purification of the enclosure wall and other elements, the generation of the forms of the deities of wisdom and method, the movement of the faces of the sky-goers (*khagama*), specific bindings, the benefits of meditation on songs, subjugation, medicinal rites, the expansion of ritual activities, and the accomplishment of *siṃghī* and so forth—are set forth; thus, it is a "section" (*prakaraṇa*), and it is the fourth. Therein, the Yoga-pīṭha is completed. Thus ends the Yoga-pīṭha in the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*.

[4.1.1] Now he speaks of the secret seat (*guhyapīṭha*): "Listen, O Vajra," and so forth. "O Vajra" means O Vajrapāṇi; the connection is: "listen to the characteristic of the one who delivers from *saṃsāra*. That by which one crosses over from *saṃsāra* is the "deliverer from *saṃsāra*" (*saṃsārottāra*), namely the Guru; his characteristic is his essential nature (*svarūpa*). To the question of how that is to be heard, he says: "according to the path" (*yathāmārgam*). A "path" (*mārga*) is that by which one seeks (*mṛgyate*), namely the scripture (*śāstra*). "According to the path" means not transgressing that [scripture]. "According to the path" thus has the sense of "by way of the path."

Vajrapāṇi spoke these words: "And I shall take up the master. The meaning is: "I shall take him up for the sake of training in the means of accomplishment; I shall know [them]. To the question "Of what kind is he?", he says: "One who knows the yoga of mantra, mudrā, and so forth. "Mantra" refers to mantras such as those for pacification (*śāntika*) and so on. "Yoga" refers to meditative absorption (*samādhi*). From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one understands the mandala and other such things. "Mudrā" refers to the mudrās of the body and so on. The body-mudrā is the hand-mudrā. The speech-mudrā is that which is performed by speech; the meaning is "the verbal secret signal" (*vākchommaka*).

The *cittamudrā* is that which is perceived through meditation as a specific configuration of color, arms, and so forth. When the *kāyamudrā* and other mudrās are meditated upon in this way, they are called *cittamudrā* because they reside within the mind. The sense [of the question] is: "The master should be one who is knowledgeable regarding mantras and the like; I now wish to hear his characteristics."

[4.1.2] "Blessed One, by what should he be seen? means: what kind of teacher should be seen? "What are his qualities? means: what are his qualities like? "How should the teacher be approached? means: how should the state of being a teacher be undertaken? "What is the perception of him as a guru? means: what kind of perception of him as a guru should be maintained?

[4.1.3] “Reality is the characteristic of all-enlightenment. The connection is: “Listen to reality. And since that refers to the Teacher (ācārya) who is the subject under discussion, it says: “the characteristic of all-enlightenment. A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that by which something is characterized; it is a designation (*saṃjñā*). Whatever is the name of that Teacher, that consists of all enlightenments characterized by omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*). Furthermore, the name is the name of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). The sense is that all enlightenments themselves are his name. Regarding the phrase “of the body of all Buddhas”:

The body of the Ācārya is composed of all Buddhas. All Buddhas are Mahāvajradhara. Regarding the phrase "abiding in the limbs that are the factors of enlightenment": the meaning is that the seven factors of enlightenment are his limbs.

[4.1.4] "The Arhats are his body hairs": the Arhats are the Buddhas, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, millions, and so forth; they are his body hairs. Regarding "the families" and so on: three, five, or six families constitute his crown. "The worldly male and female deities, Brahmā and others, are his footstool" refers to his feet. Regarding "the rays are the Guhyakas and so forth": "Guhyaka" here means Gandharvas. The rays from his body are the Yakṣas, Bhūtas, and Gandharvas.

[4.1.5] "Thus," and so forth: the body of the yogins, the teachers, possesses the aforementioned qualities. Anticipating the question, "Of what kind are these qualities? he says, "Of whom," and so forth. To the question, "Who is this teacher who consists of such qualities? he replies, "The application of whose characteristics must be stated. This means that for that wise teacher, the application of characteristics—the definition of the object of knowledge (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*)—is of the nature that will be described hereafter; his body is thus composed of such qualities. This is how it connects with what precedes.

[4.1.6] He states the definition: "disciplined" (*vinīta*), and so forth. "Disciplined" means one who has conquered the senses. "With peaceful attire" (*śāntaveśa*) means having abandoned worldly dress. Regarding "one who knows the application of mantra and tantra": *mantra* refers to mantras for pacification (*śāntika*) and so on; *tantra* refers to the ritual circles (*cakra*) for pacification and so on; their "application" (*prayoga*) consists of recitation (*japa*), drawing diagrams, and so forth; the teacher (*ācārya*) is one who knows these. Regarding "or yoga, arts, crafts, and so forth": *yoga* refers to the yoga of Vāyu and so on; *śilpa* refers to painting and so on; *kalā* refers to the science of medicine and so on; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), grammar and other sciences are included. The compound *yoga-śilpa-kalādi-vet* is analyzed as "one who breathes in (knows) yoga and so forth," thus it is without case endings (*nirvibhaktika*).

[4.1.7] "Sweetness" and so forth: the meaning is that one’s speech is pleasant toward sentient beings. "Like an only son to all sentient beings": the meaning is that one is endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*). "Generosity" and so forth: the meaning is that one is endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and the rest. "Yoga" is the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). "Meditation" (*dhyāna*) is the cultivation of the deity. [4.1.8] "Equanimity" and so forth: by means of equanimity, without distinction between enemy, friend, or neutral party, one has become a protector for sentient beings. "The ten principles" and so forth: the mandala, one’s own meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the mudrā, the ritual action (*karaṇa*), and the seat (*āsana*).
Recitation, fire-offerings, as well as worship, and the withdrawal of karma-yoga.

Thus is one who has fully understood the ten principles (*daśatattva*). These qualities, beginning with discipline (*vinaya*), are called *guṇas* because they are multiplied and practiced by those seeking the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Through association with these, one attains the status of an *ācārya* and receives the designation of a "guru," due to practicing the aforementioned qualities. As it is said: "Because of practicing correctly as prescribed—whether for others or for oneself—one is designated by the learned as a 'Guru' and by the term 'Ācārya'."

Thus [4.1.9]. With the words "by others" and so forth, he describes the action of the disciples. "Other" means different; and that is the action of the disciples. The connection is: "Listen. Regarding the phrase "the disparagement of the secrets of the teacher": the teacher himself is the secret Mahāvajradhara; the connection is that the disparager of his disparagement falls into Avīci. And it is said: "The Bodhicitta-vajra and the teacher are non-dual, without distinction."
Thus it is said. Furthermore:
"One should not create any distinction between the Guru and Vajradhara.

Again, as to what kind [of person], he says: "Yoginīs," and so forth. The Yoginīs are Jñānaḍākinī and the others. "Yoga-deities" refers to deities who have entered into union (samāpanna) through wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). The meaning is: of the Ācārya whose very nature is this.

[4.1.10] Regarding "the deity of the conduct of the pledge" (*samayācāradeva*): the pledge (*samaya*) is characterized by the five hooks (*pañcāṅkuśa*) and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). One who plays—that is, sports—by means of that conduct is the master (*ācārya*), the deity of the conduct of the pledge. Regarding "one who reviles the one joined to the secret offerings and so forth": he is a reviler of one who is engaged in the reality (*tattva*) of the bali-offerings, fire-oblations (*homa*), and so on. When does he fall? He says: "quickly. The meaning is: in this very life, immediately after death.

Alternatively, it should be explained that not only does one who reviles the Ācārya fall into Avīci, but so too does one who reviles the Yoginīs and others. Regarding the phrase "by transgressing the samaya in every case": the meaning is that even if one does not wish to do so, by being averse [to the practice] when the occasion for the samaya has arrived, one falls into Avīci.

[4.1.11] Showing that one falls into Avīci by such acts as trespassing upon the bed of the teacher, he says: "The bed," and so forth. That in which one sits is a *niṣadya*, meaning a seat. *Pādū* means a sandal. The sense is that by the act of trespassing upon the bed and other belongings of the teacher, one falls into Avīci. Regarding the phrase "one who enjoys the umbrella and clothing": the connection is that one who personally makes use of an umbrella or clothing being used by the teacher falls into Avīci. Regarding the phrase "of one who has transgressed the shadow":

"By stepping over the shadow of the guru" means by not touching his shadow, that is, by directing one's feet over it. "Of one who has transgressed": because of treading upon the guru’s shadow with one's feet. "And not saying 'no' as one would in ordinary speech": when engaged in conversation with the guru or when commanded by the guru to perform a task, if one says such words as "this should not be," "I will not do this," or "I am unable," he falls into Avīci; such is the connection [of the text]. This is stated because of the word "praśrabdha" (slackened/refractory). "This was taught by Bhadrakarmā and others regarding the feet."
Furthermore, by the words "What more? This is some kind of exclusion," etc., the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) must be indicated.

[4.1.12] Thus far has this fault been shown regarding the next world; now he asks what it is in this world, and says: "In those," and so forth. When those things—such as reviling the teacher and so on—are present as causes, there will be "seized" suffering. The sense is that one will experience pain, which is to say, suffering. He asks what that suffering is, and says: "From those," and so forth. From those transgressions against the guru and the like, there is a loss of wealth. "Fortune" (*śrī*) refers to the accumulation of merit and knowledge, or else to prosperity (*lakṣmī*). That would become distant. The rest is easy to understand.
[4.1.13] "Success in a dream" means even in a dream; this is because success follows from following the teacher.

[4.1.14–15] Regarding the passage beginning with "preceded by training" (*śikṣāpūrvakam*): the meaning is that the preceptor, possessing the previously mentioned qualities, should first provide the training in the ten wholesome actions and so forth, and then—preceded by the going for refuge to the Three Jewels and preceded by the entry into the maṇḍala—bestow the empowerment upon the disciple who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics. He states the crown empowerment (*makuṭābhiṣeka*): "the initial syllable," and so forth. The initial syllable is the syllable *hūṃ*. "Of one" refers to the syllable *aḥ*. The *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and *svāhākāra* (*svāhā*) are also to be understood. Thus, the mantra is *oṃ hūṃ aḥ svāhā*.
By means of this, one should bestow the crown empowerment consisting of the five Buddhas; such is the intended meaning.

[4.1.16] "Of that," and so forth: the meaning is that through the yoga of this crown-consecration (*makuṭābhiṣeka*), one's desired activity is accomplished. "Mantra-consecration," and so forth: at the beginning and end of the mantra-consecration and other rites, there is the placement of the eight syllables in the eight locations.

[4.1.17] Regarding "adaityābalī": the sense is that one should subsequently offer the *bali* oblation. "One should cause his consecration to be known according to the Dharma" indicates the consecration with the vajra and bell (*vajraghaṇṭābhiṣeka*). Regarding "yogena" and so forth: for one thus endowed with the consecrations, one should explain knowledge and the rest. Subsequently, after the name-consecration (*nāmābhiṣeka*), one should bestow the master-consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*). And "that which is all" refers to the embrace by her whose hands are joined with the vajra and vajra-bell; this is expressed by the word "all. Then, "guhya" refers to the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*). "Ādi" refers to the fourth consecration.

[4.1.18] He explains the sequence of consecration (*abhiṣeka-krama*): "At first, for the disciples," and so forth. Immediately after the completion of the mandala, the worship, and the offering of the bali, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple. This is as follows: having given to the disciple standing before him with palms joined at his heart water for cleansing the mouth—water over which the mantra *oṃ āḥ jihvā-saṃvartini hūṃ phaṭ* has been recited seven times—one should bestow the vow (*saṃvara*).

[4.1.19] To explain what kind of teacher should bestow the vow (*saṃvara*), he says: "The teacher," and so forth. Being a yogin of the deity seated upon the lion throne, having done what should he bestow the vow? He says: "In the hand," and so forth. Having touched the two hands of the disciple—which are placed at the heart with palms joined—with his own right hand, he should bestow the vow. [4.1.20] He states the vow: "The Buddha," and so forth... [4.1.21–23] ... up to the words "the great word for the performance of Dharma. He should cause the disciple to recite this entire passage.

[4.1.24] As to how many times [this should be said], he says: "He spoke twice and even thrice with a mind of equanimity. The meaning is that one should cause [the disciple] to recite three times through the purification of the equality of body and so forth. Following that, preceded by the teaching of profound dharmas such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is the entry into the maṇḍala; this is the procedure for the formal acceptance (*adhivāsanā*). Then, having performed twenty kinds of worship in the maṇḍala, having sounded the vajra-bell, having offered songs, and having offered praise, one should give the pledge (*samaya*).
Then, having stationed the disciple at the entrance of the maṇḍala with his eyes blindfolded and holding a handful of flowers, he should again bestow the vow (*saṃvara*).

Having caused him to recite the purification of the three bodies (*trikāya*) beginning with *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ* (25), and having established him through loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth by means of the mantra beginning with *punar virata krodhāhaṃkāra* (42a), he should cause the disciple to perform three prostrations with these three mantra-words beginning with *oṃ pañca* (39). Then, having uttered the mantra beginning with *samayas tvaṃ samaya hor* (44), he should perform the empowerment of the body and so forth (*kāyādyadhiṣṭhāna*) with this:

The syllable *A* is on the tongue (33ab); the syllable *I* is on the body (34ab); the syllable *HŪṂ* is at the heart (33cd). Then one should offer the five nectars (35–36ab). Afterwards, one should effect the descent [of the deity]. Then, with the mantra “Tiṣṭha vajra samaya pratipālaya hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ hoḥ hoḥ svāhā,” one should cause the flower to fall. Then, having uncovered the face with the mantra “Oṃ jñānacakṣuḥ hūṃ svāhā,” one should show the maṇḍala to the disciple.

Standing at the eastern gate with palms joined at the heart, the disciple should recite: "Oṃ, I have entered the great maṇḍala of the Vajra-maṇḍala; I am the one who beholds the great maṇḍala of the Yoga-maṇḍala; I am initiated into the great maṇḍala of the Guhya-maṇḍala; Samaya hoḥ.

Then the preceptor should perform the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalana*) upon him. Thereafter, the water and other consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) should be bestowed upon the disciple, who has assumed the divine pride (*devatāhaṃkāra*).

[4.1.28] With the words "kāya" and so forth, he speaks of the teaching of the Dharma. "This person does not protect the pledge"—this means that this person does not protect, nor is it necessary to protect, the pledge characterized by the restraint of body and so forth; rather, the meaning is that it *must* be protected. However, what is to be consumed is that which is characterized by the five hooks and the five nectars. Its status as a "pledge" (samaya) is due to its being inviolable. He says "samatā" and so forth to indicate that one should deliver a profound and vast teaching of the Dharma to one who is endowed with the equanimity of body and so forth.

[4.1.29] Showing that one should perform the binding of the disciple’s mouth for the purpose of entering the maṇḍala, he says: “With a cloth,” and so forth. “On the ground of offerings” means on the ground of the maṇḍala. “In the hands,” and so forth. *...†* “Then” means immediately after leading him near the door of the maṇḍala; the sense is that one should again give the vow (*saṃvara*). [4.1.30] Indicating the vow, he says: “All,” and so forth. Having caused [the disciple] to recite the previously mentioned text of the vow, he should cause him to recite “all,” and so forth. The “yoga-seat” is the maṇḍala.

[4.1.31] He says "he should explain the fourth in a secluded place" with the words beginning "the disciple, however," and so forth. "Having known" means having understood. Regarding "the lion at the head of the forest of ultimate reality": ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the knowledge of ultimate reality; that itself is the "forest" (*dava*), and he is the "head" (*ādi*) because he is the most excellent therein. He is a "lion" (*siṃha*) like a lion, because his nature is unassailable therein. One should connect the sentence as follows: "Having known the disciple who is devoted to the profundity of the nature of ultimate reality, he should explain to him the King of True Reality."

Furthermore, he describes what kind of disciple [is required]: "one possessed of yoga, for the purpose of cutting the silk-cloth. "Possessed of yoga" means one who delights in yoga. For what purpose? He says: "The silk-cloth" refers to the *paṭṭamoha*; [it is] for the purpose of cutting that.

[4.1.32] What kind of thing is that "King of the True Reality" (*sutattvarāja*)? He says: "May it destroy," and so forth. It is that reality which destroys affliction (*kleśa*). What kind of affliction? He says: "Existence," and so forth. Existence (*bhava*) refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*). That itself is "faultiness" (*doṣatā*). "Faultiness" means the state of suffering (*duḥkhatā*). Affliction is the ground from which that suffering arises—the ground of birth; it destroys that. What else might occur through the King of the True Reality? He says: "May it be accomplished," and so forth. Regarding "Yoga, the ultimate truth":

The meaning is that the yoga of the ultimate truth is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. The sense is that this very reality—just as you have understood it, and not otherwise—is what has been clarified by the words of the Guru; that alone is the "King of True Realities. [4.1.33] The passage beginning with "the letter A" and so forth is easy to understand. [4.1.34–35] The passage beginning with "five" and so forth refers to the offering of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
[4.1.36–38] Veneration is indicated by the words beginning with "of the guru.
[4.1.39–45] The arrangement of the limbs is indicated by the words beginning with "vajra. [4.1.46–48] Grammar is indicated by the words beginning with "anyā. The remainder is easily understood.

[4.1.49] He says, "One should give the instruction even at the conclusion of the consecration (*sekādi*) and so forth," beginning with the words *svabhāva* and so on. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are pure by nature (*svabhāva-śuddha*). And your own nature is the primordial essence (*prakṛti*). *Svabhāvakṛt*: it is called *svabhāvakṛt* because it thoroughly effects (*karoti*) or maintains (*bibharti*) the absence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-abhāva*) in the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth. In some versions, the reading is *svabhāvaṃ te 'bhāvataḥ*. The term *abhāvataḥ* is an ablative used with the elision of a verbal suffix (*lyablope pañcamī*). Having made emptiness (*śūnyatā*) one's own nature (*sātmīkṛtya*), your primordial essence would thus become that very absence.

Consequently, one who possesses the intrinsic nature of an existent being cannot demonstrate the sequence of awakening; for since there is an absence of awakening, that which is to be awakened, and the awakener among existents that lack intrinsic nature, what path to awakening could ultimately be demonstrated? This is the intended meaning.

Having established selflessness (*nairātmya*) in the mind, one should abandon what is unwholesome and accomplish what is wholesome; thus he says: "Patience," and so forth. For the Dharma has patience as its root. Therefore, one should not cause harm to sentient beings. The sense is that, conversely, impatience should be directed toward the afflictions (*kleśa*). Harshness is the provocation of others: speaking unpleasant words that expose their vital points is harsh speech. And that is coarse and cruel, because it produces suffering even in the next world.

Since that [distress] arises when there is distress, he says "eternal," etc., to show that one should not feel distressed. If there were such a thing as a harsh speech, it would be solely the fault of the self.

[4.1.51] He speaks of ethical discipline (*śīla*): "ethical discipline," etc. If there is a loss of ethical discipline, it is only due to the abandonment of faults such as those of one's own mind. The rest is easy to understand. [4.1.52] He speaks of abstaining from taking what belongs to others: "another's," etc. If there is the seizing of another’s property, then [in this context] it is the seizing of the property of the lotus of wisdom and the bodhicitta.

[4.1.53] He states the avoidance of falsehood: "falsehood," and so forth. "Heavy" refers to gems and the like; "subtle" refers to dust and the like. Even in that regard, falsehood must be avoided by the practitioner (*yogin*) in his actions. Why? He says: "yoga," and so forth. Yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the state of being concentrated. Those for whom such conduct is their practice are the practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*), the *yogins*; for them, falsehood is not seen. For falsehood is a lack of concentration, and *yogins* are eternally concentrated. If falsehood exists even among all phenomena... [4.1.54] He says "restraint," and so forth, because restraint everywhere is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

[4.1.55] He speaks of the propitiation of sentient beings (*sattvārādhana*), beginning with "sentient being" (*sattva*) and so forth. With the words "since" (*yataḥ*) and so forth, he expresses reassurance.
[4.1.56] The remainder is easily understood.

[4.1.57] He states precisely this point—that giving according to one's desire is contradictory—beginning with the words "giving" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of that which has grown into a sprout": of that seed characterized by giving, once sown, when it has grown—that is, when it has taken root—the "states" (gatis) that constitute its sprouts are the six realms of existence. They are called *rundhanti* because they obstruct; and "on the path" (*mārge*) means on the path to Buddhahood. By giving according to one's desire, enjoyments may arise even in the miserable states, according to the principle that "through giving, enjoyments may occur even in a miserable state."

Through attachment to enjoyments, the path to Buddhahood would be obstructed. Therefore, the sense is that the very destinies (gatis) act as sprouts of giving that block the path to Buddhahood. However, by means of that giving which is performed through the non-apprehension of the gift and so forth, Buddhahood is indeed attained.

[4.1.58] He says "kṛta" and so forth, elaborating on what was previously stated: through attachment to giving, the *ālayavijñāna* of afflictions, having obtained a body in heaven and so forth, performs (*karoti*) that which is desired, such as enjoyments. From enjoyment there arises attachment to pleasure and play; and from that, due to delusion and the subsequent absence of virtuous conduct, there will be a falling into an evil rebirth—this is the intended meaning.

[4.1.59] He states the prohibition against bowing to *caityas* and so forth for a yogi who is absorbed in meditation: "the *caitya*, etc. The phrase "one should not form hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*)" means that here only the *saṃpuṭa-yoga-mudrā* is to be performed; it does not mean that for one engaged in yoga, bowing to *caityas* and so forth is prohibited in any circumstance whatsoever. Even another yogi who is free from attachment should perform that [practice].

[4.1.60] For in all cases, constant practice is not easily obtained, whereas merely reading or hearing the scriptures is easy. Yet, the realization of the meaning does not come from mere reading or hearing alone. Thus he said:
I shall practice with my body alone; what would be the use of verbal recitation? What will happen to a sick person by the mere recitation of a medical treatise?

Thus he says: "The treatises (*śāstra*) are easy to obtain, but their practical application (*prayoga*) is difficult to find. The meaning is that the treatises are "easy to obtain" (*sulabha*), i.e., they are capable of being read and heard. The intention is: "Who is not a scholar (*paṇḍita*) when it comes to speaking? [That is, everyone can recite them. "Practical application" (*prayoga*) means practice—the performance of the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) understood immediately after reading and hearing. The sense is that while the treatise is easily accessible, its application is not possible [without further guidance]. And since that application must be demonstrated by a teacher who acts as one's own guide, he says:

"Of the teacher," and so forth. Having shown the path, the teacher himself should also demonstrate the practice of that path for the sake of the disciple’s performance; for this very reason he is "discerning. For no one ever engages in anything through mere words alone. Thus, in the case of arts and crafts, they demonstrate the actual action as well, and not merely the words. Alternatively: the teacher should show the path, but the practice must be performed by the disciple, according to the statement: "The task must be done by you yourselves; the Tathāgata is merely the instructor."

[4.1.61] Indicating that in practice one’s own mind alone is what should be practiced, he says: "The Self," and so forth. "Self" (ātman) refers to one's own body. That itself is the "deity" (deva). "The supreme deity": external objects such as cast images and the like are deities. Just as cast images and so forth are deities by virtue of being associated with an imputed deity, so too the self is a deity through the imputation of deity-status. Between these two, which brings about superior merit? He says: "The Self, the supreme deity."

Indeed, one's own body is already a deity even prior to its association with a specific color, arms, and so forth; however, due to delusion, there is no sense of "I-ness" toward it. If, in that regard, the deity itself is specifically superimposed [upon it], because of its excellence, it brings about excellent merit. The intended meaning is that the self alone should be practiced upon in the form of the deity. If this is so, why is there the making of images and the like? To this he says: "The self," and so forth.

For those who are unattached and not intent upon the deity within one's own body—the *ātma-bimba*—external objects such as reflected images or statues also bring about merit. Because there is no attachment, there is no contradiction between these two. Furthermore, external statues and the like produce only a small amount of merit;
therefore, merit is generated exactly in proportion to how one’s own mind is applied.

In the manner thus described, that treatise (*prakaraṇa*) in which the characteristics of the master, propitiation, initiation, and so forth are set forth is the Guhyapīṭha. Therein is the first chapter. Thus ends the first chapter in the Guhyapīṭha of the *Catuṣpīṭhanibandha*.

[4.2.1] To show the method for concise accomplishment, he speaks the second chapter, beginning with "Listen" and so forth. Regarding "O Vajraprabha": he is the lord or master of the *vajras*, that is, the *yakṣas*; his address is "Vajraprabha. "Practices" refers to ritual actions; the meaning is that in this scripture, they are difficult to find. The meaning is that the instruction on reality (*tattva*) is difficult to find. He asks: what is the fault in lacking the instruction on reality? He replies: "The practitioner of mantra wanders below, being one who lacks reality, revolving within cyclic existence (*bhava*)."

He who is a practitioner of mantra without reality moves below; the meaning is that he remains within saṃsāra itself. For this very reason it says: "the turning of existence. Below liberation is indeed saṃsāra.

[4.2.2] Having obtained the opportunity from the words of the Blessed One, Vajrapāṇi made this request, beginning with "Kautuka" and so forth: "O Blessed One, curiosity has arisen in me. Teach—*diśa*, meaning 'explain'—this reality (*tattva*) of the nature of the body. Regarding the phrase "What is the measure of the yoga? and so forth: what is the measure (*pramāṇa*) of yoga, that is, of meditative absorption (*samādhi*)? The meaning is: what is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? "What is mantra, mudrā, and so forth like? means: what is their intrinsic nature?

[4.2.3] What is the measurement of the body in relation to water and so forth? And what is the nature of the *balikarma* for yogins? By what means is the destination (*gati*) attained here? The sense is: by what method is which destination accomplished? Furthermore, what is the measurement and what is the defining characteristic of these destinations? Tell me—explain this.

[4.2.4] He states the Blessed One’s teaching: “Listen to reality as it is characterized, namely, the measure of the body and mind. The connection is: “Listen to reality, which is the measure of the body and mind. “As it is characterized” means as it is known; that is to say, as it is established. Regarding “impermanent,” and so forth: the elements (*dhātu*) of the self’s body—earth, water, fire, and air—all of these are impermanent. Regarding “the *bali* rite, etc.,” *bali* refers to both the ritual offering and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). “Recited” refers to the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra.

[4.2.5] “The mandala is fire”: this refers to the fire-oblation (*agnihoma*). “Of waters”: this refers to the water-oblation (*jalahoma*). “Seals” (*mudrā*): these are the hand-seals and so forth. “By those who worship with incense and the like”: this refers to external worship consisting of flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so on. The underlying thought is that all of this is impermanent. Regarding the phrase “for one who has attained the fruit,” etc.: the sense is that if a yogin proceeds by means of attachment to objects of perception and the like, he falls into the ocean of existence (*bhavārṇava*). Due to attachment to rites such as the *bali* offering, one would obtain only worldly fruits. Furthermore, the worldly fruit resulting from *bali* rites and the like would be a happiness that persists for only a short time.

[4.2.6] Showing that he asks again with the words "Having attained the state" (*gatim āsādya*) and so forth, he says: "Vajrapāṇi said," and so on. [4.2.7] "Volition" (*cetanā*) refers to the mind. What kind of measure (*pramāṇa*)—that is, what kind of essential nature (*svarūpa*)—is it to be seen as having? Regarding the phrase "if of that": the meaning is "that which is its measure. Where is that? He says: "Of the variously existing states of existence" (*pṛthagbhūtabhavādīnām*). This means in each separate state of existence: in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). And here, a doubt arises regarding the mind.

[4.2.8] He shows the words of the Blessed One beginning with "Listen" (*śṛṇu*). Listen to that which you ask regarding cyclic existence, such as the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth. Having done what? He says: "Having cleansed the mind through medical treatment. The connection is: having cleansed the mind through the medical treatment of ignorance, listen. The meaning is: having composed the mind. Regarding "at will, of the formless knowledge": consciousness (*vijñāna*) moves, or acts, within the formless (*ārūpa*); the meaning is that it arises there. How so? He says: "At will."

By the power of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), it arises according to one's own desire; thus, the meaning is "by the force of one's own desire. He asks, "What kind of consciousness is it? and says: "Moving through space" (*khaga*). It moves through space (*kha*); thus it is "space-moving. To what is it like? He says: "Like the wind" (*vāyūtīti*). It is like the wind. Alternatively, it may be construed as follows. When? He says: "When the parents emit the wind"—this is the meaning. Formless (*ārūpya*) refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyabhava*).

That consists of the gods of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

[4.2.9] "Form" refers to the material consciousness in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), which arises together with the karma and afflictions that produce it; the meaning is that it is established or produced. The realm of form consists of: the Brahmakāyikas, Brahmapurohitas, Mahābrahmans, Parīttābhas, Apramāṇābhas, Ābhāsvaras, Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, Śubhakṛtsnas, Anabhrakas, Puṇyaprasavas, Bṛhatphalas, Abṛhas, Atapas, Sudṛśas, Sudarśanas, and Akaniṣṭhas.

"Kāma" refers to the gods in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), humans and others are included. Only the gods and so forth are "possessors of desire" (*kāmin*). Consciousness arises within them. This is precisely what is said: "Desire, however, constantly seeks enjoyment. The meaning is that by the power of the karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) that produce it, there is desire; and by the power of that [desire], one experiences the fruit of karma therein. [4.2.10] These three states of existence (*bhava*) constitute *saṃsāra*; this is the meaning of the term "pertaining to *saṃsāra*" (*sāṃsārika*). Regarding "by humans": among humans and others, by the power of karma and afflictions, there is "one's own desire for the earth and so forth"; thus, through one's own desire, places and such are accomplished.

The realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) consists of the eight great hells—namely, those known as Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci—as well as animals, hungry ghosts, Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Uttarakuru, Aparagodānīya, the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. Regarding that [realm], "having removed the entities" means:
The sense is: "Listen briefly to that means by which one may rightly cross over from that saṃsāra. Regarding "Vajradhṛk," it refers to Vajrapāṇi.

"Having attained a state of existence" (*gatim āsādya*) means: having attained the latencies of karma (*karmavāsanā*) together with the auxiliary latencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), when the preceding consciousness has perished, another consciousness attains—that is, reaches—various states of existence (*gatau*). This is the meaning; that is to say, they cause it to arrive. Thus he says:
"The latency of karma, together with the latency of the twofold grasping..."
When the previous maturation has been exhausted, they produce another maturation.

Thus [it is said]. In that context, "the two types of grasping" refers to the grasping of the object (*grāhya-grāha*) and the grasping of the subject (*grāhaka-grāha*). By the term "maturation" (*vipāka*), the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is meant. This, first of all, is the general nature of consciousness. Regarding the fact that for yogins consciousness is luminous by nature (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), he says: "The consciousness of yogins arises simultaneously" (*sahajāyate*). "Simultaneous" (*sahaja*) is said to mean abiding in the nature (*prakṛtistha*).
